A number grid consisting of triangles from 1 to n, where each number is represented by a triangle with n's integer value, is first considered. This problem is transformed into a proof by showing that every k-sized triangle subset has a collateral k-sided transversal, where collateral transversals are non-disjoint k-sided transversals. Through a second transformation, this problem is linked to a generalization of a well-known lattice point problem concerning rectangular grids. This problem is resolved by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between k-sized triangle subsets and (k-1) sized rectangular grids of size (n-1) x (n-2). Utilizing this connection, a straightforward proof shows that every k-sized triangle subset has a k-sided transversal. In extension, this proof implies that there are (n^3 + 2n - 1)/4 triangular numbers up to the n cube root.

Graph Neural Networks are increasingly gaining popularity for handling complex, relationship-rich data. A major challenge with these networks lies in achieving optimal flexibility and modularity in model design. Current GNN frameworks fail to provide adequate support for this, making it difficult to efficiently modify models and achieve balanced exploration and generalization of numerous parameters. To address this limitation, we introduce Diffrn, a unique interpreter that helps with understanding and approximating the behavior of GNNs. By analyzing individual model components and their interactions, Diffrn identifies key relationships between input characteristics, network structure, and output interactions. Furthermore, it enables users to employ interpretation results to generate new, improved models with enhanced performance. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art interpretable graph classification approaches, achieving better accuracy on multiple benchmark datasets.

The X-ray emission of the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 was examined for substructure. After applying a temperature profile, no substructure was detected in the X-ray data. However, multiple radio sources within the cluster were surveyed, with one large source overlapping nearly entirely with the X-ray core. Despite being an unusual shape, this source does not indicate the presence of AGN activity and may be a star-forming driven source. A different radio source located near a prominent X-ray phase-separated filament showed signs of possibly driving the substructure in that area with an extended jet, though more data is needed for further analysis.

The Legendre Memory Unit, an advanced neural memory component, can be integrated into various neural architectures to enhance their performance and complexity management capabilities. The training of the Legendre Memory Unit relies on high-performance numerical linear algebra and transformation techniques. By leveraging the high processing capabilities of graphic processing units (GPUs), we have successfully developed and tested GPU-based implementations of these techniques using CUDA, achieving training speed-up rates of up to 60 times the original training time. Our experiments, involving the training of the LMU across three neural architectures on a range of GPU and CPU devices under various data sets and training iterations, demonstrate the substantial benefit of parallelization. Moreover, the use of parallel GPU processing enables the training of neural networks with large memory units, thereby expanding the practical applications of these architectures.

Over the past decade, theories involving feeble dark matter have been proposed, suggesting that dark matter particles do not necessarily need to possess significant speeds at the time of galaxy formation, which has long been assumed. Several types of feeble interactions with ordinary matter have been suggested, which are testable through experiments and observations. A wide range of theoretical ideas and models have been put forward, which often share certain characteristics, such as self-similarity and self-repulsion, self-singularity, and unity with dark energy. A wide array of particle candidates have been suggested, which vary depending on the characteristics and mechanisms of these theories. Decisive progress has been made in confronting these theories with observations and experiments. A turning point has been reached, in which both experimental limitations and theoretical predictions are becoming increasingly precise, leading to a critical moment for identifying the underlying nature of these theories. A deeper understanding of feeble interactions has been found within established particle theories, which undergo phase transitions under extreme conditions, resulting in temporary and potentially lasting separations between particles that interact via dark matter. A number of experiments and observations are ongoing, which are exploring the possibility that dark matter and dark energy are two distinct components of a single entity due to an underlying invariance under spatial translations.

Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply impacting how its members perceive and interact with the world around them. When exploring the origins of language, researchers frequently focus on the relationship between words and the things they represent, often using a model that mimics a naming game. This basic model, which involves associated memory pairs of language and its environment, typically consists of two interacting agents that use a naming game protocol. Studies have shown that this model can evolve into a steady state where language accurately represents its surroundings. However, real-world languages rarely ever achieve this level of perfection. Conversely, actual languages frequently contain a level of ambiguity and subjectivity that doesn't typically exist in the average naming game scenario. Additionally, population migration significantly impacts a society's linguistic diversity, which has been the primary area of study for many researchers. This paper introduces a naming game system where evolving agent populations migrate to a dynamic environment with increasingly complex connections. The results indicate that this system can reach a state in which language accurately represents its surroundings; yet, despite numerous iterations, the language will never be flawless, consistent, and complete. Instead, a natural tendency toward linguistic diversity and vocabulary growth will occur due to several underlying mechanisms, which are outlined in this study.

Momentum-based methods, widely used in traditional black-box optimization techniques, have been incorporated into neural network training through the NAD algorithm. This research, conducted on high-dimensional approximation of the Schrödinger equation using PINN with no latent variables, compared the NAD algorithm to Standard Adam using the same hyperparameters, and revealed a significant reduction in spectral bias with momentum. As momentum increases, the NAD algorithm demonstrates a decrease in spectral bias, while its generalization performance improves. Notably, non-momentum NAD and Adam methods showed equivalent results, yet struggled with severe spectral bias. This study showcases the efficacy of the NAD algorithm in efficiently training PINNs and mitigating spectral bias.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), with boundaries set by artificial damping conditions modeled as Neumann boundary controls in the Kelvin-Voigt type stiffness equation. The system has a Kelvin-Voigt type stiffness equation coupled with a dissipation term that varies spatially, with a unique coefficient within the dissipation term that goes to zero at specific points. The system's behavior is analyzed under the conditions that it reaches equilibrium around its natural oscillations. Using a temporal-galerkin scheme approach, we create a related optimality problem and use elements from the theory of operator cones to demonstrate the existence of a optimal control that ensures the system's behavior converges to its desired state.

Reinforcement learning faces a significant issue of data efficiency due to its high sample complexity. As a result, training agents using this method directly can be costly and impractical. The traditional approach involves hand-coding a system's logic and optimality criteria, which is also cumbersome and only effective for well-structured environments. The emergence of model-based RL frameworks provides a potential solution to this problem by leveraging the strengths of both data-driven and model-driven methods. The proposed HMRL framework aims to improve the performance of this model-based approach by introducing an rIRL module. The rIRL module stands for refined Integrated Reinforcement Learning using Inductive Logic Programming, a concept that has been previously explored in other contexts. The primary goal of this work is to refine the rIRL module to work within the proposed HMRL framework by utilizing abstract representations, utilizing resolution tactics to identify patterns, handling incomplete information, and addressing challenges associated with optimization. The effectiveness of the HMRL framework will be evaluated through experiments in complex simulated environments.

We investigated a specific type of nonlinear optical system referred to as an asymmetric microring resonator, an optical structure comprising two ring-shaped platforms with differing sizes coupled together. Our study, conducted using a quantum electrical field theoretical framework, demonstrated that an external field with a specific modulation pattern can trigger a phenomenon where the optical properties of the system become unidirectionally accessible, meaning they can be accessed from one side but not the other. Additionally, we observed that the optical nonlinearity within this system permits a specific type of entangled light interaction, often associated with 'quantum squeezing', which in turn enhances the precision of optical parameter measurement or data transmission by applying this'squeezed' light to the system.

This research paper investigates several minimax issues related to the sum of translates functions, an important concept in nonlinear functional analysis, originating from the study of nonlinear partial differential equations and their applications in optimization. Our approach involves developing theoretical properties for a sum of translates function with a monotone monotone-aspect component and a convex-aspect variable component. This enables us to create a minimax problem with specific properties and investigate its properties, as well as establish existence results for solutions. Our method of proving these results relies on the assignment of variational characteristics to the given function, as well as fixed point and monotone relation theories. Furthermore, we illustrate the significance of the obtained results with relevant examples.

Researchers have made four lianes, isotopes with odd spins, which have the most complicated lianes structures observed so far. By probing the unified force theory, scientists can examine the unique properties of these complicated lianes without being influenced by standard matter interactions by using shadow matter interactions. The search for dark matter has been expanded to explore novel shadow matter interactions. Our research team conducted the first experimental examination of spin-dependent shadow matter interactions by using the $^6$Li double beta decay as a detection tool. Through the analysis of the exclusion region maps, we explored the possible combinations of shadow couplings that could exist, taking into account both current LiNES data limits and proven LiNES coupling parameters. The study not only established new limits for the $^6$Li isotope but also set unique limits for the first time, effectively expanding our understanding of the lithium neutrino experiment.

This research presents a novel application of the Kernel Mixture Model (KMM) in the field of blind image restoration. The suitable prior model for the process's noise component, derived from KMM, is adapted and generalized for use in image restoration. The model's parameters are estimated efficiently using a practical approach, implemented within an iterative solution method for the restoration problem. The proposed method's effectiveness is successfully demonstrated in several scenarios, including the restoration of degraded images affected by impulse noise, poisson Gaussian noise, and mixed noise.

This paper introduces a new type of algebra called uniform and nonuniform multi-cohomology Lie Algebras, as well as their corresponding double constructions. These structures are linked to multi-Lie algebras and their double constructions via cohomological frameworks. Building on this, we develop the concepts of uniform and nonuniform multi-DG Lie algebras and double constructions. Varying the cohomology groups in multi-cohomology Lie Algebras and double constructions leads to novel equations, such as nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations and their reduced forms. Furthermore, we apply these constructions to standard Lie Algebras and use the derived structures to formulate exact mass spectra for diatonic anyons in a lattice regularization.

Formal verification has been the primary focus of this study, using the F# programming language and Hoare Logic as the theoretical basis. A custom-made F# library was created to automate the extraction of Hoare Logic from formal program descriptions, utilizing the Z3 SMT solver to validate implicit pre- and post-conditions. This process was facilitated by translating naturally expressed loop conditions and the loop body into a usable language, supported by the existing F# language framework. Although Hoare Logic is typically applied to pre-existing programs, our approach involves generating specifications from semi-formal descriptions, which are later used to verify the implemented programs, thus enabling a novel specification-oriented method of program validation. This innovative method is a rare example of Hoare Logic being used in practice, aiming to provide a more speculative approach towards a specification-oriented paradigm in program validation.

Distributed consensus is crucial for numerous distributed systems, such as distributed databases, blockchains, and peer-to-peer networks. The consensus mechanism ensures that all system members agree on a single state. Current solutions often fail to provide reliable consensus in the face of multiple failure scenarios or malicious interventions. To address this limitation, a new consensus algorithm called RCanopus is introduced. Building on Canopus, a fault-tolerant solution, RCanopus has been enhanced to not only tolerate eight possible failure scenarios but also withstand malicious interventions. The algorithm achieves fast consensus achievement with an approximate logarithmic time complexity, thereby minimizing network traffic and computational overhead. The effectiveness of RCanopus is demonstrated through comprehensive experimental testing, showcasing its high resistance to failures and malicious interventions while maintaining high performance.

Recent advancements in lipid bilayer simulations using all-atom spontaneous inflation have enabled researchers to measure properties like the shear modulus. Building on previous work, we investigated how to measure the flexural modulus of simulated lipid bilayers. First, we validated a previous approach using a force spectrum from a particular experiment and observed a high level of agreement. Next, we demonstrated that the shear modulus can be calculated using the equipartition theorem and verified that it aligns with the results from the force spectrum approach. Furthermore, we discovered that using the equipartition approach produces less statistical error. This study's methods for determining the shear modulus can be applied to other properties of lipid membranes, such as their compressional modulus, and may also be relevant to experiments with lipid nanocontainers like liposomes and nanotubes.

The loop quantum model's underlying principle is that physical quantities in a system are represented by simple operators in a complex vector space. Fundamental variables in this model govern the behavior of fundamental particles. The present study demonstrates that the_asm Hamiltonian of a star is equivalent to the Hamiltonian used in the loop quantum model. The study also shows that the ADM Hamiltonian's kinetic energy term is proportional to the Schwarzschild potential energy, and that quantum flux terms through a star's surface do not have counterparts in the loop quantum model. As a result, a star formed through the loop quantum model will not have an event horizon. The study further reveals that matter accumulating inside a star is condensed at its core and releases radiation within the electromagnetic spectrum. The radial distribution of this matter forms a determinate sequence. The study presents tables of data that show how matter accumulates inside a star, and its radial distribution forms a determinate sequence. The study does not provide a complete theoretical description of a star's structure. Theoretical descriptions of a star's thermodynamic properties and kinetic energy are missing from this model.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog listings include all the highest-energy cosmic rays, consisting of 45,378 particles, as well as 31,453 events influenced by the Earth's gravitational field. This comprehensive dataset includes extreme-energy events above 60 EeV recorded over a 20-year period of operation. This paper describes the observatory's functionality, data analysis methodologies used to examine the energy and direction of these cosmic rays, as well as the astrophysical background providing these data. No distinct source patterns have been discovered in the energy-dependent distribution of this cosmic radiation. Analysis of the energy and directional distributions of the recorded particles failed to uncover any correlation with nearby sources of ultra-high energy particles, including Centaurus A. However, the data do contain a very small number, five, of extremely high-energy particles, designated as "Eventials," each associated with distinct, fleeting, bright sources, the nature of which is unknown but does not appear to be related to any light-emission phenomena from the sources themselves that are known about so far.

Incorporating deep neural networks into automated systems requires reliable failure prediction to minimize severe consequences, as failures can breach confidentiality or trigger harmful actions. One crucial measure is estimating the detection uncertainty, especially for object detectors, though most current approaches are based on heuristic correlations and rely on inaccurate assumptions due to limited expertise in uncertainty quantification. To address this, this research presents BayesOD, a Bayesian method for object detectors that accurately quantifies uncertainty in object detection, Irrespective of the detector's design or training data. By incorporating Bayesian principles, BayesOD formulates the classification probability distribution using the mean and variance of the posterior, and derives the object detection probability distribution based on the proposal score and its variance. This is achieved without necessitating the propagation of variances through the entire network. Rather, the variances are optimized directly using a scalable approach. The results demonstrate that BayesOD outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches, offering superior uncertainty estimation capabilities. The source code of this research is publicly available at: ${https://github.com/Aler4g/BayesOD}$

When an image is divided into smaller sections called pixels, a pixel can represent a specific location and time. When a city's traffic is mapped, moving pixels create a snapshot of traffic at a particular moment. These pixels can predict basic city traffic patterns, such as seeing more cars during working hours. However, since these pixels rely solely on past data, they can only make basic predictions. Therefore, such systems have limitations in predicting more complex traffic patterns such as lunch-hour rushes or predicting events like road closures. To resolve this limitation, a new time-efective neural network called TE-ResNet was designed. This new architecture includes: 1) A new effective neural architecture called TE-ResNet that can model time-variant traffic patterns in urban settings more effectively. 2) A new method called Local Temporal Correlation (LTC) that aggregates and measures the local connectivity of scenes over a set of sequential images. 3) The integration of LTC and TE-ResNet, allowing end-to-end training, to improve accuracy in predicting traffic patterns. This new approach was tested using a publicly available traffic dataset from San Francisco, showing significant improvement in accuracy for medium to long-term traffic predictions. This method also outperformed existing predictive models with impressive results.

In categories without gray categories, units, and duals, a new approach is taken to incorporate gray categories. With these additions, unit, autonomy, and dual axioms for gray categories are formulated. It's proven that these new axioms establish a category's coherence when unit, autonomous, and dual conditions are met. Furthermore, the coherence axioms are found to be equivalent to the gray category axioms' consistency. Additionally, the study shows that the dual, unit, and autonomous gray category axioms remain unchanged for monoids, categories with endomorphisms, and 2-categories, but this is not the case for bicategories.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a crucial factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders and psychiatric illnesses. Current manual segmentation methods are complex, time-consuming, and prone to errors. Open-source MrResNet, a deep learning model, has been developed to perform automatic hippocampus segmentation. In this study, researchers evaluated the performance of several convolutional neural networks designed for MrResNet to identify hippocampal structures. Additionally, the impact of data from patients with epilepsy and those with Alzheimer’s disease was examined. Results showed that five of the six tested CNN models performed well in hippocampus segmentation tasks, with the JUPITER CNN reaching an accuracy of 0.848 for the hippocampus head and 0.792 for the hippocampus tail.

In a particular instance of the classic double-slit experiment, describing it using only first-order wave functions results in a specific phenomenon where one expects to see holes. However, when considering a slits arrangement with multiple transversal modes, describing this phenomenon becomes more complicated and requires an understanding of its phase relationships. Our analysis involves re-examining the phenomenon using an optical analogy based on a multi-stage interferometer. By doing so, we provide a specific estimate for the number of photons that would be absorbed by the observer, indicating that the phenomenon should be observable, and thus should not purely be considered as an out-of-phase emergence of the interference pattern. This particular instance of the phenomenon should be observable because it involves not just a specific form of amplitude, but rather a specific combination of amplitudes that can result in a null outcome. In order to see the phenomenon, one would need to integrate over a specific range of amplitudes that correspond to specific combinations, and it is this integration that allows one to see the phenomenon. One would not be able to see the phenomenon if one were to consider individual specific final outcomes because these amplitudes vary by a specific phase factor that results in variability and a specific relationship where one ends up with a specific result that varies by a specific phase. Our analysis indicates that the phase factor plays an important role in understanding this particular instance of the phenomenon and it's this phase factor that makes this particular instance of the phenomenon observable. Our research focuses on understanding the behavior of cosmic ray albedo neutrons decay (CRAND) particles at low Earth orbit levels. The Earth's magnetic field has a profound impact on these high-energy particles, causing them to be reflected and trapped within the Earth's vicinity. This study takes into account three key processes: neutral particle decay, inelastic scattering with the Earth's atmosphere and surface, and capture by the Earth's magnetic field, particularly for particles with charges. The paper presents findings on the distribution, trapped particle population, and longitudinal distribution using a Monte Carlo approach, with an emphasis on the Earth's shielded region. The analysis shows a significant increase in trapped particle counts at low orbit levels due to CRAND processes. To better appreciate the implications of CRAND particles, our research aims to provide a comprehensive computational framework that can be used for future applications requiring detailed orbital data.

A multi-layered graph neural network is presented, incorporating Pyramid-linked Graph Neural Network (PyLGNN), which incorporates a novel skeleton construction module and link rewriting modules. The link rewiring process creates homogeneous graph topologies through local interactions. The global skeleton construction module uses a hierarchical approach to identify node importance and reduce the graph through progressive aggregation. The built skeleton serves as a directed hierarchy graph. Integration of the node/edge rewards with a graph convolutional network and a Gated Graph Neural Network enables efficient graph scaling. The framework is applied to various tasks, including node classification, edge classification, and link prediction in networks. Testing on multiple network types validates the framework's superior performance compared to existing methods. An open-source library, PyLGNN, supports the implementation of the proposed framework. The framework's functionality is also demonstrated through online interactive visualization.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a differential privacy mechanism using the Huber method. This involves applying the Huber technique to noisy matrix completion, a concept introduced in a past study. Our research showcases the first application of the Huber method in matrix completion tasks, making it a robust solution when applied to differentially private low-rank matrix completion. Consequently, we derive the first epistemic uncertainty analysis for noisy matrix completion using the Huber technique. To demonstrate the efficacy of our method, we apply it to real-world image super-resolution tasks and provide uncertainty metrics for our generated images.

We propose a pioneering approach to describe interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust,' and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. The framework is based on a comprehensive dataset of grain sizes and compositions derived from high-resolution spectroscopic observations of distant galaxies. The model effectively replicates the patterns of gas-to-dust ratios, dust mass, and infrared polarization observed in the Milky Way and other nearby galaxies. Additionally, it generates an accurate match for the extinction and emission patterns produced by typical star-forming environments, and predictions for various types of asteroids and comets. The framework also reveals that a uniform astrodust material can produce the diverse mineral compositions typically associated with snowflake crystals. The model predicts that a typical galaxy will contain approximately 3.1 billion times more astrodust mass than PAHs, and that small galaxies tend to have more astrodust mass relative to PAHs than larger galaxies. The framework assumes that light absorption and scattering occur through a uniform system of particle arrays rather than through complex cloud structures. The model's framework provides a unified description of interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, known as 'astrodust,' and tiny particles, known as PAHs. The framework is based on a comprehensive dataset of grain sizes and compositions derived from high-resolution spectroscopic observations of distant galaxies. The specific mechanism by which planets form is still an unresolved puzzle that has garnered significant interest across the astronomical community. To gain a deeper understanding of planetary formation, scientists are turning their attention to exoplanets, especially those found around smaller, lower-mass stars. Studies of low-mass star systems, particularly those classified as M-dwarfs, are of particular interest due to the close proximity of many discovered planets to their respective parent stars. However, the disks of low-mass stars generally receive less observation time than those of larger, higher-mass stars. Thus, researchers are facing challenges in gathering the data needed to develop a comprehensive model of planetary formation. The present study seeks to close this knowledge gap through an in-depth examination of the disk around the low-mass star CIDA 1 (also known as CIDA 1 Stm), which is notable for its massive Jupiter-like planet, CIDA 1b. Utilizing data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), scientists were able to map the entire CIDA 1 disk in multiple molecular lines and develop detailed models to explain the observed data. The resulting model reveals a disk that is both tilted and warped relative to its equatorial plane, which cannot be fully explained by the action of a single mechanism. According to the researchers, the most plausible explanation is that CIDA 1b's gravitational influence is responsible for distorting the surrounding disk. With a planet of this size, scientists may

The Lights Out Problem is a well-known problem where the goal is to turn off all lights by giving a specified number of single tap commands. A comprehensive study found that the maximum number of taps required to solve the n-light version is O(n^1.5). In this paper, we prove that the exact maximum number of taps required is θ(n^2) and identify the underlying reason, which leads to a related question about how to determine the minimum number of taps needed for a given light configuration. By analyzing this question, we derive a recursive formula for solving the n-light version and validate that the maximum number of taps required is n-1 when solving from a specific starting configuration. Additionally, we present an approximation of our established lower bound with a logarithmic scale, which indicates that the original study's estimate of O(n^1.5) is indeed a tight one. Furthermore, we present an alternative tap estimation for any single tap-based change model by observing that the maximum number of taps required is n/sqrt(n) when solving from a specific starting configuration.

This paper introduces a novel, locally coupled model for image segmentation that leverages a previously developed optimization technique. The technique was initially used separately for image recovery and segmentation tasks, but we have observed that the resulting segmentation results from the breakthrough paper 'Achieving TV Morphonics via Bregman Iteration' are often accurately aligned with the input image's contours, indicating that the technique exhibits a high degree of consistency. Consequently, we are applying this technique in a new combined model to achieve more precise segmentation results, especially in cases where the contours conform to the image's details. The technique is capable of producing satisfactory results for a range of simulations, but it is worth noting that the evidence suggesting its effectiveness on real-world image segmentation tasks is currently limited to a few simple simulations.

We propose InferIO, a general abstraction algorithm utilizing an iterative and incremental approach via fixpoint monitoring, applicable to sound and imprecise abstract interpreters employing Galois connections. By continuously analyzing an iteration's impact, InferIO identifies when an iteration's initial and final outcomes can be distinguished, effectively allowing the termination condition to be reevaluated mid-process. Such overlap detection enables the early termination of unnecessary iterations, particularly beneficial in simulating infinite abstract relations. For instance, on standard hardware from 2005-2015, InferIO's performance boost ranges from 1.5 to 2.7 times compared to monitoring alone, with potential extensions like distributed computing and/or heap-based analysis predicted to amplify this advantage significantly.

We investigate theoretical perovskite oxide properties, which are highly
relevant to both sustainable energy generation and spintronics due to their
excellent optoelectronic characteristics. We utilize a tight-binding model, combined
with nonlinear sigma model theory and Bethe-Salpeter equation calculations, to
analyze the interactions of light with electrons, crystal lattice vibrations, and
spin movements in perovskite crystals. Specifically, we demonstrate that light
can induce topological crystal lattice vibrations, control their behavior, create
new topological states, control spin movements, and increase the lifetime of
excitons within these crystals. These unique light interactions may significantly
enhance the performance and versatility of perovskite-based optoelectronic devices.

Identifying unusual data points within a metric space is crucial for several key applications such as reporting anomalies, preprocessing data, and visualization. While many methods exist for doing so, they often fail to deliver rapid and precise results on large datasets. To address this, we present an efficient algorithm that calculates an exact outcome in metric spaces subject to specific constraints. Our approach produces an exact output in superstar graph, a specific type of proximity graph, and further enables more precise outcomes in more complex graph structures by adjusting the connection distance threshold. Experimental results demonstrating the algorithm's performance over real and simulated datasets are also presented.

Our research demonstrates that as a oscillating atomic cloud approaches a mirror, it continuously emits and receives radiation, stimulating itself and the mirror it's approaching, resulting in a photocurrent being generated. This phenomenon allows us to measure extremely low atomic motion speeds due to the overpowered mirror, enabling us to evaluate an integral that describes radiation emission efficiency. This method could be applied to various fields such as enhanced atomic absorption and nonlinear optical techniques, providing novel approaches to atomic momentum measurement.

Graph convolutional neural networks (GCNs) have been widely used in graph classification and representation learning. However, current GCN models are often designed to prioritize global information retention over making local connections reasonable. This leads to issues such as fair representation and potential bias. To address these concerns, we propose a new framework that prioritizes fairness at a local community level by adjusting the GCN's convolutional operator to incorporate fairness constraints. This approach will allow for the implementation of various fairness algorithms within the framework and assess the performance of different GCN parameters and transition matrices. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets (including CORA, CITeseer, and AID) demonstrate that our framework achieves substantial improvements in both node classification and graph representation tasks while ensuring fairness.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. The first approach establishes a polynomial function based on existing solutions and integrates it with the reversible Michaelis-Menten equation. The second method uses the Adomian decomposition method, which expands the nonlinearity of the Michaelis-Menten equation. The approximate solutions derived from these methods demonstrate a high degree of accuracy for both static and dynamic conditions. The validity of these solutions is supported by linear and nonlinear stability analysis, which shows excellent agreement between the approximate and exact solutions.

Theoretical models predicting supersymmetry have been tested against data gathered from proton-proton collisions between 2016 and 2018 at a 13 TeV energy level, utilizing the CMS detector at CERN. Supersymmetry scenarios involving simplified events with five or seven energy particles and significant momentum loss were examined in a single analysis. A specific edge energy threshold of 250 GeV was established for simplified spring-like scenarios. Another variation involving the division of supersymmetry theories was also analyzed, focusing on the decay of the smallest particle in a set of particles with low mass, resulting in the emergence of additional light particles with unknown mass near zero. A separate search for this specific scenario was conducted separately because it encompasses a range of supersymmetry models. Data showed that certain supersymmetry models with high energy ranges and specific particle combinations fail to match predicted models. Statistical analysis of these discrepancies yielded the exclusion of certain supersymmetry models at varying confidence levels, including certain simplified scenarios involving spring-like models and certain simplified scenarios involving gluino decays, specifically for particles with masses near the energy threshold in a set of simplified scenarios involving spring-like models. A certain division of supersymmetry models involving the decay of the smallest particle in a set of particles with low mass near the energy threshold was also excluded with certain divisions excluded at varying confidence levels.

We've developed a one-parameter model representing economists' various perspectives on financial bubbles. These perspectives can be categorized as extreme, moderate, or moderate-with-caution. Our model aligns with all three viewpoints and undergoes distinct unit root tests, which indicates that various expectations regarding financial bubbles lead to different diagnostic tests identifying them. Additionally, our analysis suggests that a widely-accepted bubble detection approach based on the Maximum Likelihood Estimator is unreliable due to consistently testing for a unit root in a stable financial system. To rectify this issue, we modified the estimator to account for data ending points, which effectively allowed us to accurately determine the bubble origins after a series of simulated tests.

This paper introduces a novel method for calculating the driven quantum harmonic oscillator's eigenvalues and trajectories using path integral techniques. Our approach, grounded in the Hamiltonian path integral formulation, maps the oscillator's time-dependent Schrödinger equation into a discrete time problem that can be efficiently simulated with Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. To test its effectiveness, we utilized the HMC algorithm for a specific case and observed consistent results when adjusting the displacement term's strength. Our findings are in alignment with existing research. Moreover, we investigated the influence of the driving force on the oscillator's spectrum by calculating eigenvalue ratios, and our results are in accordance with prior studies.

The review data for recommending products or services is typically comprised of concise, subjective statements provided by users with specific intentions, either to provide feedback or make inquiries. Existing approaches to interactive recommendation rely heavily on implicit user feedback, often expressed through clicks or purchases. In contrast, this work focuses on explicit user feedback expressed through natural language, found predominantly in the reviews written by users. Our model, called the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network, is designed to leverage the contextual information within these reviews by identifying sentiment patterns using hierarchical attention and matching the query's implicit intent using multi-head attention. The proposed network effectively merges review features with item attributes, and together they form the basis of a context-aware recommendation system that produces enhanced interactive embeddings. These embeddings, in turn, result in more accurate probability estimates of user engagement with items. Our model's efficacy was tested across five real-world datasets and outperformed several state-of-the-art methods, highlighting its potential in natural language-based recommendation tasks.

A crucial challenge in Natural Language Processing for CS datasets lies in creating diverse and extensive data to improve domain word translation performance across languages. Our investigation focuses on exploring data augmentation by replacing words with alternative choices from the same language to enhance CS data. Initially, we evaluated straight replacements by swapping CS words with monomorphous lexicals. Building on this, we developed'structured' data augmentation by replacing CS words with monomorphous lexicals that maintain the original word's suffixes. Additionally, we 'combined' both approaches to create new augmented examples. Our results showed that combining all three techniques yields the most effective CS data augmentation method. Surprisingly, a straightforward approach that only swaps words was also highly competitive, requiring minimal processing.

We demonstrate the freedom (in terms of choice) of collections of 2-dimensional surface homeomorphisms with highly irregular, disconnected topologies, and the impossibility of finding a unifying, compact structure that incorporates all such collections.

A specific class of membranes in a higher-dimensional spacetime with certain symmetries can be easily solved using the Guadagnini-Parambone method, if the impact of extra spherical surfaces on the membrane's motion is known in advance. This method works by first finding a membrane that behaves ideally without the influence of these extra surfaces. The studies reveal that these membranes maintain their intrinsic properties when the spacetime's conditions change, and a significant result is that their actions remain unchanged under specific transformations. The membrane's motion is also simplified into a set of equations governing ideal particles on the D-brane. This simplification reveals that the membranes' modes of vibration remain unchanged under certain transformations and a separate set of equations governs ideal membranes.

The measurement and representation of complex 3D surfaces utilize Hex meshes, 
which consist of a series of basic tetrahedral elements arranged in a honeycomb structure. 
An essential aspect of such an implementation is the accurate identification of existing mesh features. 
In this research, a novel mesh feature detection method is presented, which can identify up to 58 distinct hexahedral features within the 3D surface representation. 
This detection method is well-suited for processing meshes with varying levels of feature complexity. 
Additionally, a corresponding demonstration application has been developed to illustrate the functionality of the proposed feature detection approach.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share key concepts such as graph nodes and relations, making it feasible to utilize link prediction as a means of enhancing relation extraction. This can involve utilizing link prediction to create novel training instances, augmenting existing ones, or developing more effective extraction models by integrating link prediction into the extraction pipeline. This paper explores these possibilities, which have not been extensively investigated in the relation extraction literature. Our experiments using two datasets reveal that creating new training instances through link prediction yields improvements in extraction performance, while employing link prediction models directly does not result in comparable enhancements. Nevertheless, combining link prediction and extraction models leads to more consistent and accurate extraction results. This finding suggests that the benefits of leveraging link prediction to support relation extraction depend on the specific implementation and that further research is required to fully integrate these two concepts.

This study develops a pioneering, compact, and efficient model for power electronic inverters using a analytical approach based on look-up table (Look-Up-Table) models. Inverter models utilizing analytical formulas typically involve simpler computational units but often compromise on precision. In contrast, conventional Look-Up-Table models, which provide high accuracy, can necessitate more complex and slower digital signal processing units due to a larger number of input/output data points. The proposed model leverages analytical formulas for maximum efficiency and incorporates key performance-critical points from the conventional Look-Up-Table model to ensure high predictive accuracy. The model uses the least squares method with various weights and constraints to optimize specific performance metrics such as voltage, current, and d-q arm currents. The optimization strategy is inspired by the most frequently occurring operating modes of the inverter and uses a large penalty factor to ensure fast convergence. The study includes various experimental validation examples using real data from different systems. Furthermore, a practical consideration by the authors of this paper led to the development of a convenient user interface for generating the model, which is compatible with Matlab 98 and later versions.

Continuity has emerged as a key concept in reinforcement learning that facilitates the establishment of well-defined objectives and the improvement of decision-making procedures. However, the analysis of continuity in the context of reinforcement learning has generally been restricted to Markov decision processes. This work aims to extend the scope of continuity analysis to more comprehensive settings, including a broad class of stochastic dynamic systems known as metric random processes. Within these settings, our research defines a new type of continuity that is rooted in the concept of epistemic constraint and is relevant to the context. This novel continuity framework has been applied to a variety of fundamental reinforcement learning problems, including the characterization of epistemic constraints in Markov dynamic models and the development of optimal policies for metric-space settings. Additionally, our research demonstrates the practical relevance of our findings by showing their connection to existing epistemic constraint methods in reinforcement learning.

The underlying organizational principle of the human ventral temporal cortex is still largely unclear when it comes to categorizing objects. Although prior research suggested that object categorization relies heavily on a biologically-inspired dimension such as partivity (the proportion of parts that move relative to each other), it has been largely overlooked in recent neuroscientific studies. To investigate this concept further, researchers created a set of neurophysiological and behavioral experiments that focus specifically on the proportion of parts that move relative to each other and how that affects how we understand objects. The results of these experiments reveal distinct neural responses in the anterolateral STS and MT complexes' interaction, specifically in areas V5, MST, and LIP. Moreover, the data suggest that a high proportion of parts moving relative to each other serves as a indicator of complex biological motion.

In complex multivariate systems like finite element simulations, reducing dimensionality helps filter out irrelevant data, this paper shows how to do so by expanding a previously developed one-dimensional filter designed for shock capturing in hyperbolic conservation laws by Veenman et al. in JCP 2016. The proposed convex optimization-based filter maintains key solution features like steady-state exactness, monotonicity, and the conservation of nonnegative quantities, even in the presence of nonlinear governing equations. It achieves this through the application of a multidimensional generalized polynomial chaos approximation and a convex optimization algorithm for optimal projection. The approach is tested on two multidimensional test problems: a Burgers equation with a 2D smoothing effect and a 2D system of shallow water equations with multiple moving targets. Our results confirm the efficacy of the proposed filter in reducing dimensionality and preserving essential system characteristics.

Quasi-periodic fluctuations (QPFs) have been observed and analyzed from the 1.6 meV to 19.5 keV energy range in data captured by the Insight-HXMT for the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571. Its findings reveal the QPFs experienced an evolution over time, changing from type I-like to type II-like with a 1.3 s period and frequency-chirp from 0.2 to 0.83 Hz. Insights from this research on the QPFs suggest they are associated with a specific radial range within an accretion disk fraction, indicating that disk geometry and possible boundary effects may influence the evolution of a corona. Analyzing the QPFs' frequency based on a seed photon model and involving a specific spectral state, the study identifies a correlation between this frequency and the energy, which aligns with a specific radius, approximately 15 Schwarzschild radii. Its findings support the concept of a boundary-driven mechanism in the evolution of a corona.

In the field of multi-agent reinforcement learning, our approach utilizes the concept of transfer empowerment to assess and promote interaction efficiency between agents. This method evaluates an agent's behavior based on its ability to respond effectively to partner actions. However, existing empirical studies of transfer empowerment in interaction scenarios are scarce. To address this gap, we propose a simulation environment where two agents, each having different reward structures, interact and develop strategies to respond to each other's actions. The agent with a more compact action space is more reliant on its partner's actions, creating a cooperative scenario ideal for testing transfer empowerment. Our simulation experiment examines the development of various action-reaction patterns between these agents as they interact and find solutions to their joint reward structure.

Our proposed approach enables real-time material identification in any environment using anywhere, anytime imagery. To address this challenge, we leverage contrastive learning, effectively teaching a computer to distinguish between a given material and all other materials. By simulating a range of material views, we expand the scope of material observation beyond direct vision, allowing for one-shot learning of diverse material views. Additionally, we showcase a novel material editing method that allows for seamless transitions between materials. This methodology facilitates real-world applications such as augmented reality-based retail applications, supporting consumers with product color matching and other advisory services. We evaluate our approach in both controlled environments and real-world settings, demonstrating its efficacy through comprehensive experiments.

Two equivalent formulations of formal three-dimensional formal smooth manifolds are associated with the concept of Lie 2-algebras. As a result, Lie 2-algebras serve as an extension of Lie algebras, providing a way to describe the algebraic structure of three-dimensional polyforms in a geometrically meaningful way. This paper explores the different types of Lie 2-algebras that exist, with a focus on Malgrange's generic example and the superisation of these algebras. The circle 3-algebra and the M2-algebra are examined as specific examples of Lie 3-algebras that can be used to describe two different types of non-abelian formal groups. The importance of coHessians in Lie 2-algebras and formal group theories is also discussed.

We introduce a groundbreaking approach to visual local feature matching using a transformer architecture that bypasses the need for a detector. Our method, LoFTR, directly identifies corresponding points within two images without depending on pre-existing training data or covariance descriptors. When applied to the KITTI Odometry dataset, LoFTR demonstrates exceptional accuracy with a 85% success rate at a 1cm/rt threshold, outperforming state-of-the-art detectors in both point similarity and overall performance. Upon the Visual Odometry Benchmark, LoFTR displays superior performance with a 61.7% success rate at a 2cm/rt threshold, significantly surpassing the best-known results from detector-based methods.

The establishment of a data hub, filled with thousands of siphoned magnetic field data sets, is aimed at accelerating solar activity research. A significant fraction of these magnetic field data sets were derived from Stokes Inversions Using Molecular Lines, a technique prone to generating biased solutions. Investigating the bias in these derived magnetic field data, a statistical analysis of several source channels was conducted to determine the influence of noise and finite sampling on derived magnetic field data. Results indicate significant bias for some channels and that a revision of the MI^3 is necessary to correct for this bias. Furthermore, through simulation, it was found that the revised MI^3 can effectively reduce and eliminate derived magnetic field data bias. Consequently, the revised MI^3 was applied to a dataset of SSRT-derived magnetic field data to generate bias-free magnetic field data. A deep learning model was then used to generate magnetic field maps from the bias-free magnetic field data. The model's performance improved after reweighting the bias-free magnetic field data to account for observational gaps, resulting in a 20% increase in its correlation with reference data and a 50% decrease in its standard deviation deviation from reference data.

This research paper presents a novel framework for demand side management in smart grids by incorporating existing techniques such as direct load control, instant load billing, and energy consumption scheduling. An aggregative game is employed to model how consumers react to these controls and incentives, and the Ward method is used to demonstrate the equilibrium solution's uniqueness and efficiency. Furthermore, an iterative computation algorithm is offered to obtain the equilibrium solution, which is characterized by a decentralized and efficient price determined through a variational inequality, and an analytical solution is derived for the linear case. Through a simulation, the framework's effectiveness in reducing peak demand and securing benefits for consumers and the grid operator is demonstrated.

We investigate black string behavior within a framework that incorporates Rastall theory, considering how gravity's divergence influences the Hawking radiation temperature. By analyzing a nonrotating, charged black string within Rastall theory, we derive a relationship between the horizon and energy, and subsequently, a general expression for the Hawking radiation temperature. Our results indicate that the temperature is sensitive to both the horizon's gravitational potential and spin-gravity coupling parameters. Furthermore, in the context of general relativity and Einstein theory, we observe that the inclusion of gravitational divergence by Rastall theory leads to cooler Hawking radiation compared to the predictions of Einstein theory.

The convergence rate of the Ergodic Theorem for $l_1$-skew product transformations can be evaluated in terms of the lags of the spectral measure's point values. Specifically, if a spectral measure has no mass at zero, the convergence rate is directly proportional to the smallest positive lag at which the spectral measure's point values change. This conclusion not only applies to ergodic measures but also to measures with zero measure support for all lags. The same analysis can be applied to the average uniform ergodicity property, leading to a characterization based on the lags of the spectral measure's point values.

The data released by Gaia, specifically the photometric information from BP and RP spectrometers, can be used to identify metal-poor stars in a certain range. A method has been developed that accurately determines the iron content in the spectrum of G-type stars with a margin of error lower than 0.3 dex. This technique also increases the detection rate of metal-poor stars, particularly those that are very poor and early-type subgiants, compared to previous studies using Gaia data. Furthermore, it can identify metal-poor stars that are candidate horizontal branch stars or giants with a high degree of accuracy, which will greatly aid in the selection of candidates for asteroseismology and further physical research regarding these stars.

The USA Wildfire Blaze Database is a extensive collection of 15 years' worth
of data, containing 22000 fires that took place in 11 states with the highest
occurrence of wildfires. Analyzing these fires involves looking at both their
global pattern - such as simultaneous blazes - and local pattern - such as
clustered fires. Research initially focuses on identifying the most severe
blaze seasons by analyzing both daily and monthly fire data. With the ability to
predict the severity of upcoming blaze seasons using established metrics, it
becomes possible to create an early warning system for blaze severity. Furthermore,
the precision of these severity metrics can be optimized through the use of
different weighting and prioritization methods.

We've conducted a thorough examination of five distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures are applied to a collection of 94 languages, with each language represented by both its standard dictionary form corpus and a corpus enriched with inflected variants. We compare the relationships between these complexity metrics across the two corporuses, with the dictionary-based approach considered the standard. We also assess their reliability in quantifying morphological complexity and control for factors such as language family, writing system, and syntactic characteristics. Notably, most complexity measures are highly correlated with a standardized indicator of morphological complexity, regardless of whether the corpus includes inflected forms. This suggests that these measures primarily assess a language's use of inflection rather than other aspects of morphological complexity. Consequently, some complexity metrics may be adjusted to also incorporate inflection, while others should be refined to better capture the full range of morphological complexity.

Researchers at Harvard University made a groundbreaking discovery when they identified a small galaxy that acts as a gravitational lens, bending and magnifying the light from a distant galaxy within the IRAS F02152+1093 cluster. To better understand the universe, scientists used data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, the Atacama Cosmology Project, the Spitzer Space Telescope, the Atacama Star-Forming Regions Survey South, and the Atacama Cosmology Project to study the universe. By analyzing a gravitationally lensed galaxy, they found that the early universe experienced rapid star formation. Additionally, a simulation revealed that the gravitational lens affects the detection of infrared light from the background galaxy, which may change future strong gravitational lens findings in the weak lens regime. The discovery of a gravitationally lensed galaxy in the universe could provide significant insights into the mass of the universe. By applying a mass model to the universe, scientists found that the mass of the universe is composed of 0.26 solar masses of matter, 0.73 solar masses of dark matter, and 0.01 solar masses of baryonic matter. However, if self-interacting dark matter characterizes the universe, the mass of the universe is solely comprised of dark matter. By analyzing different cases, scientists found that if self-interacting dark matter is correctly identified, the mass of the universe is entirely comprised of dark matter. We've developed a new method for significantly reducing complex statistical models based on limited information about their properties. This approach is particularly useful when analyzing large data sets, as it enables us to narrow down vast model spaces to more manageable ones with much faster processing times. By initially selecting specific model components and a sub-set of model parameters to focus on, this method allows for (1) initial reduction of the extensive model space, and (2) targeted refinement of the simplified model using additional information. This innovative method, which we demonstrate to be effective through experiments, overcomes a critical limitation of existing model simplification techniques, allowing for the focus to shift from one part of the model to another based on new insights at different stages of the process.

Autonomous component analysis, a type of spectral decomposition, is a widely applied method that has been used in multiple domains since its introduction in 2007. The AC technique is particularly versatile, enabling the modeling of complex phenomena and yielding positive results in various contexts. Given its numerous applications across diverse fields, the validity of its results often raises questions in different areas of study. To address these concerns, we present an enhanced version of the AC algorithm, incorporating modifications from the m-ar-K test to improve stability and ensure a more comprehensive, accurate, and tractable component structure.

When severe weather hits, the abundance of social media data creates a daunting challenge for officials tasked with dissecting and processing it to inform critical decisions, but due to its high velocity and unpredictability, accurately identifying key incidents from a flood of posts is essential. To help officials navigate this hurdle, researchers developed RT, a real-time system designed to detect spatio-temporally significant social media incidents. By utilizing a combination of geometrical analysis and temporal evaluation, RT identifies events as they unfold and provides a conceptual framework for grounding, evaluating, and improving incident detection methods. To build RT, researchers first categorized 50,000 German tweets into 12 severe weather types, then trained an RNN within a recurrent attention network to generate situational features for each tweet. With geotagged data, RT identifies areas where tweets converge, and temporal features are derived from the distribution of timestamps. To test RT, researchers simulated three real-time scenarios: detecting tweets related to two storm systems and a flood, all occurring in 2014. RT accurately predicted 10 out of 15 possible incidents 15 minutes in advance, but performed better when considering a 30-minute prediction window. When evaluating RT using the F1-measure for each weather type, official reports showed 85% concordance with respect to location but only 57% with respect to time, due in part to the subjective nature of labeling.
