Recent advancements in computer vision research have led to the creation of powerful self-supervised image patch representation models. These models, however, face significant challenges when applied to modalities outside of photography such as microscopy, due to varying lighting conditions and the presence of occlusions, scattering effects, or samples with minimal light, among other issues. To overcome these challenges, we develop a method to leverage the knowledge of language models to improve image patch representation learning in unsupervised and few-shot settings. Specifically, we utilize a language model to create datasets with semantically-rich property labels for each image patch, which we then use to train a patch embedding model. Our method produces robust predictions on real-world datasets derived from microscopy and confocal lymph node imaging. Additionally, fine-tuning our model on a small dataset results in improved unsupervised and few-shot performance on other microscopy datasets. Overall, our approach successfully integrates the knowledge of language models and applied domain knowledge to enhance the quality of image patch representation models, which can be used across various tasks and domains.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on Advanced Speech Recognition Technology, a component that has received significant research attention over three decades. Despite contributions from industry and academia, existing open-source speech recognition platforms remain limited in their language support and performance efficiency. To address this, we assess the current state of German Open Source Automated Speech Recognition and propose an improved system, incorporating the most effective parameters from existing models. Our study involves comprehensive model evaluations, comparative language support analysis, and performance assessments to ensure high reliability in German Open Source Automated Speech Recognition.

Investigations into seven Be-type stars within the Large Magellanic Cloud's 30 Doradus star cluster were conducted through VLT/UVES spectra with a wavelength range of 379-682 nm. Four of these stars, HD 316211, have spectral properties consistent with both Be-type stars and WR subtypes, while three others are purely Be-type stars. A distinct helium and carbon abundance pattern is evident in the four hybrid stars, with helium at 2.0-2.3 times and carbon at 0.6-0.7 times the solar values. Strong lines of helium and multiple ionized species of nitrogen and carbon are characteristic of these stars, as is the metal abundance of 0.5-0.6 times the solar values. The s-process metal helium and nitrogen are prevalent, while the p-process carbon and iron are also present. The hybrid stars' fast rotational velocities of 250-340 km/s are responsible for the further enrichment of metal abundance. In contrast, the three pure Be-type stars within 30 Doradus do not exhibit the same level of metal enrichment but show an increased nitrogen line strength relative to other metal lines, which could be the initial stage of a WR-type star. The origin of nitrogen in the pure Be-type stars is suggested to be similar to hybrid stars, while carbon nitride molecules and a CNO cycle are proposed as the source of nitrogen abundance in the star cluster, as also found in the hybrid stars

To translate Audio-to-Text (AT) models' output into natural speech, inverse text normalization (ITN) is crucial; yet, its reliability is limited by the shortcomings of current language models. This study reveals that neural ITN models are prone to producing erroneous outputs, particularly on key pronunciation elements such as syllable boundaries and word stress. To address these shortcomings, we propose to utilize data augmentation techniques that simulate common pronunciation variations in real speech, thereby enriching the training data for ITN models and significantly boosting their accuracy. By applying this approach, ITN performance is enhanced by over 5% in terms of word error rate (WER) across all tested speech languages, including English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Portuguese.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and derives an optimal lower 
bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the volume of the domain and its distance 
to the equilibrium potential of a set.

Tangent space embeddings of a set of probability distributions have been gaining significant attention due to their potential to preserve crucial information about the original probability measures while enabling efficient computation of various statistical queries. A tangent space corresponds to a tangent space embedding, which can capture subtle differences between distribution functions. Notably, we develop a set of tangent spaces that encompass all exchangeable and non-exchangeable probability measures and leverage the benefits of kernel mean embedding to efficiently operate on large datasets. By applying these tangent space embeddings, we derive a consistent estimator for the covariance matrix of a discrete distribution and demonstrate its applications in establishing novel error bounds for concentration and deviation analysis of tangent space embeddings. Furthermore, we propose a general technique for constructing tangent space embeddings that can be utilized across various domains and illustrate its concrete benefits in the context of spherical embedding.

Recent discoveries in non-Hermitian topology have led to a wide variety of topological phenomena in both one-dimensional and higher-dimensional systems, notable for their exceptional phase boundaries. These phase boundaries exhibit unique characteristics such as fractional charge and unique boundary states including localized, chiral, and exceptional states. A distinct feature of one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems is the emergence of extensive phase boundaries. However, due to the scattering of bulk states with the boundary, these phase boundaries are unusually fragile and have not been fully understood. In this study, we developed models of one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems where the bulk and boundary states could be precisely controlled through rational and effective interactions. Notably, our results reveal that rational correlations significantly reduce the scattering of bulk states with the boundary, effectively increasing the durability of boundary states. Moreover, our findings illustrate that thermal fluctuations can induce correlations that transition a system from a fully chaotic state to a correlated topological phase. Through the use of exact gapless solutions and the Hamiltonian perturbation theory, we extensively examined the characteristics of exceptional states and the emergence of topological phenomena including localized, chiral, and exceptional states within one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems that are influenced by thermal fluctuations and rational correlations.

Our study delves into the incorporation of social characteristics of spoken language, specifically those attributed to social identity, gender, cultural background, and personality. We explore how to embed these attributes in synthetic speech, focusing on identifying the relevant linguistic features and fundamental characteristics of spoken language that convey social information. Furthermore, we examine the feasibility of using two potential approaches to embed social identity in synthetic speech. One approach involves utilizing existing speech data to create socially distinctive acoustic markers. Another strategy involves programming the personality of synthetic speakers using narrative techniques and allowing cultural and individual identity variations to be embedded in the language structure and content.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses emerge through one-loop interactions, resulting in a bosonic dark matter candidate within the range of approximately 0.01-50 GeV. Stabilization of dark matter occurs due to a combination of nonzero modular weight and residual Z2 symmetry derived from the U(1)_(B-L) symmetry. Indirect naturalness of this approach lies in the radiative generation of dark matter mass. Expected direct and indirect detection signatures include future prospects for ALPS-II/III, CRESST, CMB-S4, DarkLight, and DarkSide experiments to test against ongoing constraints from AME, CAMB, CDMS, XMASS, and EDELWEES.

Building on the classical movement of a rigid body concept, researchers used the Peierls-Nobel effective potential to investigate triaxial nuclei's movement as a collective entity, applying the quantum dynamics of a particle in a potential well with the minimal length concept that replaces $x \rightarrow x i \hat{\mathsb{h}}$. This approach led to a semi-classical equation of movement, and corresponding RWA equation, both of which were analyzed numerically. Studies showed that including the minimal length concept in the minimal matching procedure can account for the ground state energies of low-lying states in Al, Ga, and Zn isotopes with tolerable errors.

This paper introduces a novel class of Golay complementary arrays (GCA) with a 4-phase pattern, offering a direct extension to the existing 1-phase and 2-phase GCAs. Building on the optimal reciprocal pairs of 4-phase arrays, four possible GCA designs were created and two of them fulfilled the requirements of optimal reciprocal pairs. Notably, all four arrays, when part of a GCA, showed increased distance to the first type non-optimality defect, when compared to the existing GCAs.

This research proposes a novel unsupervised technique utilizing DCN-modules for hyperspectral change detection. Building on the concept of an unsupervised deep feature fusion network, it integrates modularity and reciprocity to effectively extract and compare spectral and spatial information from Hughes-Dictation matrices. Experimental validation on diverse datasets demonstrates the performance superiority of our approach over established benchmarks.

A thorough examination of the connection between residual entropy and viscosity was conducted in this research. We utilized molecular dynamics simulations with respect to the Lennard-Jones, Morse, Barker-Feldman, Kimur--Jordan-Buckley and other other potentials to establish this connection, specifically looking at the non-polarizable oil model, such that the Kimur--Jordan-Buckley potential can be represented as a series of the modified Lennard-Jones potential. Our research demonstrated that there exists a positive correlation between the residual entropy and reduced viscosity across a vast set of pairwise potentials, which is similar to what we've observed in real low-sulfur diesel fuel. Additionally, our research indicated that this connection can be predicted with a basic model based on the density and the energy of the potential, which is especially valuable for applying it to complex mixtures of real fuels.

We've developed a cosmological model based on cycling patterns similar to those seen in the Lambda Cold Dark Matter model, where cosmological cycles switch between expansion and contraction phases. Our research indicates that during the contraction phase, a Lambda term emerges, only to disappear again during the subsequent expansion phase. The model's primary characteristic is that it never reaches a stable equilibrium. Mathematical explanations are provided for how dark matter and dark energy evolve over time, as well as for the formation of structures through a bouncing universe scenario. An examination is also made of observations from the Cosmic Microwave Background Anisotropy and Large Scale Structure, while a brief discussion is included on the difficulties in observing cosmological cycles in the Lambda CDM cyclical cosmology model.

A noncreations-based approach to fundamental theory, known as Invariant-set theory, aims to provide a causal framework that surpasses quantum theory. This article provides an exhaustive examination of a specific variant of this theory known as ISTV, which incorporates hidden variables and addresses the quantum nonlocality of correlations observed in the Bell nonlocality phenomenon. The study first develops the underlying mathematical framework of ISTV, then constructs a protocol that achieves exact replica of quantum correlations found in Bell's original scenario within this framework. The analysis that follows reveals that ISTV, in its current form, is incapable of replicating certain quantum correlations found in the Sliwa-Zhang-Bandyopadhyay Bell scenario as well as the more extensive family of correlations found in Braunstein-Cimirov-Liang-Zhang-Buonomo-Semitekhov-Mann-Buonomo framework. The findings presented here, it is hoped, will contribute meaningfully to future discussions surrounding ISTV.

For content-based search methods in databases of audio recordings to be effective on devices such as smartphones and tablets, they must be able to rapidly locate specific key phrases within embedded neural networks. This study presents several new neural networks designed to conduct keyphrase spotting (KPS) without requiring significant offloading or relying on large storage space. The model architectures explored include a conventional LSTM-based neural network and two novel designs that combine convolutional neural networks and recurrent layers within a single model, all utilizing the same dataset post-processed using mel-filterbanks for training. The results show that these new models perform comparably to a previously successful LSTM-based KPS model while offering improved efficiency through reduced parameters and computational requirements, making them well-suited for applications on edge devices.

A dimer model with a non-zero $z$-projected imbedded in a 2D lattice exhibits some remarkable properties when $z < 2$; for instance, it has a finite entropy per site as the number of dimers per site approaches infinity. This property is shared by another model representing a free fermion system coupled with a background gauge field. A new technique for the latter model shows that its thermal excitation levels can be interpreted as embedded spin-up and spin-down particles moving across a background forest pattern composed of connected islands and roads. By applying this approach to a random gauge field, it is found that the model's thermal excitation levels behave randomly at long ranges; however, the model's thermal excitation levels per site still approach a finite value as the number of dimers per site grows without bounds. This result is consistent with known outcomes for dimers on non-random backgrounds. Moreover, it is proven that the majority of the imbedded Fermions' thermal excitation spectra remain discrete and non-dissolvable into smaller parts across a wide range of $0 < z < 2$. A convenient strategy for the imbedding construction that includes a local imbedding operator, thus connecting dimer and fermion models, is also developed. This approach simplifies previously complex relationships between these models, the hallmarks of which were previously unknown. In addition, it is also demonstrated that the model representing a free fermion system coupled with a background gauge field

Working with categorical data in high-dimensional modeling poses significant challenges due to its inherently large number of parameters, a problem that is compounded when model features need to be interpreted. The application of the Group-Lasso technique offers an attractive solution for high-dimensional categorical data. However, the technique's ability to handle data with distinct, separate groups of variables is not well-suited for data sets that require the combination of categorical variables within specific groups. Building on this understanding, a new method, Enhanced Group-Lasso (E-GLO), is proposed to improve variable selection and estimation for data sets with intertwined categorical variables within specific groups. E-GLO achieves this through the introduction of an anisotropic penalty term that adapts to the variability within each group, while also providing sparse estimates at the individual variable level. The E-GLO approach, incorporated into a new method for combined variable selection and estimation, has been rigorously tested for its performance and reliability across a range of simulations and practical applications, including a study on high-dimensional cancer data from the Cancer Genome Atlas.

In recent years, embedded systems with critical real-time requirements have been forced to accommodate general-purpose operating systems, leading to inefficient management of resources and prolonged system latency. The introduction of hypervisors has improved embedded system security and resource usage, but existing hypervisors still fall short in handling real-time tasks due to overhead in virtualization.

This research presents T-Visor, a custom-designed hypervisor that takes advantage of hardware virtualization technology to provide mixed-criticality operating environments while minimizing overhead to enable real-time tasks. The design of T-Visor focuses on creating separate virtual networks to prevent virtual machine communication, reducing context switching overhead, and implementing device allocation and scheduling policies with priority-based preemptive scheduling.

The performance of T-Visor was evaluated on an ARM-based platform using the RTAI/Linux operating system and demonstrating superior system performance compared to a monolithic operating system. Additionally, practical implementations of virtual devices such as network and block I/O devices were developed to support the hypervisor, and theoretical findings were supported by experimental results indicating T-Visor's ability to manage multiple virtual machines with real-time properties.

Creating comprehensive 360-degree models from various views relies on establishing correlations between these views, a process called panoramic joining. The key to successful panoramic joining lies in accurately mapping and aligning individual views. While existing methods primarily rely on visual cues, we propose a novel approach that takes into account the laws of physics to determine the position and orientation of partially observable cameras. By considering factors such as camera radius, focal length, and optical center, our approach generates a minimal set of possible camera locations. Furthermore, it leverages the principles of conformal geometry and Riemann surface theory to effectively organize and select valid 360-degree models from the resulting space. The proposed method not only reduces the complexity of the joining process but also significantly prunes the relevant camera positions, resulting in a substantial improvement in computation time.

Our research builds on the concept of coupled populations where one population is stable and the other induces periodic variability, but we switch roles, making the stable population unpredictable. We investigate robust slaving, or the phenomenon where chaos follows a sudden increase in parameter variability in a coupled system. This investigation uses the Beretta-Dangerfield model as a model for our chimeras, showing that a stable fixed point gives way to oscillating solutions, then chaos, as variability increases, and providing phase-plane analysis to illustrate these transitions.

Developing autonomous systems that can withstand uncertainties in real-world applications is crucial for long-term viability, yet such adaptations are often absent from current artificial intelligence frameworks. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach for designing regulators that are resistant to uncertainties using a probabilistic model-based policy search method. By constructing a stochastic abstraction of the system, we derive an uncertain policy with varying levels of robustness, and then refine it using a generalized version of the policy improvement with risk-sensitivity optimization algorithm. Our approach is theoretically validated for its ability to find a robust uncertain policy with high probability as the iteration count increases indefinitely. Furthermore, this policy has an optimal level of robustness and can be as close to its optimal value as desired. Our framework is successfully tested on two robust control challenges - the uncertain twin-tank problem and the cavity-tunnel firing problem.

Building on multi-layer diagrams introduced in a previous study, we define a higher-dimensional generalization of slice algebras through diagram-based composition. We show that this construction results in the multi-layered slice algebra, which inherently contains a monoidal category consisting of the standard slice algebra composed of diagonal diagrams. In this context, we establish colimit descriptions for the multi-layered slice algebra using diagram families with values in various higher-dimensional algebras. Furthermore, we define a multiplicative unit system within the multi-layered slice algebra with the help of generalized trace operations. Additionally, for algebras possessing a unit, we demonstrate the existence of a colimit description for the multi-layered slice algebra using specific diagram families, which includes trivial components. These results are illustrated by applying them to commutative Hopf algebras with diagonal and skew-diagonal structures.

We explore the reflected correlation, a measure that gauges the consistency of local representations within a collective ensemble in the context of random tensor networks. Specifically, for reflected correlations involving four variables, we establish a crucial link between this measure and quantum error correction capabilities, particularly regarding minimum distance. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that, in principle, individual elements of these networks can convey substantial information about the entire ensemble. Nevertheless, this property is restricted by a positive lower bound, stemming from the reflected correlation of these ensemble elements. Consequently, our research identifies reflected correlations as a crucial standard for evaluating the collective's information content within these networks.

Living organisms rely heavily on lasting patterns, such as structure and organization, to ensure their survival and reproduction. These patterns are defined by the spatial variations in their properties and are maintained through a wide array of molecular and cellular processes. The patterns seen in real-life situations typically emerge from two main factors: the initial instructions that organize those patterns and the environmental influences that affect them. To fully comprehend how these patterns evolve, it is essential to study their behavior when subject to random events or the fluctuations in surrounding factors. The patterns themselves, being physical objects with a definite history, must also be affected by probabilistic-like changes. The patterns that last depend on an intricate interaction between the instructions that define them, their capacity to resist change, and the initial conditions that lay the groundwork for their emergence. The patterns that exist at any particular time in such systems can be summarized using a concept known as relative entropy. The measures that define this concept, such as free energy and entropy, remain stable over time in systems that follow the laws of conservation and those whose evolution is influenced by correlated and symmetric random events or the equilibrium state. The patterns that exist in these systems are automatic manifestations of their equilibrium state. The patterns that exist at room temperature, and those that involve a difference in the arrangement of their parts, are relatively stable and endure for a considerable amount of time. We examine the three-dimensional generalized H\'{e}non model as introduced in (Nature (Lond.) 457, 148-152, 2009). The findings of (Phys. Rev. E 82, 046204, 2010) are extended to the 3D model, with particular focus on the influence of $\alpha$ in (2, 3 D) H\'{e}non model. Ultimately, a set of visualization tools is recommended for the 3D generalized H\'{e}non model.

The geometric interpretation of the Ricci tensor in terms of holonomy components suggests a higher, non-metric representation of gravity. This article investigates the gravitational holonomy and its relationship with the Ricci tensor, exploring its implications on a spacetime's geometry and whether it can serve as a foundation for a metric-affine geometry.

This passage explores specific cases within the symmetric functions of partitions where hook lengths are either divisible by 2 or 3, establishing a framework for generating associated orthogonal polynomials through the inversion of Jacobi-Trudi matrices, comprised of coefficients from the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials whose indices are 2 or 3 hook lengths. Additionally, the relationship between these functions and determinantal representations of partition generating functions, specifically for even and triple hook lengths, is also formulated.

Superconducting qubits rely on macro-scale electronics but use quantum mechanics for computing. The transition between quantum states within these qubits typically involves a tunneling process through a localized barrier. In this research, we demonstrate that the speed at which this tunneling occurs can be determined by measuring the Larmor clock's disruption due to spontaneous spin fluctuations in the conduit. This new method for gauging tunneling rates utilizing Larmor clocks may become a valuable addition to the toolkit for analyzing superconducting processors.

Leading twist distribution amplitudes for P-wave non-relativistic mesons are established, assuming local dimensionality and a specific form for the meson light-cone wave function. A specific gauge link procedure is employed to handle the interaction between the meson and the light-like quantization axis. To test the developed amplitude's applicability, leading twist distribution amplitudes are applied in the analysis of a specific two-body decay of a non-re relativistic meson. This analysis involves evaluating the semi-leptonic decay rate of the P-wave non-relativistic $\psi(2S)$ meson into a lepton and a photon pair, utilizing this process as a case study for the amplitude's practical use. Moreover, the analysis derives the partial decay rate for the P-wave non-relativistic $\chi_{c1}(3100)$ meson into a lepton, photon, and a P-wave hadron.

This study proposes a new set of nonlinear quantum operators for a Bose-Einstein condensate. Utilizing the Bogoliubov transformation, the authors derive one- and two-body Hamiltonians in terms of operators for both grand canonical and canonical ensembles. The authors examine the Bogoliubov inequality and compare it to the expectation value of the Hamiltonian for a system of one atom to evaluate its effectiveness. The proposed operators enable a straightforward description of mean field dynamics, and their use with a time-evolving short-range interaction yields insight into the quantum vacuum decay time, which can be easily calculated. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that the nonlinear operators can produce a pure ground state in a system of one atom. To achieve this, they incorporate a nonlinear cross-term, which is absent in previous descriptions. The resulting pure ground state, derived using a nonlinear Schrodinger equation, leads to a new expression for the one-body density matrix. The authors leverage the nonlinear operators to derive expressions for the two-body density matrix and the Bogoliubov vacuum. Additionally, they apply the nonlinear operators to a canonical ensemble to evaluate the nonlinear Hamiltonian and examine the nonlinearity's effect on the mean occupation number. The proposed nonlinear operators enable a straightforward description of occupation number fluctuations.

The extended BMS algebra includes a variety of higher-order soft theorems that come with corresponding higher-order charge principles. By applying this framework to scattering amplitudes, a key relationship is established between the extended BMS algebra and a subalgebra derived from the asymptotic symmetries of flat space-time. Specifically, this corresponds to either anti-de Sitter space-time or de Sitter space-time. Furthermore, this equivalence is used to demonstrate that higher-order charge principles derived from soft theorems through this extended BMS algebra reduce to lower-order notions for asymptotically flat spacetimes.

Online ensemble learning methods offer a valuable solution to the problem of learning in situations where there is an endless series of arriving data streams. One of the significant difficulties in this context is the issue of class increase, where new categories of data emerge, causing existing models to struggle with adapting. Therefore, there is a significant need for continuous learning techniques that can effectively handle ever-increasing knowledge domains, especially when the streams contain unfamiliar data. This paper presents a novel approach to the ensemble continuous learning problem by developing a neural structure that integrates the fusion of knowledge from individual learners with the capacity for model updating. The method's reliability in handling varying data streams is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on streams with constantly rising classes and irregular data sequences.

In the context of generalized metrics with torsion, a specific four-dimensional measure formed by the norm of the metric, and influenced by the connection and torsion, can be examined. This work focuses on the conditions necessary for this measure to be both right and left Ricci-flat. As a result, we derive a specific metric representation in terms of the commutator of the left and right connections, and we provide examples of particular generalized metrics with this property.

In the wake of several recently constructed total permutation polynomials over finite fields with square order, our focus lies on examining permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube order through a comprehensive approach. Utilizing multi-index notation, our results showcase specific types of non-weak total permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube order, thereby offering a class of weak total permutation polynomials with a significantly broader coefficient range, especially in the cases of small prime powers. Moreover, our method of analysis also reveals new permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube order that are beneficial for further research in this field.

The prevalence of intestinal parasites poses a significant risk to global public health, yet proper diagnosis often requires a costly and cumbersome light microscopy process. This research aims to explore the application of a more advanced Deep Belief Network as a reliable method for categorizing intestinal parasites. Following a discussion of the relevant background concepts and methods, the experiment's setup and results are outlined. These studies utilized 13,000 micrograph images of six major intestinal parasites, divided into three classes, and obtained impressive classification rates of up to 93%, outperforming the accuracy of human microscopists in this task. This breakthrough has the potential to greatly simplify the diagnosis process by replacing human microscopists and could eventually lead to the development of portable devices that use DBN technology to instantly identify intestinal parasites in the field.

This work focuses on a stochastic linear-expected-utility-based zero-sum investment and reinsurance model under a regime-switching framework. A weak solution approach is introduced to approximate the Stackelberg solution under a Markovian mean-variance approach and a Markovian utility approach. Furthermore, two case studies are provided to validate the effectiveness and applicability of the proposed method.

This research presents a novel method for rapidly and securely controlling fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with non-minimum phase characteristics, utilizing a Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accumulate (PID-A) controller. The proposed PID-A controller incorporates a dual simplex algorithm and a genetic filter to enhance stability and prevent oscillation, achieving controllability over third-order dynamics and non-homogeneous linear equations with multiple constraints. The integration of the genetic filter simplifies the process of specifying feasibility, reducing dependency on initial conditions and enabling automatic detection and prevention of unstable flight modes. The efficacy of the proposed controller is demonstrated in realistic simulations using a 3D model and a real UAV, showcasing its ability to provide smooth, stable flight and maintain accurate vertical flight speed in various configurations.

Historically, low-energy pion-nucleon interactions have been understudied, making up only about 10% of all pion-nucleon scattering processes but are now recognized as crucial in nucleon structure, astrophysics, and related fields. New, comprehensive experiments on these interactions are under way, which will deliver large amounts of data. This development necessitates a critical evaluation of theoretical approaches, which traditionally have not received much attention. This report analyzes the measurable aspects of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions and identifies experimental and theoretical challenges, while promoting potential solutions to tackle them. Even with limited data available, low-energy pion-nucleon interactions hold significant potential for contributing to our understanding of nucleon structure, cache, parton distribution functions, and the QCD phase diagram.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the six experiments that conduct research at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) located in Geneva, Switzerland. The CMS is designed to investigate various phenomena resulting from high-energy proton collisions at interaction points within the LHC. The CMS employs a one-inch thick superconducting solenoid to produce a uniform magnetic field for precise particle tracking. The silicon pixel pilot moduli in the CMS incorporate single-sided forward pixel sensors with 24 readout chips (RPCHs) for each side, with six moduli in the barrel and two in the endcaps. The pilot moduli utilize a novel readout system, including the 24-chip readout chip (RPCH) designed by CMS, to contribute to the development of the next-generation CMS pixel system. The CMS pixel pilot moduli were tested using cosmic rays and data from the initial LHC run in 2009-2010. The resulting analysis investigated the CMS pixel forward pixel pilot moduli' signal and noise performance, specifically focusing on charge and temperature dependence in the CMS pixel systems. The validation of these results is essential for the next-generation CMS pixel systems.

Previous studies of galaxy structures in the HSC-WS S14 dataset were limited due to the small sample size of optically identified AGN host galaxies, making it difficult to establish reliable relationships between stellar mass and galaxy structure. Our research compiles a larger sample of 307 AGN host galaxies within $0.35<z<1$ and $9.5<log(M_*)<10.6$ to extend prior findings, also including a smaller sample of 37 AGN host galaxies within $0.1<z<0.3$ and $8.4<log(M_*)<10.3$ to examine mass-dependent trends in galaxy structure. Using machine learning to select high-quality AGN host galaxies in the HSC-WS S14 dataset reduces uncertainties in galaxy structure measurement, such as the S\'ersic index and half-light radius. Our research reveals that stellar mass is the primary factor controlling the A/Sersic index and Kpc half-light radius of galaxy bulges, also establishing a weak, negative relationship between Kpc half-light radius and S\'ersic index. Compared to normal galaxies of similar mass and redshift, AGN host galaxies generally exhibit higher S\'ersic indices and smaller Kpc half-light radii. The differences in Kpc half-light radius and S\'ersic index between AGN host galaxies and similar galaxies are shown to increase with mass, in contrast, the distinction in their A/Sersic index differences with

High-energy density regions in dense matter are characterized by ultracold neutron scattering volumes that provide unique insights into short-range correlations in nuclei, a topic of considerable debate. To gain deeper insight, researchers employ dense-matter theories based on phenomenological descriptions of nuclear forces. However, conventional wave function approaches fail to account for a significant portion of the actual scattering response, a critical factor in high-energy density regions. By applying a unitary correlation operator in wave functions, researchers have found that this method can capture a more accurate picture of the scattering response, in line with quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, variations in the Wigner transformation's kernel are linked to the density matrices' anisotropic distribution of momenta, providing a second method to study short-range correlations. By using this distribution, researchers have found that density matrices preserve key correlations in dense matter, making them a reliable choice for investigating short-range correlations. By adopting a hyperbolic tangent transformation to the density distribution, researchers have found that this anisotropy can be accurately linked to the tangent hyperbolic function's argument, enabling a straightforward comparison with scattering responses.

This research investigates the behavior of complex-valued deep learning models where the input/output spaces are complex but the network uses real arithmetic. We extend previous work by focusing on models with symmetric complex output spaces and develop new expressions for their behavior. By applying techniques from function and operator theory, we derive and analyze upper limits for the norm of complex functions. Our results demonstrate that this model can approximate certain complex functions with upper limits valid across entire complex domains. We also show that this model can be represented as a collection of real-valued layers, and provide an intuitive explanation for its success. An implemented model, based on our proposed architecture, achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex Speech Enhancement tasks.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy situations, saturation momentum becomes Uncorrelated with virtuality.  Saturation in high-energy processes generates distinctive patterns - known as geometrical scaling - in observable quantities by eliminating dependence on longitudinal momentum fractions, thereby revealing hidden properties through interdisciplinary research between QCD theory and advanced experiments.  Geometrical scaling has been observed in several ep scattering events.  Scaled distributions in ep scattering also exhibit similarity to those observed in A-A collisions across varied ion combinations.  Furthermore, geometrical scaling has also been identified in two-jet production, and it's anticipated that it will be observed in multi-jet patterns.  Consequently, it's hoped that this concept - rooted in non-linear QCD - will be verified through future experiments at interaction energies of 120-130 GeV at the Large Hadron Collider.

A significant amount of amplitude scattering, observed in low-metallicity stars, can be attributed to variations in the inner barycentric space, which is driven by outer-incoming and mid-incoming dynamical processes. Furthermore, a novel computational model for amplitude scattering based on 6-body interactions is developed and utilized to better understand and replicate this phenomenon. Through a newly proposed amplitude scattering parameter, the amplitude scattering field can be quantitatively defined and analyzed. Additionally, a distinction between amplitude scattering regions and streams is established by demonstrating how these parameters correlate with known stellar streams in the Milky Way, such as the Helium-Weak Bench and GD-1. This new model and parameter also shed light on the origin of the previously observed Outer Halo population, which appears to be the result of 2D mid-incoming processes.

A novel approach has been developed for quantifying how impact tolerance varies due to inevitable uncertainties in big data, artificial intelligence, and robotic decision-making. The framework's initial testing using financial literacy data from a Latin American country demonstrates that the variations in results can range significantly, up to 5 times the initial estimate, albeit with a tendency towards lower variability for less precise outcomes. This methodology's implementation is currently accessible through a Python package named AIUtility, aimed at streamlining the evaluation of the robustness of machine learning and robotic decision-making models.

We introduce SQUID, an open-source framework for developing and machine-learning-driven quantum information processing software. Building upon the PyTorch and Qiskit platforms, SQUID combines them with a custom research-oriented programming environment to facilitate research in the emerging field of quantum intelligence. Through SQUID, users can access a comprehensive set of tools and functionality for rapidly developing, optimizing, and training quantum classification and clustering models. The framework includes an interactive environment for visualizing and analyzing data, as well as a syntax-based editor for writing and debugging quantum circuits. SQUID also features a range of advanced algorithms and tools for model training, parameter optimization, and result analysis. Currently, SQUID's source code is available on GitHub, with accompanying documentation at sqid.read.

This research focuses on examining pointwise slant submanifolds within almost contact manifold contexts, specifically looking into whether they can be viewed as warped products of submanifolds that are either totally geodesic or oriented perpendicularly to the contact vector field. Crucial to this investigation are derived formulas for the Levi-Civita connection, a second structure vector field, and curvature tensor on the relevant submanifolds.

Future direct detection experiments with exotic nuclei will utilize advanced techniques, including spectral response analysis, to detect nuclear recoil events. Current direct detection experiments face challenges due to technical factors inducing various forms of recoil events. Advanced color center materials hold promise in overcoming these obstacles, allowing the distinction between different types of recoil events, including those caused by other factors being suppressed, while focusing on the nucleus of interest. This report outlines the concept, design and technological capabilities of an innovative device called PALEOCCENE, which utilizes a new type of crystal based on the LiCaAlF6 crystal structure and contains a specific type of color center. Capable of detecting sub-eV energies, this device offers significant potential in direct detection experiments, including the capability to run at temperatures as low as 20 mK and collect data over an extensive area of over 100 square centimeters.

Colloidal particles within a fluid undergo interactions that form long-lasting associations known as colloidal molecules. Typically, these molecules emerge in situations where uniform fluid flow conditions prevail, but the focus of this study lies on the dynamic formation and evolution of these molecules in environments where a persistent gradient of fluid flow exists. A theoretical framework has been developed to track the self-organization of the particles in these molecules as they move through the gradient influenced by flow. In the initial stages, the particles exhibit homogeneous distribution until they are drawn into growing clusters in response to the increasing flow gradient. These clusters can temporarily shield the particles from the flow gradient, allowing them to temporarily stabilize before being drawn into larger and more stable structures that follow a specific size progression. A new statistical model has been created to accurately predict the emergence of these larger structures and the specific size increments within the gradient. It is found that the time it takes for the particles to be drawn into the largest structure is directly linked to the acceleration caused by the flow gradient. In cases where the particles are initially activated, this structure assumes a specific Y-shaped form. A new theoretical model has been developed to accurately predict the shape and size of this structure and its connection to the flow gradient and particle interactions.

This study delves into a theoretical model of a two-dimensional particle system with interparticle interactions, where Chern bands are formed through Laughlin Correlations. A novel type of correlation, termed "fractional topological correlations," is identified, characteristic of topological symmetries, and the research establishes a correlation between metric and spectral properties in this system. Notably, the study discovers "magnetorotons" - spectral excitations that are magnetic and rotational in nature, found to condense upon multiple quanta combinations, and the research reveals a totality rule for this combination. Central to these findings are observations of the symmetries, spectral features, and the underlying topological characteristics, yielding insights into a broader theory of topological excitations.

Although numerous disease spread models are developed specifically for complex networks, many proposed detection and prediction methods blur the line between network structure and dynamic progression, ignoring the interplay between these two crucial aspects. Furthermore, the focus on individual transmission parameters at a fine scale often hinders broader, more generalizable outcomes. To overcome these limitations, this paper incorporates a new perspective - the inherent geometry of the epidemic process - that enables the derivation of more accurate and efficient detection and prediction algorithms for outbreaks in networks. By doing so, it yields simpler, more efficient methods that outperform existing approaches in terms of accuracy and computational requirements. The proposed methods are particularly useful for real-time analysis in health emergency scenarios where resource constraints often necessitate cost minimization.

The X'es, prominent in CMB data analysis due to their impact on likelihood functions, can cause issues for Bayesian parameter estimations, particularly when evaluating the significance of theoretical models. To better understand X'es and their effect on likelihood functions, we've conducted a comprehensive study using synthetic and real-data scenarios. Our research has yielded several key takeaways regarding how to handle X'es in practice: synthetic datasets should be sufficient to assess the significance of theoretical models, even with large noise levels; the impact of X'es on an estimate's variance can be misleading, as it's affected by the variance of the underlying dataset; to accurately determine the variance of a parameter estimate, one should utilize subregions of the prior with relatively small variations; the 'internal jackknife' method is an effective alternative for estimating the variance of a parameter; finally, when evaluating the significance of a theoretical model against Planck data, one should utilize an 'outlier' method, using uncorrelated noise from a small fraction of the sky and repeating the estimation 5 times or more.

Interpreting teaching instructions that incorporate natural language is an crucial capability required to accelerate reinforcement learning in real-world scenarios.
Despite significant research in the field, natural language instructions still face significant limitations, primarily due to the difficulty of understanding the teacher's intentions behind uttered words.
This paper presents a groundbreaking approach that utilizes contextual information to decipher the teacher's intent behind instructions influenced by natural language and adjusts the student agent's exploration accordingly.
The proposed method is designed for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning and does not necessitate the student to explicitly recognize the teacher's intentions.
Empirical trials conducted on a benchmark dataset spanning across three environments (three basic versions, three medium-level versions, and three advanced versions) reveal the proposed technique achieves a 40% increase in training efficiency over existing methods (RRM and CLRL), and also outperforms CLRL on a benchmark dataset in training efficiency by 40%, and excels over random instruction scenarios by 60% in training efficiency.

Reconstructing an unknown quantum channel from noisy output measurements is a crucial step in developing quantum networks. Current state-of-the-art methods, shadow tomography and iterative shadow tomography, have significant limitations in practical applications due to the extreme number of such measurements required. In this study, we introduce a new algorithm that can accurately reconstruct any quantum channel with minimal additional assumptions, all while only needing access to a significantly reduced number of measurements. This breakthrough is achieved by leveraging the connection between quantum channels and matrix balls. Specifically, our new method involves a matrix lynchpin, the matrix ball inequality, which is a key enabler of this reconstruction. In addition, we also derive a useful application of the matrix ball inequality that can accurately estimate any quantum channel from relatively few, easily obtainable low-level statistics. This is done by first establishing a useful quantum characterisation of matrix balls that can reconstruct any quantum channel from relatively low-quality estimates. Furthermore, we also derive a useful application of the matrix ball inequality that can accurately estimate any quantum channel from relatively few, easily obtainable low-level statistics. In our numerical experiments, we find that our new method compares very favourably to the existing algorithms, with particular improvements in scenarios where the channel is nearly noise-free.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant in relation to other geometric parameters such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter for sets confined within a two-dimensional Euclidean space. These results will be illustrated by examples of shapes that demonstrate the sensitivity of the Cheeger constant, and potentially other parameters, to small changes in shape.

This study investigates how to determine the shortest time optimal flight path for an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to deliver data packets from a communication satellite to a ground station on the Earth's surface. The optimal route is calculated by minimizing a composite function of the flight distance and time, taking into account the UAV's air propulsion time, flight speed, and ground propulsion time. The resulting optimization problem is transformed into a type of Markov perfect dynamic programming problem. An approximate solution to this problem is derived by replacing the continuous flight time with a discrete step size and using a local search algorithm. The validity of the proposed discrete-time solution is confirmed by comparing it with the continuous-time solution which is already known to be optimal.

Our renormalization group analysis predicts that a bilayer graphene, characterized by low-energy interactions, is unstable to the formation of multiple fermionic collective modes, specifically Kohn effects, that may ultimately transform into two superconducting states with distinct symmetry properties. The emergence of these modes is attributed to unusual electronic properties, namely, non-zero quasiparticle weights and significant Peierls components, derived from the interaction of intralayer and interlayer Coulomb forces. Conversely, a monolayer graphene is predicted to be stable under the influence of the Coulomb interaction alone.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their abilities to respond to external stimuli and interact with their surroundings, particularly in the alteration of molecular configurations following temperature changes. The present study employs highly resolved scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to investigate the thermal-induced conformational transformation of the nanomolecule Sc2TbN@C80 on a flat tungsten carbide surface. As the temperature increases from 78 K to room temperature, all initially upright molecules on the surface undergo a vertical shift resulting in a flat configuration. Moreover, the existence of an intermediate stable configuration at around 250 K for the first time highlights the dynamic behavior of the nanomolecule and the mechanism of its conformational transformation, which has been further validated by density functional theory calculations. This investigation demonstrates the use of an ultra-stable and highly ordered single-crystalline substrate to study the conformational change of a nanomolecule at different temperatures.

A securely encrypted data transfer is crucial for Internet of Things devices to maintain user confidentiality. Although various encryption techniques are available, they may be too resource-intensive or require excessive processing power for low-power IoT devices. To overcome this limitation, a novel method utilizing the GGM (Gaussian Guided Generator) generator has been developed to enhance encryption efficiency. This new approach leverages the numerical benefits of the GGM generator to produce high-quality and unique keys. By integrating the GGM key into a conventional encryption method, such as AES, it significantly accelerates the encryption and decryption processes while providing 94% key generation rate, a high level of randomness, and superior security. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the proposed solution can effectively replace existing encryption methods like AES-Rijndael to facilitate secure data transfer among IoT devices.

Measuring Ramsey spectra provides crucial insights into the behavior of atoms interacting with optical lattice potentials and offers valuable data on optical lattice depths and atomic spin states. However, making these measurements with minimal error requires a difficult balance between the number of atoms used and the duration of each measurement. To address this challenge, a method is presented for determining the optimal number of atoms needed for a measurement by first finding the precise number required for an accurate calculation of a critical parameter. Once this baseline is established, a probability-based calculation is used to identify the most effective sequence of atomic configurations for computing the desired parameter with the fewest number of shots. This method is presented as a solution for optimizing measurements in scenarios where the atomic setup is subject to limitations and uncertainties.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. The Gromov centrality metric gauges importance at scales corresponding to node distances from the network's isoperimetric graph, utilizing the network's triangle inequality excess. It offers a multi-scale perspective combining local network interactions and global metrics, along with a nodal version and extensions that can be applied to any connected graph, making it highly versatile.

Following a groundbreaking finding by Nordstr\"om in 1917, an azimuthally symmetric theory of gravity was developed. This classical field theory of gravity overpowers relativity's limitations regarding non-Newtonian forces. Given its straightforward mathematical nature, this theory is easily derived from the postulation that its gravitational potential only depends on distance. With the potential defined as U(r), the equation of motion can be developed within the framework of the Lagrangian formalism. Since the theoretical framework starts with an unsatisfying assumption, an alternative approach is adopted using the Lagrangian formalism for fundamental theories. With the given conditions that the Lagrangian only depends on the radial distance and that energy is conserved in this simple system, the theory's equations are developed. Resultantly, the equations are compared to Newton's law of gravity, leading to the discovery that the theoretical range is limited to one body systems or systems where the theoretical and external potentials are not in conflict. This simple theoretical framework enables the creation of a one-to-one correspondence between the azimuthal potential and Newton's gravitational constant. With the theoretical framework's satisfaction of the fundamental equations, the theoretical framework's solutions are developed. This simple theoretical framework resolves the conflicts present in the fundamental equations, including the issue of the D'Alembertian's negative sign and the unsatisfying one form of the Lagrangian. This passage discusses a particular category of matrix operator bundles, denoted as $\mathfrak{M}^{\infty}(\mathbb{C})$, in the context of strict equivalence. The research establishes the criteria for two matrix operator bundles to be strictly equivalent, including the requirement that their corresponding matrices must undergo a simple transformation, either through rotation or pointwise scaling, in order to facilitate a direct relationship between the two. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any matrix operator bundle belonging to the category is inherently topologically representative and that it serves as the unit object within a binary operation under the strict equivalence relation.

We investigate a topological T-duality transformation applied to a modified cylinder based on a specific two-dimensional topological model. The primary focus of our study is to establish a one-to-one correspondence between the basic mathematical components used in the twisted cylinder's T-duality map. Furthermore, we visualize various key features, such as electric properties and a critical degenerate level in the twisted cylinder's T-duality relation. The study demonstrates that a simplified version of the AdS$_3$ solution in string theory has equivalent properties to the modified twisted cylinder when a specific condition is met. As a result, our study contributes to an ongoing research in finding a simplified version of conformal field theory that can replace the AdS$_3$ solution in string theory.

In this research, we develop a method to characterize the treewidth of graphs based on parameterized width metrics, such as tree-depth and path-width. A similar approach is taken to describe the structure of graphs with bounded tree-depth using chordal completion. Additionally, an equivalent bounded tree-depth graph criterion is established in terms of chordal completions with limited treewidth. Similarly, the concept of bounded tree-depth graphs with limited treewidth is equivalent to those with bounded path-width and can be defined using chordal completions with limited treewidth. A characterization of graphs with bounded tree-depth using chordal completions with small treewidth is also developed. A similar analysis is conducted for graphs with the minor-closed graph H and it is shown that a similar definition of bounded tree-depth using chordal completions with small treewidth applies to these graphs. A characterization of graphs with bounded tree-depth using chordal completions with small treewidth is also developed for graphs with the minor-closed graph H.

For C1-smooth maps T on R^n, including piecewise linear transformations, a set where recurrent behavior is likely given sufficient randomness is characterized. Additionally, a set where attractive behavior is likely given sufficient randomness is determined. This set where recurrent behavior is likely is characterized as the union of all positive invariant sets with maximal measure, thus resolving a problem posed by Bruck and Osborn in 1999.

A new algorithm, the Qubit-Excitation Based Adaptive Variational Quantum Eigensolver (QEB-AVQE), enhances the traditional variational quantum eigensolver by utilizing a qubit-based unitary coupled cluster ansatz that's optimized with an adaptive method. By employing a protocol that strategically adds excitation operators to reach a target energy, QEB-AVQE achieves improved performance over its variational quantum eigensolver counterpart. Furthermore, our approach maintains the benefits of utilizing a qubit-based ansatz: decreased tensor train depth and reduced memory requirement, and minimized risk of gauge invariance issues. We test our approach on small hydrogen chains and find that it outperforms traditional AVQE even with fewer variational parameters.

A novel deep neural network, known as the Deep Generative Encoder (DGE), is designed to mimic a probabilistic generative model. By assuming that two-dimensional images follow a Zipf distribution, characterized by a parameter $\zeta$, the DGE is trained to produce a representation that can generate synthetic Zipfian images. Unlike traditional autoencoders, which lack a clear objective for image synthesis, the DGE is grounded in a well-defined probabilistic model. This leads to a simple yet effective training objective: maximizing the approximate marginal log-likelihood through a fixed-point iteration of the MAP estimation of the representation.

In our research, we've established a cosmic timeline based on current data, from the patterns of fluctuations in the cosmic radiation (cosmological primordial spectrum) to the present day, including the observations of gravitational waves in the local universe. These measurements support a stiff background of gravitational waves generated during inflation, which affects primordial spectrum analysis and cosmological evolution. A close examination of the NANOGrav minipaper's analysis found that conventional sinusoidal signals can't adequately fit the evidence, although a stiff background of gravitational waves combined with pulsar array data yields a more compelling explanation. Furthermore, the study indicates that a stiff background of gravitational waves can resolve the ongoing "Hubble tension" by fine-tuning the Planck scale, which is the scalar mode amplitude at inflation. This possibility aligns with the observed spatial patterns of cosmic baryogenesis and supports a universe dominated by dark energy with a specific property, which is consistent with recent observations from the Advanced LIGO-Virgo Collaboration. An optimized cosmic timeline is suggested by these findings, which could be tested in various ways, even providing a predictive model that can be validated or rejected by upcoming gravitational wave detectors, such as the Cosmic Explorer and the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna.

Our study presents the first molecular census of the long-period comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) obtained with interferometric observations of various molecular species, including CS, HCN, CH3OH, H2CO, H2CS, and HNC. The data were collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array in February 2021, covering an extensive range of wavelengths from 84 to 236.6 GHz. Our multi-frequency observations yield diverse and continuous spectral lines from 15 to 22 February, largely influenced by water outgassing. The gas and dust temperatures were found to be around 8.7 and 5.6 Kelvin respectively, though some variations exist. Our findings reveal CS is the most prominent emission line at carbon dioxide freeze-out temperatures, with two distinct peaks, one centered at 106.3 GHz and another spanning 216.4 to 237.4 GHz. It has been concluded that the CS emission originates from a widely dispersed source rather than the comet's photosphere, as it does not coincide with other emissions like HCN and is not inclined at similar solar elongation angles. Moreover, the variations in CS line intensity at various frequencies indicate that it is mainly excited through a combination of collision with hydrogen molecules and secondary processes triggered by non-thermal desorption, as it does not arise from volume freeze-out, as it doesn't correlate with water polarization temperature.
