We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. Notably, the unsupervised system achieves this performance after training for only 24 hours on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU, representing a significant reduction of over 100 times in the amount of computational resources required compared to the traditional method.

This research employs the Tsallis statistical distribution to develop a complex form of the essence model with holographic dark energy. We examine its implications in the dark energy sector, where the essential parameter, $q_{0}$, is determined alongside other cosmological parameters through a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method using the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and Constitutional data. Our results indicate that the derived model fits the Hubble data more effectively than the complex essence model with a Lagrange multiplier. Moreover, we have found that the derived model's value for $\omega_{Q}$ lies within negative phase, while the value of $q_{0}$ is consistent with observations. The analysis of state parameters' evolution supports the dynamical dark energy hypothesis, where $w_{Q}$ transitions from a non-variating to a time-dependent state. Additionally, our results indicate underreporting in the current Hubble data as the derived model exhibits a negative value for $q_{0}$ with a high statistical significance. Lastly, our model's predictions for the dark energy equation of state have reached the phase where $w_{Q}$ is approximately -$0.95$. This study provides an alternative to the complex essence model with a Lagrange multiplier and offers insights that can be utilized to better grasp the dynamics of dark energy.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel algorithm, combining the strengths of multi-criticality branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGAII), is proposed for solving such problems. The proposed approach leverages non-dominated sorting and hybrid surrogate models to efficiently tackle the multi-objective branch-and-bound methodology. In contrast to other hybrid algorithms, this approach avoids incorporating surrogate models at each iteration, thereby significantly reducing computational costs. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithm rivals or surpasses contemporary multi-objective optimization techniques, showcasing its efficiency and effectiveness in solving various non-linear programming problems.

The abstract argues that a connected Lie groupoid is equivalent to a linked manifold. 
The argument relies on the principle that the internal version of a Lie groupoid is integral complete. 
To support this claim, the paper proves that an internal Lie groupoid is integral complete if it satisfies a specific differential invariant condition known as homogeneous homotopy invariance. 
This property essentially means that the condition must be consistent across different differential structures. 
The argument that a connected Lie groupoid is internally linked relies on the principle of internal universality, which allows the construction of a specific differential map from the original Lie groupoid to a simple manifold.

The increasing quantity of data in biomedicine has posed significant sharing challenges due to confidentiality and presentation issues, thereby restricting the development of new treatments and discoveries. To address these obstacles, secure and user-friendly systems are required to safeguard sensitive information and present data in accessible formats, thereby promoting collaboration and research efficiency. To meet these demands, comprehensive online platforms and cyberinfrastructure gateways have been developed to provide standardized data services, tailored interfaces, and compensation for capacity limitations in individual institutions. These gateways offer centralized data access, advanced processing capabilities, and collaboration facilities, enabling research and analysis across multiple institutions. Furthermore, they empower data analysis and interpretation through applied tools and services, thereby facilitating discovery and management. To promote open-access research, these cyberinfrastructure gateways promote data sharing and reuse by providing user-friendly interfaces and processes to safeguard the privacy and security of sensitive information. Through the safe and effective distribution of sensitive information, researchers can utilize shared data to support multiple use cases, including data analysis, collaboration, and education. To ensure the secure sharing of biomedical data, adherence to leading standards and protocols is required to protect confidential information. To promote data sharing and reuse, tailored workflows and processes are provided to facilitate data deposition and withdrawal, as well as the annotation of metadata and supporting documentation. These cyberinfrastructure gateways empower researchers to analyze and interpret shared information through the provision of data analysis and visualization tools, data processing applications, and expert knowledge. Additionally, they facilitate data validation by offering verification and validation

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a given aspect within written text. A prominent challenge in this area stems from the complexity of natural language and diverse distribution of sentiment datasets. Our approach addresses this issue by incorporating supervised pre-training to capture subtle emotional information in text through the connection of emotional sensitivity to sentiment judgment. A contrastive pre-training framework, utilizing a bipartite matching method, is proposed to capture emotional information in text. Additionally, self-attention masking is designed to prevent information redundancy and enhance the model's robustness. Performance evaluations on standard datasets reveal that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art models.

To analyze mediation in case-control studies, we investigate a scenario where participants have undergone an intervention and some have been selected for the study based on their treatment outcome. A participant's likelihood of being selected depends on the intervention and an additional covariate. A binary mediator is also considered, with the assumption that it doesn't adversely affect participation, but its influence on the treatment outcome is allowed. A test is developed to determine whether the intervention's causal influence can be attributed to an underlying variable, and estimation methods are presented for this scenario. The methods involve using survey weights to estimate probabilities and variance, and robust standard error calculations are allowed for repeated measurements. The proposed methods are applied to a study on a treatment for lung disease, and the findings suggest that the treatment's causal influence can be attributed to specific symptoms.

This research delves into secure communication networks with a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) that encompasses multiple individual meta-surfaces, each connected to multiple single-antenna users, and is surrounded by an eavesdropper enabled by Inverse Stable Matching (ISM). The problem of maximizing the minimum secret information rate is initially addressed through a non-convex program that is divided into two separate convex programs using the Alternating Maximization (AM) method via Drop-Inequality and Approximate Message Passing (AMP). The resulting amp-inequality-based (AMPI) algorithm is shown to converge after a finite number of iterations. The AMPI approach is compared to amp-convex and ISM in numerical simulations, displaying superior convergence and performance.

We propose the Executive Function Model, a sophisticated cognitive framework for self-modulation and perception reshaping through the use of future knowledge for improved decision-making. This model utilizes a future knowledge buffer to store observations which are then used in conjunction with a future-oriented reasoning module to refine and improve current perceptions. This refined understanding is achieved through the purposeful sampling and relabeling of past experiences by the cognitive agent. In turn, this resampled understanding is integrated into the current perception, resulting in enhanced accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model by leveraging it to address the challenges inherent in the DeepMind Lab environment, specifically in scenarios where agents are tasked with sampling and exploring unfamiliar environments. Results from our experiments indicate that our model outperforms or complements existing state-of-the-art methods, offering improved efficiency and effectiveness in similar tasks.

The solar wind's kinetic energy flux can be utilized to determine the rate at which energy is transferred from the sun's atmosphere to the interplanetary medium. A pioneering mission, the Parker Solar Probe, has enabled scientists to measure this energy flux very close to the sun, a region typically characterized by strong magnetic fields and high temperatures. By analyzing data from two different instruments - a magnetometer and a thermal analyzer - researchers have found the average energy flux to be roughly 10^3 times the flux emitted from the sun's photosphere. Interestingly, measurements near a specific point, a minimum in the corona's magnetic field, were significantly lower than expected. Furthermore, proximity to the sun's energetic reaccelerated solar wind was associated with higher than average energy flux. Studies of the solar wind's behavior in these areas may provide valuable insights into the underlying processes governing mass transport and energy transformations in the very close solar heliosphere.

The classification of countable principal bundles with noncommutative C*-algebras as fiber remains an unsolved problem. To address this issue, previous research introduced the concept of an orientable G-C*-algebra, featuring a locally compact group G that acts on a noncommutative C*-algebra. Specifically, it has a directed family of subalgebras with compact spectra, and for any given G-action, a corresponding orientable G-C*-algebra can be constructed. Building upon this concept, we establish the classification of countable principal bundles with noncommutative C*-algebras as fiber, extending topological bundle classification results from G-space actions to G-C*-algebra actions.

We establish that for any infinite, countable ordinal $\gamma$, the existence of $2^{\aleph_0}$ strongly $\gamma$-preserving sequences of ultrafilters $U_x$ on $\mathcal{P}_{\aleph_0}^{3}x$ implies $x<_{\text{nd}}^*\mathfrak{u}$. This yields a direct result stating that if a sequence of ultrafilters $U_x$ on $\mathcal{P}_{\aleph_0}^{3}x$ is strongly preserving and the length sequence is less than $\aleph_1$, the nearly disjointness number $x<_{\text{nd}}}^*\mathfrak{u}$. Moreover, it is demonstrated that it is possible to create a model in which $\aleph_1<_{\text{nd}}}^*\mathfrak{u}<_{\text{nd}}}^*\aleph_1$. As $\aleph_1<_{\text{nd}}}^*\aleph_1$ is equivalent to the existence of $2^{\aleph_0}$ stationarily invariant ultrafilters on $\sigma$-ideals of natural numbers, it follows that it is possible to create a model in which $\aleph_1<_{\text{nd}}}^*\mathfrak{u}<_{\text{nd}}}^*\aleph_1

The basic principles of optomechanical systems are expanded by introducing quantum deformations. Two versions of deformed optomechanical systems are considered within the classical Michaelis theory, where one type features a cavity made of a quantum-deformed material and the other involves a cavity with a micromaser influenced by quantum deformations. In the deformed optomechanical system, both normal and Brillouin scattering regimes are examined, where a nonlinear coupling between light and mechanical states allows for spontaneous symmetry breaking. This breaking results in the emergence of two distinct eigenstates separated by an infinite potential wall, producing light speed variations. In the slow light regime, quantum enhancement due to quantum deformation is observed, where quantum statistical parameters exhibit a quantum-enhanced parametric amplification characteristic. This is consistent with the findings from deformed micromaser systems, where double peak structures are observed in the Wigner representation of the photon number. However, only a single peak is seen in the Wigner representation of the phonon number. Both of these systems possess the capability to exhibit quantum enhancement at the quantum level.

In the Two-Rotors model, introduced in IJMPD 20, 1950004, of the current series, Adversity mechanisms are explored that cause negative scissors modes in a scenario where R-parity violates local interparticle interactions. These modes, as evidenced by existing experiments, have absolute values in the particle space that are governed solely by positive ones. Correspondingly, to introduce negativity, an odd number of particles must be involved. Specifically, configurations with an odd number of particles can exhibit negative versions of the lowest R-parity modes, whereas those with even numbers of particles lead to positive versions. The model in question is grounded in the concept of two separate rotating entities formed by paired or unpaired particles. The possibility of unpaired particles corresponds to a positive or negative scissors mode, determined by the direction of R-parity. The model's advantage lies in its ability to explain both the prevalence of positive scissors modes and situations where R-parity violates local interactions, as is usually evidenced in neutrino experiments.

A novel numerical method is introduced that combines a cell-mean based approach and a deep neural network to solve partial differential equations with Neumann boundary conditions. This method is particularly well-suited for solving heat equations and hyperbolic partial differential equations due to its ability to handle non-uniform grids and direct approximations of spatial derivatives. This approach simplifies the traditional partial mass lumping technique, which can be computationally intensive, and is capable of handling a range of problem types without modification. Results for a heat equation and Burgers equation demonstrate the method's accuracy and efficiency, with the implementation for the Burgers equation also successfully reconstructed the exact solution of the shock formation problem at test stage.

The ALICE Detector will participate in LHC Run 3 (2019-2021) and Run 4 (2021-2025) in measuring proton-proton collisions and heavy-ion collisions at energies of 6.5 TeV and 14.5 TeV respectively. In addition to the detector, a dedicated upgrade centered on the CERN-EP division will enable the fulfillment of the project named LHC Upgrade-Physics with Heavy Ions (UPWHI). This will involve installing a gas-filled cell within the existing central barrel of the time projection chamber, enhancing particle identification through the incorporation of a large-size TPC featuring six separate gas layers and the integration of a state-of-the-art electron spectrometer equipped with a 50-layer silicon detector. This will pave the way for precise measurements of the quark-gluon plasma by analyzing key signatures such as the J/ψ-to-ψ production ratio in heavy-ion collisions, as well as for exploring the potential of the ALICE Detector in studying proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions at higher energies by analyzing the production of charmonia and open charm hadrons.

The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler regions, but also between forward and backward light cones. Our analysis focuses on the geometric phase that arises from the Holographic Quantum Error Correction Code applied to the light cone entanglement. This is connected to the energy of a quasiparticle located at the origin, and its momentum is directed towards the absolute future and past. This effect is overpowered by the standard Unruh effect for particles moving between the right and left Minkowski regions. However, the anomaly in the geometric phase, occurring when a particle crosses the timelike axis with low energy and momentum, can potentially be utilized for the timely detection of the Unruh effect. This detection method is more feasible than relying on the entanglement between the Rindler regions, mainly because it leverages a stationary phase pattern that allows for a much narrower probability distribution.

This study offers a 12-language dataset for identifying crisis incidents mentioned in news articles, along with the corresponding text excerpts where each event occurs. The dataset was created by combining news articles from multiple sources and applying supervised learning models for language detection and data extraction. The resulting dataset is vast, comprising over 39,000 labeled articles across 12 languages and nearly 5 million individual data points. The collection is accessible at https://github.com/point101/MEE-Dataset. The dataset was developed as an augmentation to existing evaluation methods for identifying crisis information, filling a long-standing gap in multilingual research. To demonstrate its usefulness, the authors propose new evaluation metrics and study the effects of linguistic variables and news source characteristics on crisis information extraction. This research was presented at the second BEA 2022 Conference.

This paper delves into the global structure of vector bundles on compact connected Riemannian manifolds, examining the vector bundles' topological and geometric properties. The research establishes a connection between the holomorphic Chern forms of a Hermitian vector bundle and its real characteristic forms, which leads to a global geometric inequality. The main outcomes of this investigation are the derivation of two key theorems: the Hardamard-type inequality for vector bundles with trace-bounded curvature and the fundamental theorem of Hermitian vector bundles.

The behavior of the Hardy probe on board the BeppoSAX satellite during observations of the high-mass X-ray binary Cyg X-1 in the hard state is studied. It is observed that the probe's detector is partially shaded by corona-like structures detected through the Fourier residuals of the hard state data. These formations appear and disappear in a manner correlated with the light curve of the soft variable background seen in the soft energy band. This correlation suggests that the probe's contamination comes from the growing intial stellar atmosphere of the companion star as the standard solar model predicts. This contamination is thought to be due to a hot, thin outflow from the stellar wind rather than an expanded corona. The level of the contaminating emission is estimated at 1-3% of the hard X-ray flux, although the authors rule out the outflow as a significant source of the observed hard X-ray emission in the hard state.

The Yang-Mills system combined with an ethereal term within the framework of the gauge theory of bivectors is explored, particularly in a physical context at finite temperature. By using the zeta function regularization method, the vacuum energy density of the system is determined, yielding a known result. Furthermore, thermal corrections to the mass of vector bosons are calculated and intriguingly, their masses behave in an non-generate manner, implying a profound implication for a simulated ether within the standard model. The thermodynamic properties of the system are also investigated through the formation of an extended bag energy density at finite temperature.

Researchers in natural language have made significant breakthroughs in using pairs of models, such as sequence models and linear models, to analyze sentence structures. However, these models typically examine sentences in isolation and focus primarily on identifying the sentence's main meaning. By itself, this approach can only achieve a shallow understanding of the sentence, limiting its ability to capture complex relationships within the text. To address this issue, a new method for interpreting sentences has been developed, focusing on both the syntax and meaning by incorporating two different types of linear models into a single, unified model. This new model, known as the Joint Universal Syntactic and Meaning Parsing model, is designed to accurately predict the sentence's syntactic structure and meaning using only the sentence as input, and has been successfully trained using a combination of supervised learning techniques and special devices. Evaluations of this model have shown substantial improvements in its ability to analyze sentence meanings when compared to earlier approaches.

The merger of two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole leads to the formation of a massive, gravitationally unstable remnant that rapidly releases neutrinos. These neutrinos heat up and drive mass ejection from the merger site. Previous theoretical research employing 1.5-dimensional simulations has proposed that a disk forms following the merger and plays a significant role in driving mass ejecta. In this study, we have conducted 2-dimensional simulations of merger sites in regions outside the black hole to explore the structure of the accretion disk and any associated outflows. We have found that both magnetic fields and neutrinos contribute to the disk's shape and any formed jets or winds. We have also observed that magnetic fields reduce the efficiency of neutrino-driven winds and conversely, jets driven by the merger itself, increase the efficiency of neutrino-driven winds. These hybrid jets contain both matter ejected from the merger site and neutrino-driven winds, are less dense than previously estimated, and travel farther than initially thought. Moreover, we have discovered that magnetic fields reduce the mass ejecta produced by the merger, whereas neutrino-driven winds increase in efficiency with the accretion disk's temperature. This contrasts with previous findings by M. R. M. Borges (2017), which demonstrated that a disk forms following the merger and identified potential cosmic ray influences on the accretion disk. In this study, we have analyzed the effect of postmerger evolution on the accretion disk and

We conducted research on extremely massive galaxies from the Very Massive Galaxy Database, which was created using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis, the first to extensively examine tidal features for such galaxies, is based on early-type galaxies weighing more than 11 billion solar masses and spanning a 140 million light-year section of the galaxy universe. Through a statistical approach, we discovered that tidal features' brightness relative to the parent galaxy's is higher for smaller galaxies and less massive tidal features. Our findings support the idea that galaxies of various sizes have similar internal structures. Our study shows a relatively low rate of tidal interactions for massive galaxies, which is about 2-3 times larger than the rate of spiral galaxies. This suggests that dense tidal features may be less common in massive galaxies, which could be due to a larger number of interactions where one galaxy remains largely unchanged. Our research indicates that interactions with a 30% chance of significant impact are common among spiral galaxies, but this probability is lower for galaxies that are unusually massive.

The distinctive signature of bipolar outflows in AGN and Young Stellar Objects has long fascinated astronomers. A novel theory of gravity, the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation, is applied to replicate the patterns observed in these objects. According to this theory, gravitational repulsion occurs when the gradient of gravitation is stronger than the gravitational force itself, a phenomenon that can occur in spherically asymmetric environments. By setting specific boundary conditions and assuming radial symmetry, the necessary conditions for gravitational repulsion to occur in bipolar outflows are derived. Using a simplified cosmological case as an example, the theory demonstrates that repulsive forces can arise near the equatorial plane, contrasting with the traditional concept of gravitational attraction. A computational model of an accretion disk is also used to show that the patterns observed in bipolar outflows can be modeled using the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation.

We have gathered a vast dataset of lower-than-threshold Fast Radio Burst (FRB) candidates from radio telescopes, totaling nearly 202,000 entries. Following thorough analysis, we established 121 confirmed FRBs and 28 likely FRBs, accounting for roughly 6% of original detections with significant period derivatives. Furthermore, our findings optically quiet the FRB sourcecount, confirming that about half of lower-than-threshold FRBs are expected to exhibit significant period derivatives and indicating a derivation-hosting population largely consisting of neutron star magnetospheres. In the process of identifying the source population, we established a dataset with nearly 3,000 FRBs that can be used, such as in our analysis of the FRB 200428's 87-inch optical counterpart, to explore light curve and polarization correlations. Subsequently, we utilized this dataset to derive optical emission upper bounds for FRBs, namely a 1 sigma flux limit of 8.0 sigma 10^-9 flux limit for simultaneous emission and a 1 sigma flux limit of 6.5 sigma 10^-4 flux limit for delayed emission a year following the event, both far surpassing the FRB 200428's flux limit of  sigma  10^-3.

Advancements in high-power laser technology are highly dependent on the effective execution of three critical phases: system conceptualization, improvement, and reverse engineering. Each phase necessitates distinct skills sets, yet they share common goals such as achieving high average and pulse power, maintaining narrow spectral and temporal profiles, and ensuring high beam quality and precision. Effective application of computational models plays a vital role in all three phases, which we will discuss in detail. Furthermore, we examine the cutting-edge laser systems created by the NLHPLB network, highlighting the substantial progress the community has made in high-power physics and technology over recent decades.

Fine-tuning large language models using reinforcement learning significantly
enhances their performance across various text generation tasks.  Visual inputs,
however, have not been fully utilized in previous studies, with few experiments
featuring tasks that require processing visual data to produce meaningful text.
We are the first to explore visual inputs in text generation by controlling LLMs
with visual cues, demonstrating that visual information is crucial in tasks
such as describing images, creating dialogue, and crafting descriptions based on
emotions expressed through gestures.  We developed a generic framework that
integrates visual inputs with language models to produce text and showed that
visual features significantly improve the quality of generated text according
to human evaluations and quantitative metrics.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The proposed method accelerates the transaction verification process in comparison to the combined Monero-EOS system.
Our modifications encompass the majority of RingCT features, including variable-length outputs, sub-commissions, and a distributed hash table-based transaction identifier system.
The Delegated RingCT scheme comprises six core components: a public key cipher, a secret key cipher, a unique identifier generator, a stealth address generator, a transaction format transformer, and a commission calculator.
We utilize the generative approach for creating unique identifiers and stealth addresses in order to expedite transaction creation.
The research also integrates code snippets in multiple languages to facilitate easier understanding of the protocol.

A key feature of a bright sunshine beamline is its large, roughly circular format, making it an ideal choice for transmitting intense light to multiple areas simultaneously. Researchers can take advantage of this characteristic through brightness scanning, which involves moving the circular beam across a sensor to reveal its spatial intensity profile. This technique offers highly accurate means of measuring the transverse beam size and thus provides vital information for optimizing a light source's performance. In addition to its applications in system diagnostics, brightness scanning can also be used to investigate the light source's fundamental characteristics, such as its time and spatial stability. This paper outlines a basic method for implementing brightness scanning and discusses its capabilities and potential limitations.

Since the 1960s, collaborative modeling has encompassed various forms of model development where multiple disciplines come together to create a cohesive approach and meta-disciplines have played a crucial role in this process. Recently, the emergence of computational power has given rise to significant advancements in model-based design, empowering engineers to find innovative solutions to complex problems through advanced modeling techniques. In the fields of engineering and research, there is often a disconnect where researchers from different backgrounds cannot find each other due to varying priorities and expertise, despite their shared goals. In an effort to address this issue, this work provides a range of tools and concepts designed to facilitate collaborative modeling across various domains, incorporating methodologies from the systematic development of models and models with intrinsic uncertainties. Through the use of probabilistic uncertainty quantification, this work ensures that model uncertainties are accurately represented in order to inform decision-making. Additionally, this work incorporates a variety of computational models that have shown to be effective in numerous applications and provides a collection of model-driven methods for analyzing and interpreting results. By combining these tools, concepts, and models, this work aspires to empower interdisciplinary collaboration and facilitate problem-solving in a variety of real-world scenarios.

This research presents observations of specific decay types of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ state, namely $\Upsilon(10753) \to \Upsilon(2S) \pi^+ \pi^- $ and $\Upsilon(10753) \to \Upsilon(1S) \pi^+ \pi^- $ with estimated branching fractions of $ (2.15 \pm 0.19 \pm 0.14) \times 10^{-2} $ and $(1.72 \pm 0.17 \pm 0.12) \times 10^{-3}$, respectively. The studies were carried out using Belle II data stemming from $4-2019 $ run. Furthermore, vertical bars minus signs and parentheses containing estimated CMS/WA105 charmonium branching fractions are applied. Additionally, horizontal ellipses indicate additional research needed.

This method efficiently trains neural networks that use the integer weights found in quantized neural networks by applying a randomized, iterative process that adjusts parameter ranges during optimization. Initially, the method sets very wide intervals around each integer weight, allowing stochastic gradient descent to take large steps while minimizing gradient computation. With each iteration, the algorithm gradually narrows the intervals, converting the problem into a series of regular optimization tasks within increasingly narrow range intervals by the next iteration. This approach guarantees convergence to a local optimum. Our experiments with AskewSGD on quantized neural networks demonstrate significant speedup over traditional SGD and randomized smoothing methods on CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets, with some cases training 6 times faster while achieving comparable accuracy. All source code is available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/pari4e/AskewSGD.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible structures to accomplish tasks that traditional robots struggle with. This joint research project offers unique opportunities for experimentation, however, due to its high degree of flexibility, it is necessary to account for the movement of multiple endpoints when implementing motion planning, greatly increasing the computational demands. As a result, the project requires innovative, efficient, and adaptable control systems that utilize feedback from various sensors. This study aims to provide an in-depth review of the current state in research related to controlling continuum robots and to identify areas for further improvement and potential application in the near future.

The Jacobi group $G^J_2(\mathbb{R})$ - specifically its semi-direct product of ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ with $H_1$ - does not form a nilpotent group. This contradicts a previous finding by I. S. Ulger, which was recently brought to my attention.

Verifying facts through language is an integral part of how we typically converse, as humans naturally seek confirmation or denial of existing claims. Current NLP solutions for fact verification, which involve analyzing natural language to confirm or deny a statement's accuracy, are still limited in their capacity to handle intricate facts. Our proposed solution tackles this problem by leveraging the functionality of fact verification to facilitate the breaking down of intricate facts into more manageable forms, thereby enabling the verification of novel combinations of information. Two key aspects that NLP research still needs to improve on include handling complex factual expressions and integrating verified facts in a way that allows them to contribute meaningfully to future fact verification tasks. Our method involves employing a multi-step approach that uses both language models and knowledge graphs to facilitate fact verification. The DisFactVer system, which executes this approach, was tested and validated in a competition organized by the Fact Verification Shared Task of the 2022 NLP4SLU Challenge.

By conditioning a generative adversarial network with hidden space, the produced images not only match the target data distribution more closely, but also contain information about the input to the network. This is similar to how conditional GANs work, but our approach differs in that it doesn't rely on additional condition input. Additionally, the input to the network can be images, words, or any other form of data. Our method involves modifying the latent space to create a continuous relationship between the input and generated images. Experimental results demonstrate that the necessity for conditional GANs in visual conditional generation could be questioned. This research builds on a 2018 paper by Radford et al. and demonstrates that the latent space can act as a condition for generative adversarial networks.

To choose the next sample in Nested Sampling, a Step Selector must be used,
deciding which candidate samples to advance and which to choose anew. The choice
of Step Selector greatly affects the performance of Nested Sampling analyses,
with different methods achieving very different computation times for the same
posterior approximations. This study investigates four Step Selectors: 
    1. A method developed by Vickers-Church (2016),
    2. A random candidate approach,
    3. A candidate based on the largest log-likelihood,
    4. An importance weighted approach, resampling from a dynamic
    importance distribution that places more weight on candidates with
    higher observed posterior densities. The proposed importance
    distribution aims to achieve a more efficient exploration of the
    posterior. The algorithms can be studied using a Python package,
    nsspy, publicly available on GitHub.

In the distance labeling problem for graph G, a label t(v) is assigned to each node v, indicating the shortest distance from v to all other nodes in the graph. For graphs with n nodes, optimal distance labels have a size of O(n, D, ϵ) and can handle node failures by withstanding Ω((n/k) 2/3) failed nodes on average, where k being the number of removed nodes. For most practical graphs that are sparse with a fixed constant degree, (n, D, ϵ) is essentially equal to the optimal distance ordering, which is O(log n). Our main finding is that, in order to improve the resilience of distance labeling in graphs that are weakly connected with (n, D, ϵ) being equal to O(log n), the distance ordering needs to assign labels that are at most poly(log n) larger than the actual shortest distance from a failed node to all other nodes in the graph. Furthermore, for graphs with a fixed constant hop-diameter to any subset of m vertices, (n, D, ϵ) is equal to O(log n), and our characterization is the first to limit the influence of removed nodes in the 2-hop distance closure of the graph. Moreover, for most practical graphs that are sparse with a fixed constant degree, the size of the optimal distance ordering in the 2-hop closure of the graph is equal to O(log n). In this theoretical study, we explore the dynamic correlations of two bosons within a discrete Bose-Hubbard model that is subject to dissipative processes and an external driving force. Our findings, particularly in the time-domain, show how the effects of dissipation and non-conservation of particle number manifest in observed patterns. Furthermore, the interplay between these processes is analyzed through comparisons with the undriven system in both time and frequency domains, with a focus on the discrete nature of the system.

We present a significant improvement to de Giorgi's theorem in the context of partial differential equations with coefficients drawn from the Sobolev space $W^{1,p}$. Our study specifically examines elliptic operators in divergence form that take values in the $L^2$ space. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of these operators as linear operators within the $L^2$ space.

To identify invalid or suspicious test data, out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is crucial for utilizing machine learning predictions with confidence in data validity. Recent studies on Gaussian process (GP) based OOD detection have achieved impressive results. Nevertheless, these GPGP methods have suffered from limited interpretability and performance issues when dealing with large-scale problems. In our research, we introduce a novel, computationally efficient approach to GP-based OOD detection that incorporates the benefits of distributional Gaussian processes (DGP) and hierarchical clustering. By utilizing the DGP's posterior distribution, our technique provides enhanced interpretability and improves the scalability of GPGP methods for large-scale problems in theoretical settings. Our empirical analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in various real-world applications compared to existing GPGP methods and other competing techniques.

Many-body quantum systems are difficult to study due to the limited access to precise measurements of large numbers of particles at a time. However, an artificially created excitation, known as a Quasi-Degenerate Autler-Townes Line (QDATL), can serve as a precise pointer to the dynamics of such systems. This study shows that applying a certain type of excitation, which remains stable despite repeated interactions with an external environment, to an optical lattice and driving it with a specific type of laser light can lead to a condensation of bosonic particles into a narrow part of the energy spectrum around this stable state. This outcome is attributed to persistent heating caused by weak interactions with a surrounding bath at very low temperatures. This process is predicted to result in a range of interesting phenomena, including a blockage to heat transport and the emergence of correlated entanglement between particles. This research offers a practical method to achieve strong entanglement of bosonic atoms with minimal losses in an optical lattice.

The primary objective of this research is to demonstrate the existence of a smooth solution for the Monge--Amp\`ere equation on a strictly convex domain with a nonempty bounded interior, given that the right-hand side of the equation is smooth and bounded and meets certain geometric constraints. This solution is also known to be uniformly H\"older continuous. Previous studies by Bir\"okin and Chtioui in 1999, along with Caffarelli in 2005, had established the smoothness of such solutions, although they did not provide estimates for their norms in a space of smooth functions. In contrast, our findings are analogous to those achieved by Gilbaut and Trudinger in 2004 with their uniform H\"older estimate for the gradient of solutions to the Monge--Amp\`ere equation with a bounded right-hand side. Additionally, our method of proof relies on an enhanced version of the Alexandrov maximum principle, applied to the viscosity solutions of an associated upper semi-continuous perturbation equation.

Counting the recurrence of periodic beeps can accurately determine time, and by using different frequencies, multiple clocks can sync up when their frequencies match a common multiple time cycle. But what about optical clocks that don't give regular beeps? We've developed a mathematical tool to find a consistent time-keeping pattern in these types of optical clocks by using their measurement data to calculate a time variable. Our method starts by breaking down the data into fixed-length time segments and calculating how often they occur. Next, it connects nearby segment frequencies to create a coherent timeline. Our research found that two distinct types of optical clocks, Rubidium and Ytterbium, exhibit different frequency patterns when plotted against time, and these patterns match the expected behavior based on how they naturally operate.

This research centers on an optimized service delivery model for real-time applications that integrate fog computing to enhance SDN's agility and adaptability. The proposed service delivery model addresses two key challenges faced by network administrators: fault prevention through predictive maintenance and real-time fault detection followed by rapid service restoration. To tackle these challenges, the research develops an optimization framework for effective resource management in fog-supported SDN networks. The framework's objective is to prevent failures, minimize service disruption duration, and reduce network operational costs while considering factors such as energy efficiency and adherence to quality-of-service requirements. The optimization framework algorithms operate at the application, fog, and network levels, utilizing specific models tailored to each entity to achieve optimized service delivery. The research evaluates the proposed framework through simulations, achieving improved results in terms of fault detection frequency, service disruption duration, and energy consumption with the current implementation.

Researchers have been experimenting with loss functions beyond the default mean squared error to improve the performance of deep networks, but the success of these alternatives isn't always due to the expected reason - some methods work by reducing the system's complexity, for example through a consistent prediction output. To shed more light on this, a new method called gradient surgery was developed to analyze the effects of various loss functions on deep networks. Gradient surgery involves modifying the gradient flow in a network according to different loss functions, which reveals significant differences in the behaviour of loss functions. The results show that loss functions can improve performance by altering the system's training resistance, changing the way the network's weights evolve over time and influencing the way the network makes predictions.

In holographic tensor networks, reducing entropy quickly is crucial for creating useful approximations.  Research has shown that minimizing entropy should prioritize areas of high interaction, but this often conflicts with the requirement for a one-way causal timeline.  High-entropy regions, where entropy grows rapidly, are particularly problematic.  Existing methods for managing this issue, such as minimizing entanglement, often fail to address these regions or can become time-consuming to calculate.  As an alternative, researchers presented the Hyper-Invariant Matrix Product State (iMPS) algorithm, which can efficiently create holographic tensor networks with power-law dependencies by prioritizing entropy growth rather than reduction.  This algorithm has been expanded to apply to higher-dimensional networks, now known as Hyper-Invariant Multiscale Product Codes (iMPC) and hyper-invariant iMPC algorithms.  These new approaches can provide significant improvements in computational efficiency and runtime.  In practical terms, researchers created a complex model of a symmetry-breaking phase transition and demonstrated that the hyper-invariant code could capture both the area where the transition happens and the properties of the system's spectrum, all while efficiently managing computational resources.  Additionally, the hyper-invariant code was found to power a quantum algorithm that identifies certain types of disorder more effectively than current algorithms.  As such, the hyper-invariant code may offer a practical approach to modeling complex systems and deriving useful insights from their behavior.

This study presents the results of an investigation regarding the spacing between magnetic filaments at the heart of the Milky Way. Initially, a graph illustrating the density of these magnetic structures in relation to their size is shown. The same research earlier examined the distribution of filament widths and this current segment focuses on the inter filamentary distance. The results show that large magnetic filaments are separated by an average distance that is 2 times the width of these wide filaments. The space between smaller magnetic structures, however, appears to be randomly distributed in relation to their width. The findings suggest that broad magnetic filaments such as those seen along magnetic equators are not independent entities but rather part of an interconnected network while smaller magnetic structures may take on independent existence at a later stage. Possible explanations for this phenomenon exist. It is also hypothesized that magnetic structures may be influenced by a hierarchical organization pattern which can be further validated through statistical analysis.

A proposed method for distributedly optimizing conservation voltage reduction (CVR) across distributed networks demonstrates the potential for significant energy savings without necessitating any modifications to existing equipment. The method is built on an iterative model that asymptotically converges towards the optimal solution by leveraging distributed optimization algorithms such as the distributed subgradient method. To ensure model accuracy, self-reporting of node voltage and current is required from smart devices, making it suitable for deployment on contemporary smart grids. The method's reliability and effectiveness are substantiated through application to actual distribution networks in the United States. The results reveal that through optimal tuning of the tuning parameter $\alpha$, energy savings of up to 5.42% can be achieved with minimal voltage variations at end-use nodes. With this approach, the required iterations to achieve optimal results is demonstrated to be directly correlated with $\alpha$. The method's adaptability is also illustrated through its application to systems of varying sizes.

This research investigates two related problems, delayed advisor recommendations and delayed arms of a multi-arm bandits. We develop a criterion for determining when minor delays in reception or processing of information will not hinder achieving nearly optimal results within a constant factor, considering scenarios characterized by non-stochastic environments. Our investigation employs a model with uniformly distributed, potentially significant delays to examine the impact of receipt of advice or arm selection. This models real-world situations such as medical diagnosis guided by health professionals or various multi-arm bandit scenarios with differently long setup or exploration phases. Our findings also address situations with a small number of delayed arms, bringing the problem closer to a setting where delayed arms are known in advance, for which we establish tight bounds on the performance loss. Additionally, we present a general method allowing to sample delayed arms at a rate dictated by their relative lengths or differences in lengths. We apply this approach to derive improved results for specific scenarios: (i) cases with delayed arms where distribution of their lengths is known in advance, (ii) settings where number of delayed arms is known in advance and they have uniformly distributed lengths, (iii) general conditions under which we achieve nearly optimal results within a constant factor, (iv) scenarios characterized by adversarial actions.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can produce accurate responses but often lack a human touch. To fix this, researchers have been exploring ways to incorporate natural language patterns and nuances into these systems. To tackle this challenge, we developed LEATHER, a theoretical framework for improving text generation. By building on existing theories, including n-gram models and decision-making processes, LEATHER creates a common language for creating new dialogue systems and enables existing models to incorporate new knowledge. We demonstrated the effectiveness of LEATHER by applying it to various successful dialogue systems and saw significant improvements in their output. Specifically, we updated a proven system, called GoalCode, using LEATHER and saw a 40% increase in its similarity to human-written dialogue. Additionally, we updated another system, Dialecto2, using LEATHER and saw a 13% improvement in its accuracy in producing coherent text.

Following World War II, scientists made remarkable advancements in understanding the strong force described by Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), with the field growing exponentially. Initially, QCD was tested through its predictions for deep-inelastic scattering and jet production at high-energy collisions, confirming that the strong force is a fundamental aspect of nature. In the 1970s, scientists in the field of lattice QCD worked to establish that the force has a underlying order, proving that quarks and gluons are not independent but rather part of an underlying massless theory. This work laid the groundwork for the formation of the American Physical Society's top physics journal, Physical Review Letters. Today, scientists continue to explore QCD under conditions far from that which is normally observed in nature, namely high temperatures and dense matter. This article provides an update on their latest achievements.

As the offshore wind-energy sector expands rapidly, designers of massive, multi-million-dollar offshore wind turbines need more efficient method to evaluate and optimize their designs for minimal stress under unpredictable loading conditions, covering various weather scenarios like wind, waves, and sea currents. In this research, a sophisticated statistical tool, utilizing two interconnected Gaussian processes, is developed to accurately simulate the complex interactions between stress and input parameters for individual tubular components of an offshore wind turbine. The approach incorporates practical limitations on stress, a crucial aspect often neglected in existing statistical models, by utilizing, partitioning the stress-stress curve into different sections with unique stress potentials and introducing correlated noise among Gaussian processes through a statistical transformation and the "leave-many-out" cross-validation technique for predicting stress under unfamiliar conditions. The proposed model significantly outperforms existing statistical methods in predicting stress for new scenarios and simulating stress distributions across various weather conditions. The research involves a collaboration with Irwind, an industry leader that provides software for designing and analyzing complex structures, including offshore wind turbines.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Natural disasters like the 2020 Izmir earthquake, which resulted in significant losses and 110 lives lost, highlights the importance of rapid crisis information dissemination. Social media platforms like Twitter can facilitate rapid information dissemination but include a substantial amount of irrelevant, low-quality, and noisy content that hinders critical information retrieval during crises. This study examines Twitter data related to the Izmir earthquake, focusing on developing a web scraping method that collects and filters relevant content efficiently. By employing specific keywords related to the earthquake, our method successfully scraped over 750k tweets, yielding excellent results with improved precision and accuracy due to the incorporation of BERT-based noise types classification and content filtering techniques that utilize decision clustering and labeled data annotation. The final dataset after filtering contained 94,550 tweets, yielding outstanding results in classification, with our proposed model achieving 97.58% accuracy, accompanied by high recall and precision values of 0.9691 and 0.9969, respectively, indicating the method's potential applicability to future cases.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all non-identity elements of G's quotients by nilpotency correspond to positive powers of a single generator, for example, the group's nilpotent quotients have a presentation of $\mathbb{Z} \wr \mathbb{Z}$, for any n greater than or equal to $2$. In this study, we determine the $R_\infty$ property in the nilpotent quotients of the generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups for any n greater than or equal to $2$. Specifically, we prove that these nilpotent quotients possess the $R_\infty$ property if and only if they have a nilpotent rank less than or equal to $3$. Additionally, we find that a nilpotent quotient of the generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar group has the $R_\infty$ property if and only if it is isomorphic to either $\mathbb{Z} \wr_{n-1} \mathbbZ$ or $\mathbbZ_{n-1} \wr \mathbbZ$, for any n greater than or equal to $4$.

A novel framework is introduced for handling time-resolved data in experiments with substantial temporal dimensions. This new approach leverages an efficient algorithm to perform optimization-based inversion, where simulations are conducted using a trajectory model that encompasses critical factors such as parameters, geometry, and boundary conditions. To ensure accuracy, high-resolution grids are adopted in time and space, facilitating precise trajectory simulation. This method's main strength lies in its ability to efficiently process time-resolved data with high temporal resolution, approximately one trillion times faster than real time. Furthermore, this technique effectively handles complex data such as those involving fluid dynamics and reaction kinetics by integrating multiple observation operators. Additionally, this method's capacity to handle various data types is demonstrated through a range of applications, including the analysis of experimental data obtained from molecular physics, fluid dynamics, and reaction kinetics.

Current advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles mostly rely on high-resolution RGB cameras for decision-making, with the majority of available training data sourced from structured, top-down perspectives. However, real-world driving predominantly involves looking downwards towards the road due to its lower luminance and more predictable features. The Road Above Eye-Level (RAEL) dataset, though providing an alternative view point, still falls short in replicating real-world driving scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present a new naturalistic driving dataset called SceNDD, which is unique in capturing the dynamic nature of driving environments. The dataset is derived from around 24 hours of recorded traffic footage from a front-facing camera positioned at eye-level during various driving situations, ranging from urban to rural environments. To evaluate its usefulness, we conducted multiple baseline experiments using top-performing road segmentation models and found that the models performed significantly better when trained on our SceNDD dataset, as compared to existing datasets such as the Urban Road Dataset and RAEL. The annotated SceNDD dataset, including automatic road segmentation, is available for free at https://github.com/5force/SceNDD.

This article extends Reflected Entropy, initially explored in arXiv:2006.14933, to conformal field theories at boundaries/interfaces through the application of conformal field theory's commutator technique and universal correlation functions' expansion. As a result, relevant boundary/integral reflection currents are identified, and their connection to relevant currents established in relevant conformal field theories. This advancement allows for entropy calculation in relevant events in relevant conformal field theories, specifically in events involving multiple relevant boundaries, resulting in the annotated outcomes.

Our work involves a major improvement to the hardware-assisted Rank Insensitivity (HARIS) method, which originally relies on the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) for effective Rank Insensitivity Factor (RIF) design. However, due to the inherent characteristics of ELM, its convergence can be quite slow. To resolve this, we've developed a Majorization-Minimization (MM) approach to reformulate the original nonlinear ELM problem into a series of convex optimization tasks, ensuring computational efficiency. Our novel MM-based ELM will serve as the core solver in HARIS and is further refined by incorporating the impacts of limited cyclic prefix and hardware imperfections into the HARIS criterion. Ultimately, HarIS aims to achieve optimal RIS reflection patterns that minimize out-of-frame power, while considering these extrinsic factors, thus yielding superior performance compared to existing schemes in various scenarios, including cases with 64 QAM signals and high percentage ratios of cyclic prefix limitations and hardware imperfections.

The integral variation theorem is a confirmed principle, however its standalone measurement counterpart remains unproven. Theoretical findings suggest that under specific non-projective measurement conditions, the theorem may hold true, and this concept is currently being experimentally explored. Our study has a key implication: even when measurements fail to project onto a particular subspace, the theorem still applies. This knowledge has significant implications for the advancement of the quantum sense of sight technology.

We're developing a theory of deformations for G2instantons by combining the deformation theory of G2instantons with that of nearly G2 manifolds. The resulting theorem shows that if a nearly G2 manifold has a vector field that significantly affects the G2 structure, almost preserving the primitive 7-form, the resulting deformation space will be equivalent to the space of Killing G2instantons on the manifold. This applies to manifolds with a hypersurface of this nature, and includes manifolds such as C-Dubrode transformations of hyperkähler manifolds. This type of deformation is an essential aspect of a broader theory of deformations for nearly G2 geometries initially developed by the authors.

The global spread of the novel Coronavirus has led to the implementation of various measures to curb its progression, including the adoption of national contact tracing programs. To manage the pandemic more effectively, the use of Mobile apps has become a widely considered approach. While contact tracing apps aim to protect public health, they also pose significant risks to users' privacy. The emergence of widespread COVID-19 infections has prompted governments to devise new correlation-based contact tracing methods, further emphasizing the need for private contact tracing systems. Our analysis focuses on the security and privacy aspects of contact tracing apps, specifically evaluating the susceptibility of the Coronavirus-SUS Centralised model to server-based attacks. The model's server plays a crucial role in processing and storing users' data, yet its vulnerability to potential security breaches has not been extensively explored. Our investigation aims to identify and assess the risks associated with the server, as well as propose countermeasures to mitigate any security compromise of user data.

Researchers are working to develop quantum versions of neural networks that can process data in a quantum format. In physics, studies indicate that both classical and quantum systems can process data, with the latter requiring a defined number of qubits based on logarithmic scales. In biology, neural information is understood to be a combination of chemical and electrical signals, with the latter occurring only in specific types of cells. Studies in the field have primarily focused on processing capacity rather than the actual data itself. Our work involves analyzing a particular type of neural data found in the brain, specifically in dolphins, as part of a broader project involving data analysis in different systems. In this study, we compare the data in terms of its classical and quantum processing capabilities using Shannon entropy and q-information entropy metrics. To determine the quantum processing requirements for the dolphin data, we apply a particular transformation. Our findings demonstrate that the data has the capacity to process both classical and quantum information, with the quantum version necessitating approximately 36 qubits.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 functions into C code and verifying the correctness of the generated code using proof obligations within ACL2. A a subset of C is embedded in ACL2 as a language, allowing for the direct compilation of C expressions into ACL2 expressions. The tool uses a C-to-ACL2 shallow embedding to generate these proof obligations, allowing for the identification of correct C code implementations. The tool creates a C function equivalent in behavior to an ACL2 function, producing a set of ACL2 hypotheses to validate its correctness. The tool creates C code for a subset of ACL2 functions with basic data types, including recursive and non-recursive functions. Furthermore, the tool can translate ACL2 functions that utilize structs to C code incorporating structs. The tool produces a set of C code and corresponding ACL2 hypotheses for each input ACL2 function. The tool generates the C code based on the specified shallow embedded subset of the C language within ACL2. The tool outputs the generated C code along with the produced ACL2 hypotheses in a format compatible with the ACL2 proof producer, ACL2P. The tool allows users to specify how the C code and ACL2 hypotheses are displayed. The tool can operate in two modes: a mode that produces ACL2 hypotheses for C code and a mode that optimizes the C code while generating the corresponding ACL2 hypotheses. The tool creates C code for a subset of ACL2 functions with basic data types in both its single-pass and optimization modes

A notable phenomenon known as the "fluting effect" or Floricóvich fluctuation phenomenon is observed in asteroid families, causing variations in their residual infrared brightness. These variations reach their peak when an asteroid's size corresponds to its distance from the Sun, typically within a specific, relatively narrow range. A distinct "fluting effect" is observed in certain C-type asteroid families, whereas others exhibit different behaviors. A study conducted using high-resolution taxonomic data from the Three-Color Band Model and the Water Bond Albedo Parameter found that 16 families demonstrate the "fluting effect," with two being C-type families, (39991) Iochroma, and (11170) Highwater. By analyzing the water absorption bands in Iochroma, this study found evidence supporting the "fluting effect" in C-type families, confirming previous observations and understanding the phenomenon better. With its high spectral resolution, this analysis provided precise ground-state absorption frequencies and a degree of level energy states, offering new knowledge that can be applied to other C-type families and Cgyra, correcting Water Bond Albedo Parameter errors in Iochroma and Highwater, and enabling the accurate detection of the "fluting effect" in Iochroma. A comparison of Iochroma's water absorption intensity to other C-type families revealed that its water content is relatively low, approximately 0.32 weight %.
