Overcoming the class imbalance issue in text classification can be achieved through various oversampling techniques. The enhancement of minority class instances can be carried out using different methods such as word addition, part-of-speech replacement, back-translation, and generating synthetic texts. A notable technique is oversampling through word addition (OWA), which enhances the accuracy of classification by increasing the representation of underrepresented classes. Another method is the application of a synthetic text generator (STG), which directly produces textual examples to counterbalance the imbalance by creating new samples specifically for minority classes. Prior studies have been conducted to investigate the word-level class imbalance issue; however, research on text-level oversampling for class imbalance remains scarce. Therefore, this research aims to evaluate the effectiveness of oversampling methods in improving the classification of underrepresented classes in text classification tasks, with a focus on comparing the performance of recent synthetic text generators (STGs) against existing word-level oversampling techniques (including OWA) using word embeddings. The findings show that using synthetic texts, generated with an STG equipped with a rotary system for point-to-point translation, leverages contextual information to produce high-quality texts that lead to improved accuracy in classification tasks, with benefits particularly apparent in scenarios where the dataset is small but contains many classes.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between news coverage, COVID-19 cases and deaths, and audience engagement. It aims to fill a gap in research on COVID topics by utilizing real-time, community-specific data. The results reveal that more aggressive reporting of government responses and public adherence to health measures are associated with higher COVID case and death rates. Conversely, cases and deaths are inversely related to audience attention, implying that people are drawn to areas with lower infections. Furthermore, audiences in areas with higher government involvement and public compliance tend to be more engaged. Smith-Molina et al.'s categorization of news topics based on coverage and audience response is expanded to include new categories and subtopics, reflecting a broader public agenda. Policymakers and public health officials are advised on strategies to effectively manage the pandemic by influencing community attitudes toward government interventions and public behavior. Additionally, the study provides real-time, data-driven insights into audience perceptions of local news topics, contributing to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between COVID coverage, community attitudes, case and death rates, and audience behavior.

The Fast Multipole Method, a primary algorithm in real-time physics simulations, efficiently calculates the interactions between numerous bodies in space by reducing the complexity of higher-order mathematical representations when distant from one another. This technique has a widespread presence in physics simulations, particularly in scenarios involving collisions between many particles, where preserving accurate angular momentum calculations is crucial. Research has highlighted a long-standing issue with the Fast Multipole Method where the angular momentum component calculations become inaccurate as the bodies transition from higher-order to lower-order representations, ultimately affecting consensus metrics and accuracy. This paper addresses the inconsistency by implementing a novel verification framework designed to preserve angular momentum during translation, rotation, and interaction applications of the Fast Multiple Method. The proposed framework also accommodates multiple forms of representation, such as spherical harmonics and vector harmonics, as well as varying types of matrices used in intermediate computations. The verification framework involves evaluating and optimizing the conservation of angular momentum in multiple scenarios, including a 2D test case, a 3D test case, and two additional 3D test cases involving collisions of multiple particles. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in ensuring accurate angular momentum conservation across various scenarios.

Numerical calculations have been conducted for the $Q^2$ range from 0.1 to 1.0 GeV$^2$ using lattice QCD results for the non-perturbative target proton structure functions, specifically $\mathbb{G}^M_{1}$ and $\mathbb{G}^M_{5}$, to compute the polarization transfer function $\gamma_5$. Calculations have also been done for the Feynman-Murray $\kappa$ parameter, which when compared to the Peterson-Pillot-Lalonde-Liu parameter $\gamma_5$, provides insight into their proportionality, with both showing similar behavior across the specified $Q^2$ range. This indicates that the proton structure functions, rather than receiving significant contributions from higher-order terms, derive a significant portion of their non-perturbative content from the polarization transfer function $\gamma_5$, which in turn is extensively studied in relation to the proton-proton scattering reaction.

In a collaborative learning setup, members, or 'experts', share their modified versions of the basic data to optimize their accuracy without revealing their modifications, or 'parameters', to protect their autonomy and prevent influence. The indoor environmental condition expert, for instance, shares data with a high temperature, or 'criterion', similar to what an autonomous vehicle sensor would record. The goal is to train each expert using the standard, or 'natural', data rather than artificially created 'artificial' data. A challenging implication is that some experts may benefit from more training data than others, but sharing limited, natural data with all should benefit all. The standard method, or 'balanced training', where each member is given the standard data in proportion to the supposed amount of training data they need, is not ideal as it doesn't account for potential disparities between experts and results in slower overall progress. A proposed solution, or 'asymmetric balanced training', is to have members estimate and use varying amounts of artificial data to enhance their training, ensuring each expert receives what they need the most. The new training method has proven efficient in several situations, including experts working with sensor data and recent models that make predictions based on probability rather than plain value, or 'categorical', when tested in simulated, real-world conditions for studying autonomous vehicle vision.

A study of the interaction between the Higgs boson and the electroweak sector is performed by observing simultaneous occurrences of a Higgs boson pair and a vector boson (W or Z). The investigation, carried out using 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV gathered by the ATLAS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, has determined an effective cross-section for the observed phenomena. After adjusting for expected Standard Model activity, the analysis discovered an excess with a significance of 3.8 standard deviations for the combination of $ZH+Z\rightarrow \ell \ell q\bar{q}q\bar{q}$ and $ZH+Z\rightarrow \ell \ell \nu \bar{\nu}$. This result has not been observed in individual channels and further analysis is required to interpret these results within the Standard Model's framework. Furthermore, the study set upper bounds on the predicted probabilities for the creation of a vector boson paired with two Higgs bosons, based on the Standard Model's interference with the electroweak sector's coupling of a Higgs boson to two photons. The results of the analysis also set new standards for the probability of a Higgs boson paired with two W bosons in a phenomenon known as vector boson scattering.

The exceptional properties of alkali vapors make them ideal for generating highly coherent light with specific frequencies. However, creating electrons with sufficient frequency fluctuation to drive a laser of this specie is complex due to their strong intermolecular interaction, which necessitates specific fueling techniques. A novel approach has been developed to produce a high-coherence laser at 633nm frequency by using a digital laser control mechanism combined with a specific cooling process. By digitally modulating the laser setup and applying a 1.5GHz frequency filter, the researchers achieved low frequency fluctuation of around 221kHz while maintaining a temperature of 1070K, thereby yielding a high coherence time of around 7ns. This innovative method allows for the creation of high-coherence alkali lasers with tunability to different frequency ranges.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Siegel disk's modulus of rotation aligns with the logarithmic trace of the automorphism's action on the homological symplectic representation, which in turn equals the Picard value of the K3 surface's moduli space, thereby being an integer with absolute value greater than 1. Furthermore, applying Bogomolov-Mori-Sur l's inequality to K3 surfaces allows derivation of a bound on the moduli space's Picard number. Moreover, an explicit example demonstrating 4 distinct Siegel disks for the same K3 surface is presented.

In the context of the dark matter's annihilation process, we find that neutralinos with masses ranging from several hundred to thousand geometrically-based parsec masses, and with reclining gaugino masses, produce a decaying particle with properties similar to neutralinos. The study shows how this particle, resulting from GUT-breaking instability, influences the dark matter's behavior and further calculates the resulting gamma-ray spectra from proton-proton and helium nuclei annihilations in the Milky Way's center for masses between 10^3 and 10^7 geometrically-based parsec masses, and for the galactic center's radius at 8.6 kiloparsecs. The analysis presents favorable scenarios for detection by future missions, such as CTA, AGIS and GLAST, based on the assumptions of 50% efficiency and instrument sensitivity limits of 10^-14, 10^-13, 10^-11, 10^-9, 10^-8, 10^-7, 10^-6, 10^-5, 10^-4, 10^-3 Joules per second and above, and further compares these with the observations of nearby galaxies observations. The study presents tables illustrating the various masses and their corresponding gamma-ray production rates in the Milky Way, nearby galaxies such as M31 and M33, and in future missions' detectable ranges. The analysis further uses its results to derive constraints on the galactic halo's spatial extension and mass-based parsec units in

The problem of finding a minimum surface into which a given graph can be projected has been proven to have an efficient computational solution. A new algorithm was developed that approximates this solution to within a specified fraction of the minimum surface required, and can be run in a short amount of time that increases only logarithmically with the desired level of accuracy. This algorithm was itself derived from previous research into simpler graph problems, and is seen to be computationally equivalent to solving these smaller problems.

A novel stochastic Newton algorithm has been developed for solving large-scale convex optimization problems over networks. This algorithm utilizes individual node processing and inter-node communication to update solution estimates at a fast convergence rate locally, with convergence to the optimal solution occurring in as few global communication events as the order of the problem's data dimension. Convergence properties and performance bounds have been theoretically established for this algorithm, with empirical studies confirming the proposed approach's efficiency in practical applications.

Our research involves developing a neural network-based system to identify hate speech in two popular Indian languages, Hindi and Bengali. This initiative is particularly timely as these languages are rapidly gaining traction on social media in India, with over 100 million users. However, the danger of social media being exploited for spreading hate has become a significant concern. Previous studies primarily focused on datasets in English, but our investigation aims to tackle hate speech detection using recurrent neural networks for Hindi and Bengali, leveraging the highly informative semantic space of word embeddings. We utilized the Twitter datasets for both languages and carried out a thorough analysis of different models including RNN, LSTM, and GRU, as well as exploring transfer learning using pre-trained models like LSTMs and word2vec. Moreover, our study also involves creating and utilizing a universal vocabulary to represent words that are commonly used in both languages. Through extensive experimentation with varying architectures of RNN-based models and employing cross-entropy loss functions, our analysis reveals that the transfer learning approach using LSTMs yields the most effective results for both Hindi and Bengali. In the case of Hindi, the model exhibited an impressive accuracy of 0.82 with a balanced dataset, while for Bengali, the accuracy was found to be 0.74.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to detect the influence of a nucleus in motion is a crucial element for determining the location of any detected ions or electrons emitted from it. This capability isn't offered by the most common methods of detection, so scientists employ alternative, more specialized technologies that can detect even the smallest amounts of nuclear movement. A particular detector called the Gas Time Projection Chamber, specifically its high-definition variant, is already being used in various experiments to study individual nuclei and also as part of a future neutrino experiment to gain a deeper understanding of how neutrinos interact with nuclei. Unfortunately, even the advanced technologies used don't provide enough information to accurately account for a nucleus's motion when it interacts with detected electrons. To overcome this limitation, researchers are using a technique called "recoil feedback" to effectively simulate a nucleus's movement, providing a more accurate understanding of this interaction. Although this method has its limitations, scientists are able to improve its effectiveness by applying more precise conditions to their model of the interaction and also by applying advanced techniques to accurately understand this interaction. This ability to detect the influence of a nucleus's motion also provides a means to study a nucleus's movement even after it has interacted with electrons, providing even more accurate information about this interaction.

In various industries such as transportation, self-driving cars and automated trucking are being deployed, relying on judgment and skills tested in professional driving contexts. However, their ability to make sound judgments when faced with challenging situations like heavy rain, poor visibility, or unexpected events is a concern. The issue stems from whether AI systems can truly replicate human judgment without bias. To address this concern, we introduce the Role of AI in Commercial Vehicle Operations (RACVO) dataset, which aims to improve artificial intelligence in complex driving scenarios. The dataset consists of video-footage of experts performing alleged negligent actions on highways and subsequent moderated evaluations of the AI's performance. The results reveal that AI-driven models struggle with certain environmental conditions and complex situations, but with human input in critical situations, their performance improves significantly. The data set is now available on open datasets.

The Out-of-Category challenge held in conjunction with CVPR 2023 presented an new type of competition where multiple top model submissions were possible, yielding significantly more submissions than previous contests.  With this new challenge, the typical issue of a single best solution being identified was resolved. Analyzing challenge results revealed that performance gaps between the highest scoring models and the rest were very large, with the top model's accuracy increasing by over 16\% in comparison to second place. Further examination found that there was no distinct best approach for tackling the challenge, indicating diverse ways to address the problem. Looking ahead to future competitions, the challenge organizers suggest considering multi-priority evaluation methods to further enhance competition rules.

Random fields define probability distributions over functions, defining a probability measure on a space of functions defined by a specific stochastic process. Determining the most likely path between two functions in a space of functions is crucial for various applications such as statistical inference, decision theory, and machine learning. This research develops a theoretical approach to geodesic paths in the space of functions, demonstrating that these paths are consistent with the manifold's Riemannian geometry and establishing their consistency in two distinct contexts, including a scenario where functions are defined by a Gaussian process.

This note outlines the reasoning behind the length counting principle in a physical context. It investigates a finite particle system that walks along a loop S1, using the Cantor comb topology, and calculates its thermodynamic properties. The study demonstrates that the parabolic law holds, along with an specific partition function, and identifies a significant turning point in the free energy. The length counting principle is then established as a sufficient condition for the thermodynamic properties of a S1 gauge theory with an arbitrary gauge group to be calculated. This is illustrated in a simple example of a U(1) gauge theory. A companion letter explores the mathematical foundation of the length counting principle.

For a modiform f and an infinite place ρ, a unique real value ρ_0 is said to be distinctive if it's the only real root of the L(s,f) conjugate equation, excluding its integral multiples. This paper proves that the L(s,f) denominator for distinctive real values ρ_0 is generally bounded, with more specific bounds applicable at its special point 1/2.

In a study on the transport properties of graphene nanoribbons, researchers explored the role of spin-dependent interactions. They found that spin interaction with a gate voltage can be used to control spin-dependent transport in GNRs, where the spin-orbit effect plays a significant role. An investigation into GNRs with defect sites revealed that spin interaction is essential for maintaining spin polarization in these structures. Additionally, the spin-Holstein model was used to study spin-dependent transport in disordered GNRs, revealing non-equilibrium many-body effects and spin polarization in these systems.

Theorems ensuring the almost everywhere convergence of certain sequences of linear operators applied to inputs within a specific class of continuous functions on a compact manifold have already been established. Similar 'Korovkin type theorems' for nonlinear operators, requiring only monotonicity, have not been identified in previous research. In this study, the convergence of nonlinear, monotone operators on a compact manifold is demonstrated, utilizing a concept based on weak Starry Sky patterns and incorporating localized assumptions compatible with Lebesgue measure zero. The theorem is applicable to any nonlinear operator defined on a Banach space with the following characteristics: it is continuous, monotonic, and satisfies the closed graph property. The proof involves a simple and logical sequence of theorems.

A graph parameter is a way to assign a specific value to each graph of a certain size. Two graph parameters are said to be similar if there are small graphs where their values differ by a certain amount, and identical otherwise. In this paper, we explore relationships between three parameters: Hamiltonicity, independence count, and pancyclicity. By developing a technique that identifies a certain type of graph with relatively small size and independence count, we establish that independence count is a parameter that can be distinguished from Hamiltonicity. We achieve this by proving that there is a limit to how small a graph can be while having independence count p and Hamiltonicity q such that pq is greater than a certain constant. This solves a problem first brought up in a 2008 paper by Bogdanowicz, Kaw 藤, and Tancer. Furthermore, we introduce a new method of proving Hamiltonicity and apply it to generalizing a result from Erdős and Galvin, and we also prove that there is a limit to how dense a pancyclical graph can be.

The trajectory of extremely rapid particles in certain collisions is crucial for understanding the initial conditions and properties of the matter created in these collisions. 
A specific calculation, known as the transport of heat, Q, and v1, is used to simulate the movement of energy and a particular component of the matter's movement, v1, in various types of particle collisions.
When this matter is simulated, it exhibits a certain pattern of movement in certain types of particle collisions - a pattern that can be measured by observing the direction of rapid particles in certain collisions.
Research on the movement of particles in different types of collisions shows that a certain type of matter, Au+Au, exhibits a certain pattern of movement that can be understood using a theoretical model, but another type of collision, Ca+Cd, exhibits a different pattern of movement that does not match this model.
A theoretical model used in this research shows that a certain type of rotating matter, called a Cr-Cr collision, exhibits a certain pattern of movement that is similar to Au+Au, but another type of collision, a Pi+Al collision, exhibits a different pattern of movement that does not have a clear explanation.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to capture complex system dynamics in the small-scale regime. Although it offers high accuracy, constructing the Koopman tensor requires significant computational cost. This cost is proportional to the size of the state space, making ASK prone to high computational costs when dealing with multi-dimensional systems. This drawback is alleviated by applying a sparse grid method, which reduces the computational complexity by creating a condensed grid structure based on importance factors. This method can efficiently select optimal evaluation points for the Koopman tensor, thus offering improved efficiency for complex systems. Our approach also incorporates a localized tensor decomposition technique, which reduces the size of the Koopman tensor while preserving solution accuracy. This method can efficiently solve multi-dimensional systems, providing a significant computational advantage. Its effectiveness is demonstrated using two test systems: the extended Duffing system and a set of ordinary differential equations representing the evolution of a hurricane. These case studies show that the proposed method can compute solutions at a speed up of several orders of magnitude compared to conventional Koopman method results.

Our studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of an outer complex scaling method in tackling the challenges associated with diversity and non-diversity of eigenvalues in strong DC fields for atoms and molecules. This method involves scaling the coordinates with a field-dependent vertex $\eta(\mathbf{z})$ while applying the Riesz projection operator to transform boundary conditions into the bulk of the complex plane. As a result, it enables the separation of eigenvalues into distinct groups corresponding to different symmetry subspaces, even those without a hidden symmetry structure. This method facilitates the numerical computation of eigenvalues using an Arnoldi decomposition based on finite basis expansions. This approach has been applied to numerous scenarios, including the classification of alignment transitions in DC-field hydrogen atoms, the characterization of eigenvalue clusters in few-electron ions, and the investigation of the non-Divergent (ND) eigenvalue in some DC-molecules. Interestingly, it turns out that the ND eigenvalue is a limiting case of a diversity pair as the scaling parameter $\eta$ approaches infinity from below. To achieve reliable finite basis results for the ND eigenvalue, we introduced a fixed-point iteration scheme with an intrinsic convergence guarantee. Furthermore, the outer complex scaling method has been combined with the local optimization of the vertex $\eta$ using the barrier method with a Newton restoration procedure, leading to the identification of the ND eigenvalue in some molecules. This approach has also been used to derive the inner classical turning points of eigenvalues by applying the phase function based on the L

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains widely utilized for solving the Schrödinger problem within the framework of the Sinkhorn scaling. However, it's well established that this algorithm converges to a solution only when the Schrödinger issue has a solution. In instances where the transport plan does not align with the product of the marginals, it is demonstrated that the Sinkhorn algorithm may converge to a semi-stationary state that fails to satisfy the dual problem's value. A theoretical analysis is presented in order to investigate the long-term behavior of the algorithm in such a scenario and it is shown that the Sinkhorn algorithm converges towards a semi-stationary state consistently, which does not correspond to the optimal solution. It is also shown that a modified algorithm, incorporating a cyclic projection, converges towards the optimal dual value consistently. It is also established that the algorithm converges at a linear rate in the case where the transport plan does not align with the product of the marginals. These findings are verified through numerical experiments presented in the paper.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC has published data on the top quark pair cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a specific energy. This energy, 5.02 TeV, was recorded in 2018 for a designated dataset known as the U--U collisions. For these collisions, the entire dataset consisted of an accumulated luminosity of 25.43 inverse picobarns. A particular analysis was utilized to determine the top quark pair cross-section, relying on events with identified electrons and jets. Multiple corrections were applied to the data to accurately account for detector readings. Ultimately, the measurement yielded a top quark pair cross-section of 43.4 millibarns, with a corresponding uncertainty of 6.6 millibarns. This measurement agrees with the standard model predictions from two specific calculation methods, with the calculations aligning with the data within 2 standard deviations.

This research investigates the localization phenomenon in a specially designed, symmetrical system linked to a central node, with each node having a random disorder. Using a unique approach to calculating critical conductance, we studied the local conductance of this disorder-prone system. Our results revealed a distinct pattern of conductance distribution as the disorder strength varied, which could be explained by a straightforward percolation model. Additionally, we observed that the system's behavior near the center node changes when the disorder extends beyond a specific reach, leading to a break in the otherwise clean conductance curve.

The conjecture that all smooth convex functions u on the right half-plane, whose second mixed derivative u$_{xy}$ vanishes at infinity, can be expressed using generalized Bessel functions from the janowski class is presented.

The COVID-19 pandemic led to a significant shift in how people behaved in public. People who lived in denser urban areas were more likely to limit their movements due to the stricter social distancing measures that were put into effect. As a result, there was a change in the diversity of interactions among those who did go out, largely as a consequence of the reduced mobility of city dwellers. Data from mobility reports was used to model and analyze this change in diversity of encounters, comparing the differences in diversity of encounters in urban and suburban areas before and during the pandemic. Additionally, a representative population model was developed to formally study the impact of individual mobility restrictions, leading to a more uniform distribution of encounters in suburban areas and a decreased diversity of encounters in urban areas.

Researchers have developed several methodologies for partitioning complex systems into multiple fields to simulate two-phase flow in irregular media, such as porous rocks. In this study, we evaluated several techniques for dividing the system into multiple fields: distinct partial oxidation, double oxidation, and a straightforward mathematical algorithm. We analyzed how these methods affected precision, computation time, and memory requirements using actual field conditions and Irregular Hexahedral Grids. The results showed that distinct partial oxidation and double oxidation techniques performed similarly, requiring less computation time and memory compared to splitting the system into many fields. However, a straightforward mathematical algorithm was less efficient than the other two methods, prompting further optimization to make it more effective. Additionally, we discovered that dividing the system into only two fields might overlook local and systemic effects, such as reservoir cycles and micro-scale entrapment of fluids.

An innovative approach is introduced to create optical resonators with a singular optical property, namely left- or right-handed circularly polarized light reflection. The design hinges on leveraging the inherent symmetry properties of a specifically curved optical waveguide and polarization-dependent reflections within a proprietary reflection structure. According to the design specifications, the waveguide features a unique 'S' shape, which allows for reflections that exhibit chiral properties through carefully calculated polarization-dependent optical path length differences for left- and right-handed polarized light. The proposed resonance model relies on a two-part system consisting of semi-infinite left- and right-handed optical pathways with manual control of the waveguide's curvature to adjust the resonance frequency. The study presents a detailed framework for calculating polarization-dependent optical path length differences, which serve as the foundation for chiral resonance. Additionally, an antiferromagnetic metal film is suggested to further enhance the proposed chiral resonance phenomenon by implementing a specific pattern of spin-dependent reflections. The concept of using a curved optical waveguide for chiral resonance has the potential to open new avenues in the development of technologies requiring circularly polarized light, such as quantum computing and advanced biological imaging applications.

This study establishes a specific connection between the Liouville CFT and a non-interacting free fermion CFT, both of which are based on the same central charge, $c=1$, and are extended in one space and one time dimension. Subsequently, we derive the gravitational limit of the free fermon CFT using the duality between the free fermon CFT and a non-linear sigma-model, and compare it with the separate derivation of the Liouville CFT gravitational limit made by Matteo Seiberg in a different work. Both methods are then combined to conclude that a specific four-fermion interaction in the free fermon CFT, when taken to the ultraviolet, does not lead to a divergence in the two-point correlation function of two fermions; the function remains finite in this scenario.

A new set of analytical solutions is derived for an improved warp drive model incorporating both an ideal fluid and a cosmological constant in its framework. By employing a modified pressure assumption, these solutions are obtained through a combination of derivative expansions and an algebraic equation for the Kretschmann scalar, resulting in a general spacetime metric that can be expressed in a coordinate-independent manner. Additionally, the study investigates the stability of the derived solutions and examines the geometry and properties of the obtained spacetimes.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their residents' high expectations for efficiency and comfort. Cities strive to manage their underground Subsurface Urban Space and the infrastructure embedded within it, but this task poses technical difficulties and financial burdens. To aid in these efforts, a novel engineering approach known as GUIDES offers a comprehensive framework for compiling, maintaining, and analyzing Subsurface Urban Space data. This approach, supported by a unifying set of abstract components, ensures that various types of infrastructure are represented uniformly, and their 3D mappings accurately align. The GUIDES software suite includes tools for compiling and analyzing Subsurface Urban Space data, silent infrastructure surveillance, and infrastructure modeling. The implemented system encompasses algorithms for detecting and matching 2D and 3D patterns, and demonstrations of its capabilities are showcased through the use of data from Chicago. This research presents the GUIDES engineering approach and its associated software, highlighting its potential applications and model limitations.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized optical resonance between states with parallel spin and angular momentum alignment. This resonance, sensitive to translational movement of the ions, was exploited to study both low-frequency oscillations and trapped ion heating. By examining how these oscillations change in response to dephasing, we were able to accurately determine the average temperature of the ions, which would be challenging to achieve with traditional single-particle measurements. Furthermore, we were able to determine the frequencies and amplitudes associated with specific modes of movement, utilizing this information to develop an in-depth model of the ions' motional state distribution. This model is based on an assumption about the initial distribution of energy among the ions, which we found to be in good agreement with the actual result. Ultimately, our method of analysis has significant implications for the study of quantum many-body systems using trapped ions.

TERS is a spatially resolved imaging technique that uses Raman spectroscopy and near-field microscopy to provide valuable insights into the chemical composition of a sample. The technique leverages a localized and highly controllable electromagnetic field generated by a metal nanoparticle to excite and detect vibrational motions in substances. Nevertheless, the fine detail of this electromagnetic field also confers a considerable non-thermal, abiotic influence on the sample's molecules, inducing distinct electronic and geometric distortions. Despite its relevance, the precise nature and strength of this ancillary effect have long been the subject of debate. To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying processes, an advanced computational method was developed that simulates the joint electromagnetic and quantum mechanical interaction between TERS's key components, namely the sample, Raman scatterer, metal nanoparticle, and light source. The framework consists of two interconnected parts: a cutting-edge quantum mechanical simulation of the electron states in the Raman scatterer and the substrate, which encompasses the interplay of electromagnetic interactions; and an accompanying approach to calculate the distribution of the extremely local electromagnetic field in the scatterer and the substrate. This sophisticated field simulation takes into account the complex interactions among all the components, including mutual influences between the electron and photon states in the system. Our findings from the simulation match the experimental observations in recent research, showing that the strength of the abiotic influence can be substantial and potentially surpass the primary chemical effect in some cases, with the electron and photon states becoming equally essential in

Our study aims to discover low-intensity radio radiation in nearby galaxies. We conducted
K-band observations of 28 galaxies, including 24 Magellanic Cloud objects, using the
Sardinia Radio Telescope. We analyzed the spectra of these galaxies to identify
radio emission discrepancies. The non-thermal radiation of spiral arms in galaxies
was compared to previous values. The non-thermal radiation of the Large Magellanic
Cloud was consistent with previous values, while the non-thermal radiation of the Small
Magellanic Cloud deviated with a lower radiation intensity at 20 GHz than expected.
These results will contribute to a comprehensive database of extra-galactic low-intensity
radio emission through the E-MERGE project.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated ferroelectric behavior belies complex dynamics between protons, electron charge and energy in the system. Using computer-powered simulations, the dynamic movement of its units below and above the ferroelectric transition temperature has been investigated. It's discovered that at higher temperatures, subtle changes start as early as 10K above the transition and gradually grow in magnitude, largely due to the breaking down of a crystalline lattice structure, causing a significant shift in entropy. This process is found to be nearly entirely connected to the movement of the ammonium bond orientation. However, the story doesn't end there - further analysis reveals a second contribution to the entropy change which originates from the teaming of polar units within the lattice. This finding implies a more intricate interpretation of the ferroelectric phase transition than previously considered.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a sub-optimal strategy to overcome uncertainty, uncertainty-reducing habits, or complete reliance on chance. This study discovered midbrain activity in patients being taught a gambling game, trained with either fixed or variable rewards, resulted in optimal model fitting that captured implicit and explicit decision-making processes. Notably, the variation in choosing the sure win option was best explained by the ability to accurately represent negative surprises in the brain, specifically when this accuracy increased, it encouraged exploration of better options. Furthermore, the level of this accuracy influenced how often patients chose the sure win, while it did not affect their ability to learn from rewards. This research signs off by highlighting a more dynamic role for the midbrain in uncertainty-related choices than previously estimated.

We're exploring the potential for core systems based on complex versions of the $E_8$ lattice to serve as foundations for quantum computations, potentially leading to more powerful capabilities than traditional quantum computers. Studies have shown that core systems in 4D spaces have properties that could enable quantum computations, but they also fall short of being fully quantum in certain context-dependent tasks. To overcome these limitations, we're proposing the use of complex versions of the $E_8$ lattice to create a more robust core system. However, our research has found that even with these complexifications, the resulting core systems may still fail to meet the requirements for full quantum computations in all context-dependent tasks. Nevertheless, we've found evidence suggesting that complex $E_8$ systems have the capacity to exhibit quantum entanglement and contextuality simultaneously, paving the way for novel computational applications and insights.

The challenge of close neighbor searching in time series under the Fr\'echet distance has been thoroughly investigated. Despite its relative simplicity, this problem has proven to be computationally demanding. For its approximation, a logarithmic query time and logarithmic approximation ratio were initially proposed. Later studies enhanced the approximation ratio while maintaining logarithmic query time. Our research presents a new algorithm with a linear processing time that offers a logarithmic approximation ratio, surpassing previous results with the same approximation ratio but a smaller query time. Our result relies on a new lower bound on the Fr\'echet distance between two pieceswise linear functions, an approach not previously explored in the literature.

The process of quantum unfold folding, which reconstructs the quantum system's underlying physical values from quantum measurements with inherent errors, plays a vital role in quantum research. However, applying the standard folding method to correct measurement inaccuracies in experiments that use Scanning Tunneling Microscopes is impractical due to the large amount of collected data. In this research, a highly scalable approach to correct measurement errors based on the quantum folding concept is developed. The proposed method computes the likelihood of each measured event and determines the corresponding actual value based on that event and previous measurements, which enables iterative correction without storing vast amounts of data. The new method's performance is verified using simulated data with various characteristics and real-world experimental data from a non-contact scanner, demonstrating high accuracy and the ability to efficiently process data under any condition.

Effective communication between humans and robots is crucial for successful collaboration in unfamiliar environments.  Existing methods of teaching robots via instruction are complicated and demanding, unrealistic in emergency situations, and do not account for the human's perspective.  To address this, we have developed a novel, user-centered approach to teaching robots via observational learning.  Our system utilizes a user-friendly interface to record and compile sequential human actions and robot movements, and then applies machine learning techniques to create a set of common, optimized protocols.  These standardized protocols are available for immediate use, and can be further refined through subsequent observations.  Our approach was tested in a kitchen simulation and found to be a more efficient and accurate method of teaching robots compared to existing, non-observational methods.

We present an unsupervised learning method for developing a navigable map, comprised of sequential sections with inherent directions, by training a multi-layered neural network to analyze an environment's topological structure from overhead satellite images. By identifying ports, roads, landmarks, and intersections, this map dynamically captures an environment's changing configuration due to construction or destruction. To enhance our map's utility, we incorporate a representative geometric model that translates the diagram's elements into a usable spatial format, facilitating various tasks such as route simulation, location calculation, and chart design. Upon achieving optimal performance, we applied our system's capabilities to real-world scenarios in multiple cities.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-user detection properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in wireless technologies that increasingly encounter multiuser interference problems. This work focuses on inter-group complementary code sets that enable pairwise arrays to have zero cross-correlation off the grid, thereby benefiting multigroup wireless communication systems by reducing interference between different groups. To this end, a novel inter-group complementary code set is presented, along with a 2-D Z-supplementary array code set, both of which can be synthesized using multivariable functions. Notably, the proposed code set can accommodate up to 16 groups, whereas conventional approaches are generally limited to 2 or 4 groups. Additionally, the 2-D Z-supplementary array code set offers improved performance compared to conventional two-dimensional arrays, such as interleaved arrays and pseudo-orthogonal arrays.

We've developed a novel statistical framework to jointly reconstruct CT images, remove background noise from sensors, and separate materials during data acquisition. Since CT measurements are inherently non-parametric and multi-modal, traditional variational methods are often ineffective or prone to producing 'artifact-filled' results. To overcome these limitations, we've engineered a sophisticatedly designed data-driven prii from the sensor signals. This prii leverages the decision theory-based method, 'Information-theoretic Meaningful Image Reconstruction using Sensor data (MIRSE)', to create detailed CT images. Our proposed framework includes: first, reversing downsample operations through a size-preserving CT inverse model; second, reducing noise through a sophisticatedly designed data-driven prii from the sensor signals using the 'Information-theoretic Meaningful Image Reconstruction using Sensor data (MIRSE)' method; and third, separating materials through a multi-class random field model that utilizes Kullback-Leibler divergence and divergence of density functions, and where each density function is derived from the CT measurements of a specific material. Our method's effectiveness has been confirmed through successful tests using diverse multi-spectral CT datasets as well as data captured from an optical sensor during concrete drilling operations.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two concentric metallic spheres connected by a narrow neck. Using the discrete surface current approach, we generate a numerical solution that considers both local and nonlocal electron dynamics. An equivalent continuous model based on the hyperbolic Drude model is also developed to replicate the nonlocal effect. Calculations reveal that as the gap narrows, gap plasmons shift from the visible to the infrared frequency range. An increase in electron cutoff momentum reduces the gap plaston lifetime and amplifies its spectral width. When the gap width approaches the electron mean free path, the hyperbolic Drude model's prediction of the damping time diverges from the discrete model's result. Nonetheless, the hyperbolic model provides a reasonable estimate for gap plasmon resonance positions within the visible spectrum, even for relatively large electron mean free paths.

In many retrieval tasks, like question answering, a question serves as a context, enhancing the relevance of responses by aligning with the question's meaning. For Named Entity Retrieval in context, a new problem called Term Relevance Response (TRR) is proposed to improve conventional retrieval metrics. In TRR, assessments have two key components: first, scores of how well query terms match the context, and second, scores of how relevant the identified entities are to the context. These scores are based on a small dataset and can be viewed as a multi-dimensional ranking. Experimental results from a small dataset show that when using context for both queries and entities, context-based metrics like TRR perform better than traditional metrics, while also demonstrating the potential of more complex models in the future.

The increasing availability of detailed data through various sources has made modeling complex relationships between different variables appealing. However, statistical software typically excels at analyzing single time series but falls short when dealing with links between multiple variables. This gap challenges researchers who must simplify intricate data patterns to effectively communicate results, which is particularly essential when engaging stakeholders outside of a data science background. To bridge this divide, we developed tools facilitating exploration, understanding, and collaboration on multivariate data sets, including the examination of long-term trends. By combining interactive visualizations, we demonstrated that users can rapidly develop shared insights into their data.

Developing trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems is essential to support decision-making in the healthcare sector, and this task is complicated by the existence of imbalanced datasets. Such unbalanced datasets can negatively affect the performance of AI models, resulting in biased predictions and reduced accuracy. To overcome these limitations, AI researchers use transfer learning and ensemble methods, however these methods have theoretical constraints and may compromise model reliability. This study proposes a novel Graph Neural Network (GNN) approach called Heterogeneous Resemblance Graph Neural Network (HRGNN), which uses a holistic observation transcription to establish node and edge similarities within the graph. The model then generates electronic health graphs based on these similarities and applies GNN to improve the representation of observation features and enable the diagnosis of unobserved diseases. Experimental results demonstrate that HRGNN surpasses Baseline GNN models and maintains a high level of model explainability while reducing the impact of dataset biases.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle shapes and solvent properties, we model the electric double layer (EDL) formed between a charged soft material and an electrolyte solution. By accounting for the static distribution of ions and water for various oriented flat elements, we explore how hexagonal packing affects EDL charging and compare our results to Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data obtained from tension measurements on black lipid bilayers. Our study shows that taking into account the distribution of water molecules significantly impacts EDL characteristics, such as capacitance and charge density, especially at low salt concentrations. Conversely, the effects of orientation are relatively minor. To facilitate application to different particle shapes and sizes, we create a set of parameters that allows for generalized modeling of EDL formed by charged soft materials.

The significance of software retrieval in the development cycle has been emphasized, yet this area is underdeveloped when comparing to other industries such as law, medicine, and the humanities where detailed search techniques are common. Current methods for extracting information from software text typically rely on external knowledge without assuring the extracted information accurately represents actual specifications. What if a developer could effortlessly retrieve and understand a software's precise specifications from publicly available sources such as product manuals, without needing specialized knowledge or external references? We introduce a groundbreaking method for extracting a comprehensive set of standardized software specifications from unstructured text documents based on the ISO/IEC 26550 standard. These specifications include definable attributes like purpose, scope, and applicability as well as other modular attributes that facilitate their application to various software contexts. We implement this method using computational models for extraction and assessment, evaluating its effectiveness on a collection of product manuals. This method reveals that multiple standards define the same specification, with many specifications not related to software quality or functionality as per the ISO/IEC 26550 standard.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in wireless networks using cooperative network coding with joint schedule and power optimization. Firstly, a theoretical bound on energy consumption is established for networks employing traditional ARQ, SRARQ, and network coding methods. These energy consumption models are then utilized to devise an optimization problem aimed at enhancing energy efficiency in cooperative network coding with joint schedule and power allocation. However, this optimization problem is of a mixed-logical and real-variable type, making it difficult to solve. Consequently, a concise programming problem is derived to reduce search space and solve it directly. Furthermore, a lower approximation algorithm is developed to achieve a near-optimal solution for the optimization problem. Simulation results indicate that the proposed solution yields superior energy efficiency compared to conventional approaches.

A comprehensive understanding of the electronic structure of magnetic adatoms and clusters on surfaces involves a critical examination of spin-dependent low-energy impurity states localized within the energy gap of the host material. Research has demonstrated that these states can be described by the combined theories of impurity and host materials. Notably, an Mn impurity on a superconducting surface creates a unique environment characterized by an unusual spin-dependent Yu--Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) state extending far beyond the impurity itself, extending into the host's conduction band and displaying distinct changes in energy with magnetic field applications. This study develops a theoretical framework to describe YSR states as a consequence of magnetic impurities based on a unified theory for both impurity and host systems. By employing first principles calculations, the theory is validated for an Mn impurity on a Nb surface and shows an excellent match with the recently conducted experimental results. Furthermore, this theoretical framework is applied to examine YSR states in larger systems, such as Mn clusters consisting of up to 4 atoms. An essential aspect of these systems is the emergence of a distinct spin--orbit coupling, originating from within the cluster, which significantly distorts the shape of the YSR state for a singly occupied impurity and alters its behavior in multi-atomic clusters, thereby affecting magnetic excitations and spin dynamics. This theoretical framework is poised to unlock a deeper understanding of magnetic impurities and clusters on superconducting surfaces, thereby revealing the underlying complex physics of this phenomenon

Navigation systems for mobile robots often rely on inertial sensors, combined with data from various sensors that provide information about the robot's environment, such as cameras, sonar, and lidar. However, these sensors aren't always available or suitable for certain robot types or environments, particularly when there are no visible landmarks. As a result, navigation systems often depend on lidar data for accurate positioning and map localization. However, even with lidar data, common methods for selecting features, such as the NormalDistrubution Mixture (NDM) and Associated Tracking (AT), can introduce biases in the map localization process. These biases can cause problems when the robot operates in different environments than those used in the training data for the navigation system. As a solution, this research proposes a new method, called the Normalized Distribution Association with Deep Neural Filter (NDADNF), that aims to mitigate pose estimation biases by using a lidar data filtering approach. By removing some lidar data points, this method can reduce the impact of features that cause navigation system bias. Navigation system bias is caused by the overlap of multiple distinct distribution patterns, a issue that the NDADNF method addresses by using a deep neural filter to match the local features in the robot's perception only with those from the map localization system. As a result, this method can eliminate the overlap of distribution patterns, a key factor in reducing pose estimation bias. In addition to eliminating bias, the NDADNF method also helps to navigate

This paper tackles the challenge of enhancing the visual clarity of satellite imagery by applying a straightforward edge detection algorithm. Unlike commonly used deep learning methods, our approach relies solely on predetermined parameters and avoids complex training or sourcing of satellite-specific data. By combining a convolutional operation, an edge detection mechanism, and refining processes, our method yields comparable results to those obtained from deep learning techniques while being significantly more efficient and adaptable to any image. Furthermore, this efficiency enables our algorithm to function effectively in environments with limited computational resources, making it well-suited for applications on hardware with restricted capabilities, including resource-constrained IoT devices.

To better understand XANES measurements in dense matter, researchers need to combine traditional atomic models with the collective behavior of free electrons surrounding ions in plasmas. There's a critical point where a group of electrons transforms from a more traditional Mie model to a higher-level density of states, and our new approach outlines this transition for X-ray absorption across various fields of ionization. This research offers a theoretical framework for grasping how multiple energy states arise in X-ray absorption, and it may be expanded upon to study the movement of electrons in X-rays.

This study introduces an innovative Deep Neural Network architecture, specifically designed to enhance the robustness of modulation classification networks against adversarial attacks. By integrating a similar Blend GAN approach to improve classification performance across various scenarios, we tested its effectiveness in modulation classification tasks. Results show that the proposed architecture's ability to produce adversarial-resistant and robust classes is superior to a conventional GAN method. Moreover, the network's ability to maintain its original accuracy on clean datasets and its ability to classify malicious samples are significantly improved compared to a conventional network.

Creating a comprehensive multiple sclerosis segmentation toolkit remains a pressing need given the scarcity of publicly accessible clinical data and the fast-paced advancements in deep learning. Establishing such a toolkit could greatly simplify clinical research and diagnosis. A notable challenge in building this resource is associated with diverse segmentation models that have been developed in response to a lack of clinical data, with many employing transfer learning with pre-trained models. A comparison of several segmentation methods that utilize transfer learning with those that have been trained from scratch on clinical data is presented in this work, using data from over 600 patients across five hospitals in the UK. A newly developed model is introduced, incorporating detailed anatomical prior information, along with an efficient, iterative approach for training the model in a unified fashion. A thorough evaluation of all approaches is conducted using a combined dataset of 632 patients (260 training, 172 testing) in a blind study, including measurements of model performance in blind tests on data from hospitals that were not used in training. A key finding of the research is a demonstration of the need to continue developing and refining clinical resources, as data-driven approaches may significantly trail behind domain-specific designs that have been fine-tuned for specific datasets.

Recent breakthroughs in neural survival forecasting enable the creation of contrastive pairs of life span predictions, which can be employed as a crucial input for learning to predict remaining time spans. Current methods for generating these pairs are grounded in random procedures, hindering the effectiveness of the model. To address this limitation, this study proposes an innovative technique for creating contrastive pairs based on natural processes of life span prediction, which can capture essential features for accurate prediction. Additionally, this technique is capable of leveraging large-scale paired data without requiring labels indicating the correct prognosis. Experimental results on critical care units and cancer patients showcase that the technique can facilitate accurate prediction when employed in conjunction with a neural network based on attention that incorporates bipolar contrast.

A flexible framework has been created to learn how systems of equations with multiple variables behave when there's an error, which can be used for various types of models, including small and complex ones. This framework's key component is a mathematical function called an error map that describes the relationship between a small change in one part of the system and the resulting change elsewhere. To develop a reliable error map for a given model, we suggest training an artificial neural network (ANN) using a method called machine learning. We have developed an algorithm that simulates how a system changes over time and uses these simulations to test different ANN approaches. Our experiments, which included simple mathematical equations and models of ocean currents, show that it's possible to accurately train an ANN using a relatively small number of calculations, which is a promising result. This breakthrough could make it easier to use models with known errors for decision-making tasks, which is especially exciting for complex models that are too big for typical computers.

We conducted a research project to study the characteristics of isolated infrared dark clouds (IRDCs) using the Submillimeter Array (SMA) to observe cooling emissions in three IRCDs, including Dragon. Our findings indicate that one of the clouds, known as IRDC25, displays a unique pattern of emissions that suggest its center is expanding as a result of massive star formation (MSF). This expansion most likely initiated the formation of massive stars, causing the cloud's core to break into multiple distinct components. Two other clouds, IRDC2 and IRDC32, did not exhibit this same pattern of motion, yet we did detect a range of emissions in their respective spectra. Our analysis of spectral lines from nitrogen compounds in these IRDCs reveals a correlation with molecular outflows, indicating their potential to form extremely massive stars.

The dark matter composed of primordial black holes exists throughout the universe, with a potential to be detected in various experiments. Determining the abundance of these black holes depends on two key factors: the power spectrum of the cosmic density fluctuations and the density threshold for the formation of these black holes. The primordial black hole dark matter candidate can be evaluated using different scenarios for the abundance, based on the amplitude of the primordial fluctuations. Measuring the abundance requires either direct detection or indirect evidence, such as the effects of the black holes on the large-scale structure. Our population-level code for calculating primordial black holes, called PopSyCLE, can determine the density of these black holes and their distribution within the universe. Using PopSyCLE, we calculated the density of these black holes under specific conditions - when the power at a specific wavelength is three times larger, and when the density threshold for the formation of these black holes is 1.4 times larger, compared to the conditions in our current universe. Our model shows that this results in a density of these black holes that is significantly higher, at about four orders of magnitude higher than their density in our current universe. Our population-level model allows for a more precise determination of the parameters and can predict the possible effects of these black holes on the structure of the universe and its evolution.

We utilize molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the structural organization of triangular shapes composed of six spheres that vary in size, focusing on the impact of shape asymmetry on their packing patterns. The results reveal the existence of a distinct phase where the triangular shape exhibits a gradient in the direction of one of its arms, accompanied by a specific pattern of hole arrangements that becomes more prevalent with increasing asymmetry. As the degree of shape asymmetry increases, this phase undergoes a transformation from one with fluid-like hole arrangements to one with rigid holes, reminiscent of hexagonal close-packed structure, but with alternating layers of loose and dense particle arrangement. Additionally, we discovered another distinct phase with a pentagonal prism structure that becomes more prevalent with increasing asymmetry.

The performance of large language models can be enhanced through fine-tuning, but this process is costly due to the large number of parameters.  In order to make adjustments more resource-efficient, we suggest a method of fine-tuning an LLM for a smaller transformation task without modifying the underlying weight structure.  Previous methods of adapting large language models involved modifying the vocabulary to match the task-specific tokens, however this approach has several drawbacks such as requiring extensive vocabulary updates and handling potential token-mapping errors.  In order to mitigate these issues, we implemented a unique special token adaptation technique that uses a set of predefined control tokens to match tasks, thereby avoiding token-mapping errors and reducing the need for extensive vocabulary updates.  Our proposed method was then put into practice by adapting it for five different tasks and evaluating its effectiveness in adapting large language models efficiently.  The results revealed that our method achieved superior results on these tasks when compared to standard adaptation methods, also highlighting that our method had minimal adverse effects on the original LLM performance.  Furthermore, through experiments and analysis, we validated the effectiveness and reliability of our method.

This paper investigates how context impacts preference evaluation in multi-item scenarios where the context is a subset of available options. It's crucial to consider the context optimally to make the best final choice. The study compares two approaches: context-free, which doesn't account for the context except when it's the only option, and context-aware, which takes the context into account at every step. The results showed that context-aware outperformed context-free under most circumstances. However, both approaches faced challenges with context ambiguity, which could often lead to the context-free method making the better choice. The paper discusses the implications of these findings.

Our investigation into polymer fluids, which are crucial in understanding 3D printing, packaging, and other industrial processes, focused on the connection between heat and the movements of particles within the liquids. By using the generalized Eyring theory, we demonstrated that there's a clear correlation between a fluid's ability to flow and its overall energy, which is also influenced by the fluid's movement patterns. To validate these claims, we used computational models to analyze several types of polymers and found that the fluid's behavior does indeed follow the expected patterns. This discovery allows us to not only study the thermal movements of particles but also use the fluid's temperature to predict its behavior in various industrial and natural processes.

Our investigation into how neural language models process cognitive Rejection labels has led us to an unexpected discovery. Since Rejection isn't a word found in standard language data, we initially assumed it would be difficult for models like Transformer GPT-2 to recognize and process. Yet, our research across 12 datasets from diverse sources (including generated fake Rejection data, as well as datasets with varying levels of cognitive Rejection labels) revealed the contrary. Not only can GPT-2 accurately detect Rejection, but it can also effectively generalize this detection to unseen Rejection labels despite never having seen the word before. Moreover, our findings across 5 distinct datasets indicate that GPT-2's Rejection processing performance is on par with that of leading supervised models like RoBERTa and BERT, all without any formal training on Rejection. We also found that GPT-2's ability to effectively reject based on its understanding of the context, rather than just the specific Rejection label, is a testament to its robust cognitive processes. Our findings also shed light on the possible limitations of traditional supervised approaches to Rejection and highlight the potential future developments that will be needed to fully develop Rejection processing in language models.

To improve focused, coherent and informative generation in neural machine translation, this study proposes a Look-ahead Focus (LAF) loss technique. LAF encourages the model to concentrate on specific parts of the translation, by measuring how focused and informative the generated text is, by looking ahead. We've modified the FocusLoss by removing the auxiliary translation task and modifying the predict function to allow looking ahead several steps. Experimental results on three datasets show that LAF achieves a higher focus score, better translation quality, and is more interpretable than existing focused generation methods. Additionally, we found that models optimized with LAF are more resistant to various forms of noise and are capable of effectively focusing on specific parts of the translation both pre- and post-translation.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on a structured six-dimensional manifold with U(3) and SU(3) Lie groups as the fundamental gauge and symplectic groups, with the associated symplectic structure merely serving as a starting point for a general connection. This study expands prior research, as previously such calculations have only been successfully executed for structures with SU(2) and U(2) Lie groups. Moreover, a well-documented example is given of a five-dimensional manifold with the spinor group as its associated Lie groups. This example serves to illustrate the complexity of calculations for curvatures when the associated Lie groups have spinor representations. Lastly, a theoretical proposal is presented that connects curvature weights to Chern-Weil theory.

This research involves determining whether the thermodynamic behavior of a specific class of CFTs can be attributed to information gaps, like those found in holographic CFTs. To explore this, we've collected and analyzed the second-order large-N approximations for both the free energy and spatial entanglement entropy in a group of CFTs with interacting CFTs as well as gauge theories with three colors. These calculations were possible thanks to a recently discovered method involving the use of representative j-planes. Our findings show that the spatial entanglement entropy exhibits the same temperature-dependent behavior as the free energy in this group of CFTs. However, this shared behavior does not necessarily imply that the entanglement entropy represents the thermodynamic entropy since they can behave differently at fixed temperature. In the case of the O(N) CFTs with interacting CFTs, our analyzed orders suggest that the spatial entanglement entropy accurately represents the thermodynamic entropy, based on our findings. These results also indicate that the adS/CFT duality, which applies to gauge theories with large group sizes, implies that the spatial entanglement entropy accurately represents the thermodynamic entropy as well. In contrast, this research dismisses a previously proposed method for determining the thermodynamic entropy from entanglement entropy, which was previously thought to be accurate up to large-N approximations.
