Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect but recent discoveries in gapped graphene with an asymmetrical sublattice potential suggest an alternative known as the orbital Hall effect. Our investigation provides evidence for this effect by combining analytical and numerical methods to evaluate the Berry curvature in gapped graphene with a uniform external field. The results confirm that the orbital Hall effect occurs when the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the graphene and validate experimentally observed patterns of the orbital polarization described by Chern Simons theory.

Machine learning models' (ML) accuracy is consistently compromised by data corruption caused by deliberate or unintentional tampering with existing training sets, which includes fabricated data. Existing research into GNNs has either developed effective but limited solutions to address corruption or employed generic machine learning techniques that don't account for the unique characteristics of graph data. This study presents a method (GraphCLEAN) that utilizes reinforcement learning (RL) to rectify corrupted training datasets by focusing on the most detrimental examples for model accuracy. By prioritizing examples with the highest impact on model performance, GraphCLEAN is capable of both identifying and correcting correlations within graph data more effectively than existing approaches. When tested on GraphCLEAN outperforms existing approaches (including a self-correction method, a semi-supervised learning method, and a strong deep learning method) on graph datasets, demonstrating its superiority. All code and resources can be accessed at https://github.com/mehdi-oz/graphclean.

The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue and improve the accuracy of object matching. A novel technique has been developed to utilize the cross-correlation of magnitudes in conjunction with precise astrometry for cross-matching catalogues, boosting the overall quality of the matches obtained. Results demonstrate that the method can achieve a high quality of matches exceeding 80% using photometric catalogs of average brightness. Additionally, the technique can also be employed in future surveys to anticipate and prepare for the changes in photometric catalogs due to varying brightness and time frames, thereby enabling the accurate cross-matching of sources between different photometric catalogs.

In this paper, we investigate the largest possible size of minimal vertex subsets in infinite hypergraphs with specific properties. A vertex subset is considered minimal if the removal of any of its vertices results in the inexcusable (non-hypertouchable) vertex subset. We explore the sizes of these minimal subsets in various types of infinite hypergraphs and establish the optimality of the obtained results by demonstrating corresponding hypergraphs for each of the obtained bounds. Additionally, the paper examines an extension of a well-known result due to Bollobás, who found the asymptotic value of the $r$-th hyperedge density in systems of $n$ vertices. We revisit this question in an infinite context and identify the corresponding infinite hypergraph.

Transcriptome analyses, a crucial aspect of modern healthcare and research, heavily rely on domain-specific ontologies, particularly gene ontology. These complex ontologies, comprising thousands of nodes and relationships, aid in making genomic data interpretable, but their sheer scale often hinders their comprehensiveness. When researchers investigate novel phenomena, they typically start with comprehensive ontologies, but as new findings emerge, existing understandings are challenged, necessitating revisions. In order to stay updated, researchers must be informed about changes to the ontology that have led to these revisions, especially when new pathways are discovered. However, existing visualization tools fall short in providing this insight as they mainly focus on visual representations, neglecting the underlying connections and modifications in the ontology. this problem. This paper presents OntoPlot, a new visualization framework that informs researchers of comprehensive and hierarchical associations within gene ontology by integrating an intuitive plot of hierarchical relationships with an interactive sunburst representation of associated concepts. Sunburst's transparent nature showcases which additional entities are linked compared to the starting point, and the integrated plot reveals the point of divergence, offering a shared understanding of the hierarchy. OntoPlot's sunburst view is groundbreaking as it is the first to seamlessly incorporate cyclical associations found in GO, enabling researchers to visualize three types of circular associations: algebraic, residual, and redundant. Sunbursts reveal the entity responsible for creating a circular association by showing an invisible 'entry point' in the plot and the ability to highlight entities involved in residual and

We introduce an innovative technique to leverage unlabelled speech data from a domain diverse from our trained model through a cycle-consistent, cross-domain cycleGAN-based approach. By training this cycleGAN, we can map untained audio to a domain comparable to our model's input, effectively utilising more valuable data in speech recognition tasks. In addition, our method incorporates inter-domain contrasts to facilitate speech recognition across different domains. This approach is particularly useful because it allows us to harness a broad range of unlabelled data without being limited by a specific domain. Our experiments, involving both a mainstream ASR framework and a novel recurrent neural network structure, demonstrate a notable improvement in speech recognition performance with the adoption of this cycleGAN-based domain adaptation method.

This study presents an innovative technique for directed autonomous navigation in environments challenging for robots. By harnessing the power of Bayesian learning and active prediction methods, the approach achieves flexible and versatile control of robot movements. Utilizing simulated time-series data, the algorithm promotes the creation of a diverse set of autonomous trajectories that are optimized to stimulate the target system's outputs and facilitate robust understanding of its internal dynamics. It does so by repeatedly applying a Bayesian generator network to generate and sample new states from the target system, and then guiding the robot towards these dynamically probed states to foster in-depth exploration and systematic progress. The proposed method is successfully evaluated in a complex autonomous navigation task, where a soft actor-critic robot navigates towards a goal by selectively interacting with a dynamic multi-agent simulation model representing other robots. Experimental findings demonstrate that this novel method leads to notably improved targeted understanding and system state sampling, thus offering a versatile framework for directed autonomous navigation in a wide range of robot contexts.

Our research focuses on the Soret effect in mixtures of rigid molecules with rotating symmetries, and also in mixtures of rigid molecules coupled to internal degrees of freedom, and those that include both rigid and flexible molecules. We found that in mixtures of rigid molecules with rotating symmetries, the Soret effect is negligible, regardless of the temperature gradient. This is because the movement caused by the temperature gradient does not result in a significant change of average orientation, which is the primary factor contributing to the Soret effect. On the other hand, mixtures of rigid molecules coupled to internal degrees of freedom exhibit a non-negligible Soret effect, as changes in temperature affect the movement and arrangement of these molecules. Theoretical calculations we performed revealed the Soret effect in mixtures of rigid molecules coupled to internal degrees of freedom strongly depends on size, flexibility and arrangement of the molecules. Additionally, we investigated the Soret effect in mixtures of rigid and flexible molecules and found that the movement caused by the temperature gradient has a limited impact on the average arrangement of the flexible molecules. However, we do observe a significant contribution to the Soret effect from the internal degree of freedom of the flexible molecules, which overpowers the effect caused by the temperature gradient. Theoretical calculations we made clear that the Soret effect in mixtures of rigid and flexible molecules is influenced by both the movement caused by the temperature gradient and the internal degree of freedom of the flexible molecules, as well as the size

The evaluation of written texts in extensive assessments is generally accomplished through a labor-intensive and costly process involving the examination of numerous written works by human examiners. As a solution to this issue, Automated Essay Assessment is investigated, employing state-of-the-art transformer models like BERT and RoBERTa. Yet, these models are typically trained on a broad range of tasks, which may lead them to perform inadequately when applied to specific educational objectives. Our research centers on the efficacy of utilizing fine-tuned BERT, RoBERTa, and BART models for evaluating various grade levels of English compositions and understanding the underlying reasoning, as demonstrated through evaluation on standardized tests developed by Educational Testing Service. According to our findings, fine-tuned BERT is the top-performing model in predicting grades across multiple tests. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the performance of the transformer models is mainly influenced by compositional characteristics rather than textual content. Finally, our study explores the advantages of using fine-tuned transformer models for producing scoring keys in the context of Automated Essay Assessment and demonstrates their capacity for consistent evaluation across various grade levels and examinations.

Domain adaptive pedestrian detection faces a critical challenge due to varying conditions across different domains, resulting in a high number of false positives in real-world scenarios. To tackle this issue, a new method called Box Re-Ranking is proposed, which ranks boxes of the same class to reduce false positives, even without labeled data. To facilitate positive pedestrian detection, a new technique called Anchor Matching is introduced, which creates a favorable adaptation environment by matching pedestrian box anchors. Furthermore, a new loss function called Box Remapping is designed to promote positive adaptation by linking similar positive boxes, thereby advancing the boundary of a class-agnostic box towards a class-specific boundary. Extensive testing has been conducted on benchmark datasets for domain adaptive pedestrian detection, showing significant improvements in reducing false positives and gaining domain adaptation performance gains.

This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions, background noise, and echo effects. Inspired by the remarkable face renewal capability of the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), specifically the Progressive Growing GAN, we adapt this concept to develop an image translation model that can remove unwanted digital camera distortions from log-power spectra representations of music. Furthermore, we utilize a conditional Variational AutoEncoder based on the VQ-VAE architecture to create a robust and efficient spectrum-to-waveform converter, which can transform the refined log-power spectra into a viable audio signal. Finally, we incorporate a pre-trained WaveNet model to melancipate the output of the conditional VAE, producing a native waveform that is entirely consistent with a professional studio recording.

Motivating users to perform the right arm movements can be challenging, particularly when it comes to complex actions such as throwing. To encourage users to mimic authentic throwing motions, we introduce FauxThrow, a technique that discretely inserts brief glitches into users' natural motion execution. Our research focuses on identifying the most effective time and duration for these glitches in order to minimize the noticeable difference between actual and simulated throwing motions. The results show that incorporating brief glitches can successfully mimic throwing motions, reduce subjective perceptions of artifice, and lower objective discrepancies in motion dynamics. This approach has the potential to expand the applicability of rendering realistic motion trajectories, especially in the creation of more interactive and engaging virtual training environments for sports.

To incorporate syntax in neural machine translation, this study proposes an innovative approach that seamlessly integrates syntax into the translation process by using a single model handling both tasks simultaneously, thereby enhancing efficiency and interacting syntax in a unified environment. A novel decoding method is developed based on a refined syntax-aware translation model, built on top of a generalized tree structured autoencoder, which enables it to produce more accurate translations and handle complex logical representations, especially with ambiguous words, by breaking down the translation into manageable segments and using syntax to link these parts together. In order to handle ambiguous words, this decoding method automatically splits these words into their component parts and considers the most appropriate version in the context of the rest of the translation. In order to handle multiple possible translations, this decoding method uses a predictive pointer, which actively predicts when to use the syntax-dependent translation instead of skipping it, thus making the translation process more efficient and robust to ambiguity. As a result, this decoding method yields significant improvements in performance and robustness, especially with ambiguous words, from multiple testing environments, covering a range of English-French and Chinese-English language pairs.

Accurate calculations of binding energies between molecules and dust grains, such as those involved in ice growth, are crucial but often plagued by uncertainty due to the granular nature of dust and varying attachment sites. To establish a standard for astrophysical applications, we compiled a platform with pre-computed binding energies for over 500 molecule-dust combinations, based on time-averaged calculations. To determine the time-averaged binding energy, we analyzed the distribution of binding energies for each molecule-dust combination, finding that this approach is statistically valid. As part of this platform, we also provide graphs demonstrating the time-averaged binding energy distributions for different grain sizes. This comprehensive database, comprising extensive binding energy data for over 500 reactions, is available online at www.bep.uwyo.edu.

A multiplicative stochastic process representing yearly carbon emissions is explored, where each subsequent value relies on the previous year's output, a random increase factor, and a baseline emissions level. When addressing the inherent uncertainty of carbon capture technology in energy production sectors, utilizing probabilistic lower bounding becomes a valuable approach in evaluating the carbon emissions process. By employing stochastic rounding and a sample-dependent lower bound, the carbon emissions analysis can be reformulated to determine whether a given emissions threshold is met with high probability, while taking into account the inherent uncertainty of capture technology in specific energy sectors. This method is crucial in planning regional energy strategies that account for carbon emissions restrictions and industry-specific capture technology uncertainties. Furthermore, the approach may be generalized to apply to other multiplicative stochastic processes possessing similar characteristics as the carbon emissions example.

We offer a practical method to estimate the average measure of any given qubit in a particular state $\rho$ generated by a random quantum circuit, all while keeping the depth minimal. Our approach builds on the'shallow shadows' technique introduced in 'Readout of a quantum computer' (arXiv:2106.08926), which we enhanced to calculate the trace norm of the difference between two states $\rho$ and σ, now achievable with an additional logarithmic number of calls to the expectation assessment oracle. We complement this with a novel technique, dubbed'shadow clustering,' which enables us to assess the expectation value of any given Pauli operator for a collective state $\rho$ with a polynomial improvement in tolerance, now attainable with just a logarithmic number of calls to the expectation assessment oracle. Our research includes an experimental evaluation that demonstrates the effectiveness of shadow clustering across various complex multi-qubit circuits.

The researchers who studied the initial value problem for Davey-Stewartson II equations extending beyond two dimensions found a consistent long-term behavior in the spectral scattering theory. A modified reflection coefficient was introduced and its long-term behavior was analyzed. It was discovered that the behavior depends on whether $|k|^2$ or $|k|^4$ terms are dominant. This led the researchers to develop a long-term behavior theorem for the modified reflection coefficient, which holds true for both equally and infinitely weighted FIOs. Furthermore, the dominant behavior was confirmed by specific calculations for soliton resonance, the two-dimensional cubic Schrödinger equation, and equations such as Yukawa and Helmholtz.

The reliability of sequential models like BERT can be compromised by input data alterations that involve word substitutions, removals, and rearrangements. To address this, we suggest an approach where multiple sentence structures are combined in a single model. This "Sibylvariant" framework generates distinct paths for word substitutions, thereby enhancing the robustness and reliability of the model. We implement this approach with a transformer-based structure and evaluate it using various natural language processing tasks. Our experiments indicate that the Sibylvariant approach offers improved robustness and reliability compared to existing methods. Moreover, we find that it is compatible with existing language models and can enhance their performance without adjusting hyperparameters.

Our focus is on meta-learning through the implementation of a neural network
that automatically adjusts its internal connections in response to various
training datasets. This study delves into the potential capabilities of such a
system, particularly under the assumption that a linear connection framework is
employed. In the conventional sense, metagenral systems are trained with a
predefined fixed structure of connections. In contrast, a linear system learned
by backpropagation will generally produce a unique configuration for each new
dataset, which poses significant limitations. On the other hand, certain
sequential tasks sharing a common thread can be effectively processed using a
linear system through the elimination of dependencies via backward reasoning.
Moreover, metagenral systems aim to generalize across various tasks using
shared, code-generating neural cell representations. However, existing
implementations of this concept are susceptible to modifications in the
representational framework. Instead, we introduce a more comprehensive,
automated approach for generating code, which is derived from a linear system
trained in an end-to-end manner. This study examines the potential limits of
linear metagenral systems, while also exploring a new theoretical framework for
identifying the commonalities among a group of related tasks, which in turn
enables knowledge transfer and improves overall generalization.

Developing efficient multilingual models has become a growing concern in modern research. This issue was investigated by applying knowledge distillation to create lightweight versions of a highly accurate Transformer model utilizing a much smaller vocabulary and a smaller hidden state size. The evaluation showed that leveraging a smaller vocabulary has a far more significant impact on model efficiency than reducing the hidden state size. Furthermore, quantization presented itself as a relatively straightforward technique to develop lightweight models, largely due to its minimal influence on model training data and the availability of pre-existing frameworks. The advantages of distillation over quantization were mainly observed in sentence translation accuracy. Although it resulted in smaller gaps between the student and teacher performances, distillation's results showed superior robustness to changes in vocabulary and hidden state size. The findings indicated that in low-resource MT settings, it is highly probable that the primary obstacle will stem from the need to reduce the vocabulary rather than decreasing the hidden state size. Ultimately, the research identified distillation as a more effective method for developing such lightweight models, particularly in comparison to quantization.

To accelerate medical image analysis tasks like pneumonia segmentation, researchers have proposed using augmented training datasets.  This approach involves generating more training images through popular data augmentation techniques such as rotation, reflection, and Procrustean analysis to have multiple copies of the original training set. Notably, a study by Liu \emph{et al.} in 2019 demonstrated that using rotation and reflection transformations increased the effectiveness of deep learning models for pneumonia detection in chest X-rays. Conversely, using rotation and Procrustean analysis transformations has shown improved results in the segmentation of pneumothoraxes and pneumonia. This research investigates the efficacy of these augmentation methods in the segmentation of pneumonia and compares their impact on augmentation. A time-series analysis is also performed to quantify the performance decline of the model over time. Our analysis reveals that using rotation and Procrustean analysis transformations yields better results in the segmentation of pneumonia. A preliminary experiment indicates that increasing the size of the augmented training set leads to decreased performance decline. This research is the first to study performance decline of segmentation models due to data depletion and offers recommendations for maintaining model accuracy in resource-constrained settings.

There's a growing need for videos with clear explanations in various domains like commerce, education, and transportation. Current techniques struggle to provide explicit and nuanced descriptions of video content, which is crucial for understanding complex scenes. This research introduces a novel paradigm for generating detailed and context-specific descriptions of video footage. Our approach employs a language model that is guided by specific words or phrases to produce video-centric sentences. Additionally, we develop a set of predefined prompts that encourage a video-generating model to describe different aspects, such as characters, settings, or actions, resulting in more coherent and relevant sentences.

This paper delves into the concept of harm, with a claim that more severe forms of harm are better characterized as causing obstacles to agents' goals.  We build on this idea by analytically defining a concept of harm that encompasses both physical and emotional suffering, as well as being aligned with intuitive examples.  An instance of harm, according to this definition, diminishes an agent's capabilities by restricting what they can achieve.  This conceptualization of harm has a multitude of advantageous attributes, as evidenced by our causal analysis.  The properties of harm, derived through a structural definition, include common-sense expectations, such as the transitive nature of harm and the idea that similar cases should be treated similarly.  An illustration of the difference between being transitive in cases involving harm is provided through the consideration of three characters - Phillip, Carol, and Alex.  Additionally, our framework showcases Philp's distinctive approach to resolving ethical dilemmas through the management of consequences.  The properties we derive also enable us to encode common moral maxims, including the idea that one should maximize benefits and minimize harms, as well as the principle of do no harm.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Cognitive Toolkit and Apache Spark by introducing Java bindings and new components. The integration with OpenCV and the development of automated PyTNN converter from Python is also highlighted. The research further explores the benefits and challenges in utilizing this library in developing machine learning applications, accompanied by code snippets and experimental outcomes.

Voice translation technology has seen notable progress in the last few years. 
However, its fully automated counterpart, zero-shot voice translation, is still underdeveloped due to a lack of suitable training methods and benchmarking datasets. 
The main hurdle in implementing zero-shot voice translation involves synchronizing acoustic signals and translations without any manual interference. 
Furthermore, evaluating its effectiveness poses an enormous challenge due to the sheer complexity of the data involved. 
The solution to this problem is proposed by introducing a new method that breaks down translation data into sentence, word, and character levels to combat the entropy inherent in language translations. 
Additionally, a novel approach called the SynVoice encoder is suggested for generating the voice of any given text, and a method for measuring evaluation accuracy is offered. 
The proposed techniques were tested on a large-scale English to Mandarin Chinese dataset and have proven to be highly successful in translating voices effectively. 
The results indicate that our method compares very favorably with existing approaches on both the COMET and METEOR evaluation metrics. 
The success of the proposed techniques has paved the way for the practical application of zero-shot voice translation in fields such as social media monitoring, speech-based learning, and the automatic creation of multimedia content.

This research extends the scope of modified Finsler-Ricci curvature equations and related theories, incorporating dynamic boundary conditions and resultant curvature equations within a broader framework. Our study examines the boundary problems of these equations, with dynamic boundary conditions influenced by a scalar $\eta$ that adjusts the boundary's evolution, along with related flow problems. Furthermore, we investigate the theoretical properties of the dynamic boundary problems, such as existence, uniqueness, and regularity of the solutions, with numerical examples provided in the concluding section to illustrate the dynamic behavior arising from the dynamic boundary conditions.

We investigate the techniques and data required to accurately forecast low voltage electricity load with a high degree of precision and uncertainty, particularly during peak demand hours. Our model combines a basic load model with discrete Gaussian Process ensembles, each reflecting uncertainty around load sub-half-hour forecasts. Introducing a new process, $\texttt{prophet2gp}$, we demonstrate how integrating exogenous data with popular forecasting libraries can significantly enhance forecast quality. Our approach improves upon current state-of-the-art prognosis methods, significantly reducing errors in forecast analysis. Furthermore, we develop an adaptable procedure, $\texttt{pfp}$, for pinning precise forecasts during peak hours, while maintaining uncertainty characterization. The proposed methodology significantly outperforms existing methods in both mean absolute percentage error and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, particularly when analyzing uncertainty metrics like the quantile loss and the expected absolute deviation from the forecast distribution.

Domain knowledge integration is a critical challenge when combining human expertise with machine learning. This paper develops a systematic approach to translate domain knowledge into machine learning algorithms. This framework consists of two main components: refining domain knowledge through data analysis and representation, followed by an algorithm that incorporates this knowledge into existing machine learning models. Our approach targets knowledge integration at the feature selection stage, leveraging the power of gradient boosting machines. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in various real-world applications, showing that integrating domain knowledge significantly enhances performance.

Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans requires high-quality annotations, which can be scarce. To produce better results with limited data, self-supervised learning methods can be used. One strategy, weakly supervised autoencoders, learns to compress CT images without labels for pneumonia, while an unsupervised segmentation model is applied later with classification results to identify positive scans and their detailed structures. The method outperformed three baseline models and demonstrated the effectiveness of this self-supervised approach for COVID-19 detection tasks.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, these tasks are difficult to perform accurately due to variations in posture and scanning type. In this paper, a breakthrough method is presented that uses in-flight X-ray filtering to create standardized spine orientations in 3D image stacks, enabling the application of advanced optimization techniques. By incorporating anatomical constraints, such as intervertebral angle limits, into a optimization model, accurate vertebrae localization and identification are achieved. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated across 4 different datasets, comprising 350 scans with diverse anatomical configurations and scanning parameters. By utilizing standardized spine orientations, the optimization model can accurately determine the vertebrae position, even in non-aligned 3D image stacks. Our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art approach, known as LFPF, providing more accurate results on all tested datasets. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits greater resilience to errors and variations in vertebra identification and positioning, thus ensuring robustness and accuracy in spine imaging.

Scattering electrons can trigger chemical reactions and significant light-induced transformations in molecules. An electron impacting a core-excited atom may either trigger a chemical reaction or change the atom's electronic configuration. However, how does an electron's velocity influence the probability of such reactions or modifications is still unclear. In this research, we examine how a high-speed electron interacts with atoms in an extremely short, strong laser pulse when placed within a confined space. The simulation reveals that as the electron approaches the speed of light, it starts to experience a novel form of temporary attraction due to the confinement of virtual photons within the enclosed environment, which in turn accelerates its approach towards the atom. This enables it to spend more time near the atom's core, increasing the likelihood of it being diverted or interacting with a second atom, or transitioning to a excited state. In contrast, a slower electron impacting the same atom at the same velocity would only experience repulsion, resulting in significantly reduced core impacts and a lower chance of it interacting with a second atom. This discovery of light-induced temporary attraction at high speeds has a wide range of potential applications in fields such as chemical reactions, quantum computing, and optomechanics.

In the field of robotics, utilizing spring-like actuators as locomotion mechanisms has gained interest. This study involved modifying existing quadrupedal robots equipped with traditional actuators to integrate elastic actuators, which require no additional hardware besides replacement of the actuators' elastic characteristics. The goal of this research was to demonstrate the ability to learn and adapt the control parameters of these robots without expert knowledge, as well as to showcase elastic actuators as a promising technology to enhance quadruped locomotion. We focused on a VCO-based elastic actuator, which simulates the properties of spring constants, damping, and inertia through electronic adjustments. To seamlessly integrate this model with existing control systems, a new architecture was developed, separating the robot's dynamics into two parts: standard and elastic components. The latter was optimized using reinforcement learning, based on pseudo-actions that represented variation in spring characteristics, damping, and inertia. To accelerate this learning process, Bayesian optimization was employed, providing a more efficient protocol for training the robot. Additionally, we successfully adapted existing control parameters from traditional actuators to the new elastic actuators, reducing the need for extensive reinforcement learning. We evaluated the proposed method in both simulated and real-world scenarios, successfully achieving a stable quadruped locomotion using the elastic actuator technology over an extensive period of time. The study's results show that elastic actuators can be seen as a versatile solution to enhance quadruped locomotion, offering opportunities for the creation of agile and agile-like robots that

A new approach has been developed for resolving the quantum separability problem by utilizing variational optimization methods with both classical and quantum algorithms. It was discovered that applying a specific classical algorithm to a separable state yields rapid convergence, while a quantum algorithm achieves significantly better results in comparing the entanglement of mixed states. Additionally, this method enables convergence measurements for bipartite systems on exact entanglement values and applies to both pure and mixed states in the Hilbert space.

A phenomenon known as the "ripping mode" occurs when electron isotropy is disrupted due to interactions with parallel electric fields, causing hot isotropic electrons to become aligned and heat up along the field lines. A theoretical study has analyzed the mode of this phenomenon in a particular type of plasma, identifying key factors that drive and stabilize the mode. When certain conditions are met, the mode can transform into a turbulent state due to the Kelvin-Hokkins-Loitsianski mechanism, potentially producing a large-scale chaotic effect in a star's convective core that could influence the star's late-stage evolution. A one-dimensional model has been used to demonstrate that this phenomenon could occur in a certain type of star and may be responsible for observed irregularities in the star's magnetic field behavior. A accompanying simulation has also explored the nature of this phenomenon, revealing that when certain conditions are met, the mode can cause a small-scale feature in a star's magnetic field to become arranged in a specific, whirlpool-like pattern. This phenomenon is an example of small-scale physics that could influence a star's overall behavior.

A crucial capability for internet search engines is image retrieval, and it is becoming increasingly significant in fashion due to the vast amount of fashion images available online. However, current fashion search engines are inadequate, often failing to provide relevant outcomes. To boost retrieval precision, the concept of fashion style transfer has emerged, enabling images to be searched based on a specific fashion style. In this paper, we enhance fashion style transfer by modifying only the attire aspects of images, preserving other fundamental features. To achieve this, we propose a novel, efficient method for manipulating individual features of images at a detailed level. Experimental results on a prominent fashion benchmark validate the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating significant improvements in retrieval accuracy compared to numerous baseline solutions. Notably, our proposed technique outperforms the current state-of-the-art in subjective quality assessments by a substantial margin, showcasing its ability to effectively change image attire while preserving other fundamental features such as face, body, and background of images.

The main goal of this research is to develop a mathematical solution for resolving certain types of ill-posed problems, specifically those that involve operator equations in Banach spaces and are subject to noise. By applying the principle of minimizing a Tikhonov functional, smoothed solutions can be obtained, and the study establishes a convergence criterion for this approach based on the source condition and the ill-posedness of the problem. Building on this framework, a dual gradient method is introduced to approximate the solutions of these problems, and the method is shown to be effective in a free-nonsense setting. Moreover, a convergence rate for this approach is demonstrated under the assumption of source condition with order 2.

Capturing a complete 4D light field within a single capture area poses significant challenges, largely due to the inherent problem of missing data caused by catastrophic occlusion of the sensor's limited sub-pixels. Consequently, most existing algorithms for estimating depth in light fields are severely hampered by this missing data problem, leading to their overall performance degradation. To effectively address this issue, a groundbreaking change is made here by introducing a novel, holistic approach based on the cost of missing data for estimating light field depth. By using a specially designed, iterative cost builder that calculates the cost of the missing data for each distinct scene category, it's possible to address the inherent disparity between the different types of sensor data, namely, epipolar planes and intensity images. By focusing all the distinct cost elements on the depth information, it becomes possible to obtain a refined depth map. Experimental results show that our approach yields a notable improvement in estimating light field depth with the aid of a single intensity image as a reference.

This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a comprehensive range of solutions for the reduced Fokas-Lenells equations. Several solutions are illustrated through asymptotic analysis, including periodic, kink, and bell-shaped solutions. Furthermore, through the bilinear method, consistent Fokas-Lenells hierarchy is derived, and a direct link between the Fokas-Lenells equations and the Nizhizkovsky-Lenells integrable system is established.

Effective field theories encompassing generalized metrics with vanishing Bethe-Bloch sum have been proposed recently. These theories not only incorporate non-Riemannian spacetimes but also alternative theories of gravity such as loop quantum gravity, which may help resolve quantum gravity paradoxes like the cosmological singularity and black hole information loss. Double field theory provides a framework for constructing action principles for these effective theories, and specifically, three distinct action formulas derived from double field theory have been shown to be equivalent to the polynomial invariant action formula proposed by Hoare. An alternative formula derived by Fairlie and van Holten has been shown to be equivalent to a string-inspired gravity action with a cosmological constant.

To optimize performance in IEEE 802.11n and above home WiFi networks, using extension devices can be beneficial. However, these devices may interfere with the signals used for management within the network. To resolve this issue, a proposal exists where extension devices can actively prevent their operation from being controlled by the access points when needed for maintenance purposes. 
Our method prevents this interference by leveraging the control features provided by IEEE 802.11k and v standards to enable seamless handover between the access point and extension devices. 
Results from various simulations indicate that performance in terms of data transfer rate and signal quality can be significantly improved. 

This improvement is achieved through the engagement of extension devices only when necessary, thereby reducing unwanted interference and the likelihood of data packet loss. 
This approach offers a practical solution for managing home WiFi networks that incorporate multiple access points and extension devices. 

To demonstrate this, two scenarios were simulated - one with a single access point and multiple extension devices, and another with multiple access points and extension devices. 
These extensions operate within the network using three modes - equal, two-tier, and three-tier. 
To maintain signal integrity, handover occurs between the access point and extension devices based on signal strength. 

In addition to performance analysis, another simulation assessed the time it takes for maintenance commands to be transmitted and received by the extension devices. 
This simulation revealed that during extension device operation, access points receive maintenance commands in a relatively short time. 
This is a practical consideration for
